t.hadrian s wall and vallum between birky:
Just east of Carlisle, near the village of Scotby, the Wall leaves almost no mark on the land. Here, at the western end of the Roman frontier, it was built first of turf and timber before being rebuilt in stone, and much of that stone has since been carried off to build farmhouses, churches and field walls. What survives is mostly buried, a faint line in the pasture or a slight ridge followed by a hedge. The vallum, the great earthwork that ran behind the wall, sometimes shows as a shallow trough in the fields. Yet this quiet stretch is part of the same World Heritage site as the dramatic crags further east, and walking the Hadrian's Wall Path through it gives a sense of continuity across the whole country.

Carlisle, a few kilometres away, was a Roman town called Luguvalium, and later a fortress city disputed between England and Scotland for centuries. Its red sandstone castle and cathedral are well worth a visit, and the Tullie House museum has excellent displays on the Roman frontier and on the reivers, the border raiders who terrorised the region in the late Middle Ages. Carlisle is also the home of Carr's biscuits, founded in the city in the nineteenth century, and the smell of baking sometimes drifts across the town.

The riding here is not about the Wall itself. To the south-east, the A686 climbs from the Eden valley over Hartside into the North Pennines, one of the great motorcycle roads of England, with long sweeping bends, a big climb and huge views across the Solway to the hills of Scotland. The Eden valley has quiet lanes through red sandstone villages and green pastures, and to the north, the border country has empty roads through forest and moor. Avoid the M6 if you can, unless you need to cover ground quickly.

Weather in Cumbria is famously wet, and the Pennines can be cold and windy even in summer, so pack for all conditions. The roads are generally good, but mud from farms and sheep on the moors are common hazards.

Carlisle, with nearly eighty thousand people, has fuel, workshops, shops and plenty of pubs and cafés. A pie and a pint in the city, or a sandwich by the river Eden, makes a good pause before heading east along the Wall.
t.skinburness@54.9,-3.4:
Skinburness is a scatter of houses at the tip of a shingle spit on the Solway coast of Cumbria, just north of Silloth, looking across the wide, shimmering estuary to the hills of Scotland. When the tide goes out, the Solway empties into vast expanses of sand and mud, with channels winding through them, and the light changes constantly as clouds race overhead. On clear evenings, the sunsets over the Scottish hills, with the dark bulk of Criffel opposite, are spectacular.

The Romans did not stop their frontier at the western end of Hadrian's Wall near Bowness-on-Solway. They continued a chain of forts, small fortlets and towers down the Cumbrian coast to guard against raiders crossing the firth by boat, and these coastal defences are part of the Hadrian's Wall World Heritage site. Near Skinburness and Silloth, the remains of towers and fortlets have been found, though little is visible on the ground.

Silloth was built in the nineteenth century as a port and seaside resort, with wide cobbled streets, a large green and a promenade along the shore. It still has a quiet, old-fashioned charm. The Solway coast is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, with saltmarshes, dunes and mudflats that attract huge numbers of birds, especially in winter, when tens of thousands of barnacle geese arrive from the Arctic. Rare natterjack toads breed in pools in the dunes, and their croaking can be heard on spring evenings.

The riding is gentle: flat roads along the coast and through farmland, with long straight stretches and few cars. The open landscape means wind can be strong, especially when it blows in from the sea. Inland, roads run towards Wigton and the northern fells of the Lake District, which offer more hills and curves.

A word on the map: Annan appears as the nearest larger town, but it lies across the firth in Scotland, and reaching it by road means a long detour around the estuary through Carlisle and Gretna. For fuel and supplies, look to Silloth, about three kilometres away, or Aspatria and Wigton inland. Silloth has cafés and fish and chip shops, and a walk along the promenade at sunset is the perfect way to end the day.
t.burrow walls roman fort@54.7,-3.5:
On the northern edge of Workington, near the mouth of the river Derwent, a fragment of stone wall stands alone in a field, a jagged piece of masonry rising above the grass. It is part of Burrow Walls, a Roman fort that guarded the Cumbrian coast, one of the chain of defences that extended from the western end of Hadrian's Wall down the shore to watch for raiders crossing from Scotland and Ireland. Much of the fort's stone was reused in a medieval building on the site, and what survives today is modest, but it is part of the Hadrian's Wall World Heritage site and has a lonely charm, with views over the sea and the river.

Workington is an industrial town that grew rich on coal and iron, and it was famous for making steel rails that were exported around the world. The steelworks have closed, and the town has had a hard time since, but it retains a strong identity. Every Easter, it hosts Uppies and Downies, a chaotic, ancient ball game played through the streets and river between two teams of hundreds of players, with few rules and a lot of mud.

The real attraction for riders lies inland, in the Lake District, only a short ride east. Cockermouth, a pretty market town where William Wordsworth was born, is the gateway, and from there roads lead into the fells. The Whinlatter Pass climbs through forest towards Keswick, while the Newlands and Honister passes offer steep, narrow and spectacular routes through the mountains, with gradients that test both rider and machine. Further south, the Hardknott and Wrynose passes are among the steepest roads in England, with hairpins and gradients of up to one in three. These roads are narrow and busy in summer, with cars, cyclists and walkers, so take care and be patient.

Weather in Cumbria is famously wet, and the fells can be cold and windy even in summer. Roads can be slippery with rain, mud and sheep droppings, and visibility can drop suddenly in mist.

Workington, about two kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and cafés. Try a Cumberland sausage, a long coiled sausage seasoned with pepper, served with mash and gravy, or stop at a Lake District pub for a hearty meal by the fire.
t.durham castle and cathedral@54.8,-1.6:
The river Wear loops around a rocky peninsula in a tight horseshoe, and on top of it, rising above the trees, stand Durham Cathedral and Durham Castle, one of the most impressive views in Britain. The Normans built both in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries, soon after the Conquest, as a statement of power in the turbulent north. The cathedral is a masterpiece of Romanesque architecture, with massive columns carved with zigzags and spirals, and its stone rib vaults are among the earliest of their kind in Europe, pointing the way to Gothic architecture. Together, castle and cathedral were listed by UNESCO in 1986.

The cathedral was built to house the shrine of Saint Cuthbert, a seventh-century monk and bishop of Lindisfarne, whose body was carried around the north by monks fleeing Viking raids before finally coming to rest here. The tomb of the Venerable Bede, the great early medieval historian, lies in the Galilee Chapel at the western end. The castle, once the palace of the powerful prince-bishops of Durham, who ruled the region almost like kings, is now a college of Durham University, and students live and dine in its great hall.

The city is compact and hilly, with steep, narrow streets, many of them cobbled. Access to the peninsula is restricted, with a road charge for vehicles entering the area around the cathedral, so it is best to park outside the centre and walk up. The riverside paths below the cathedral are beautiful, especially in autumn.

For riding, head west into the North Pennines, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty with wild moors and deep valleys. Weardale and Teesdale offer winding roads through open country, past old lead mines and stone villages, with views across the moors, and High Force, one of the most impressive waterfalls in England, is in Teesdale. These roads are quiet but exposed, with sheep wandering freely, and weather can be harsh, with rain, wind, fog and snow in winter.

Durham has fuel, shops and plenty of pubs and cafés. Try a stottie cake or a bowl of pease pudding, local north-eastern specialities, or simply a cup of tea in the cathedral café after a visit.
t.hadrian s wall vallum from a6071 to the@:
Do not expect a great stone wall here. Near Brampton, on the stretch running out toward the A6071, Hadrian's Wall is mostly a matter of earthworks and imagination: a line in a field, a softened ditch, the long parallel banks of the vallum to the south. In this western sector the wall was originally built of turf and timber before being rebuilt in stone, and centuries of farmers and builders carried off the dressed stones for barns and churches. What survives is listed as part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and once your eye tunes in, you start seeing the line everywhere.

The vallum is the most puzzling part. It is a broad flat-bottomed ditch with mounds on either side, running behind the wall, and it seems to have marked the military zone, a boundary between the army and the civilian world, rather than a defence against enemies to the north. Walking it on a misty morning with sheep looking on, you understand how much this frontier was about control and administration as much as war.

Brampton is a small market town of four thousand that played a part in a much later conflict: in 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie stayed here while his Jacobite army besieged Carlisle, and the city's surrender was accepted in the town. Nearby, Lanercost Priory, founded in the twelfth century and partly built with stone from the Roman wall, is a beautiful ruin by the river Irthing. Carlisle, eleven kilometres west, has a medieval castle and cathedral and was a fortress town for centuries on the edge of the Anglo-Scottish border wars.

The riding is gentle and green, with narrow lanes between hedges and dry-stone walls, rolling hills to the north toward the Bewcastle fells and the busy A69 cutting through the valley to the south. The lanes can be muddy and slippery, with farm traffic, and the weather changes fast: drizzle, sun and wind all in an hour. Brampton has fuel, a few cafés and pubs, and Carlisle has everything. A pot of tea and a bacon roll will get you going, and if you are staying, the local ales are worth it.
t.charlestown@50.3,-4.8:
Charlestown is a harbour carved out of a beach. In the 1790s, a local landowner called Charles Rashleigh built a port here, cutting a dock into the rock to ship copper ore and, above all, china clay from the pits around St Austell, and the village took his name. Little has changed since: the stone harbour walls, the lock gates, the Georgian cottages and the old warehouses survive almost intact, which is why the harbour is part of the UNESCO Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape and why film and TV crews love it. Tall ships often moor in the dock, and you may have seen it as a backdrop in more than one period drama.

The china clay is the story of this whole area. Just north of St Austell lies a strange landscape of white spoil heaps and flooded pits, nicknamed the Cornish Alps, where kaolin has been extracted since the eighteenth century for porcelain, paper and paint. One of those pits now holds the Eden Project, with its giant biomes full of plants from around the world. Along the coast, the fishing village of Mevagissey has narrow lanes, a lively harbour and fresh fish straight off the boats.

Riding in Cornwall can be wonderful and maddening in equal measure. The main roads are good but busy in summer, while the lanes are narrow, often single-track, enclosed by high hedges that hide oncoming traffic. Mud, gravel and tractors are common, and the weather is unpredictable, with sea mist rolling in without warning. Spring and autumn are the best times, with fewer tourists and milder weather; in summer, expect queues at every pretty village.

St Austell, just a kilometre away, is a market town with fuel, supermarkets and all the essentials, and Par has more services along the bay. Charlestown has a few pubs and cafés around the harbour, perfect for a break with a view. You cannot leave Cornwall without a proper pasty, the half-moon pastry filled with beef, potato, swede and onion, or a cream tea, and here the jam goes on first and the clotted cream on top, a point the Cornish defend with passion.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between the disman:
West of Carlisle, Hadrian's Wall heads out across flat farmland toward the Solway Firth, and the closer you get to the estuary, the quieter it becomes. Along this stretch, the wall itself has largely gone, robbed for stone over the centuries, but the vallum, the wide ditch with its mounds that ran behind it, can still be traced in places, and the line passes the sites of Roman forts and the civilian settlements that grew up around them. At Stanwix, now a suburb on the north bank of the Eden, stood the largest fort on the whole wall, home to a cavalry regiment of a thousand men. Further west, at Burgh by Sands, another fort lies beneath the village and its fortified church, built partly with Roman stone.

It was on the marshes near Burgh, in 1307, that Edward I, the Hammer of the Scots, died while leading yet another campaign against Scotland, and a stone monument stands alone on the marsh to mark the place. Out at Bowness-on-Solway, the wall reached its western end, and the views across the firth to the hills of Dumfriesshire are wide and wild. Just across the border lies Gretna Green, famous for runaway weddings since the eighteenth century, when Scottish law let young couples marry without parental consent.

The Solway coast is a place of big skies, salt marshes and huge flocks of geese in winter, especially barnacle geese arriving from Svalbard. The riding is easy and peaceful, with narrow lanes across flat land, lined with hedges and farms, and very little traffic. The road along the marsh can flood at very high tides, so watch for warning signs. The wind is often strong, blowing straight in from the Irish Sea, and the weather can turn wet in an instant.

Carlisle, about six kilometres away, is the regional capital, with a medieval castle, a cathedral and all services, including fuel. Smaller villages along the coast have pubs that serve lunch, and a pint by a fire after a cold, windy ride is a fine reward. Try Cumberland sausage, coiled and peppery, or a plate of Morecambe Bay shrimps if you see them on a menu.
t.low mire@54.8,-3.4:
Low Mire lies in the quiet farmland behind the Cumbrian coast, near Dearham and Maryport, where the land slopes gently down to the Solway Firth and the hills of southern Scotland rise across the water. It is an area of small fields, hedges and scattered farms, with the Lake District fells visible to the south-east on clear days.

The Roman presence here was significant. Hadrian's Wall ended at Bowness-on-Solway, but the Romans extended their defences down the Cumbrian coast with a series of milefortlets and towers, to watch for raiders crossing the firth. Maryport was the site of a large Roman fort, Alauna, and the Senhouse Roman Museum, on the cliffs above the town, holds a remarkable collection of altars found on the site. The fields around Low Mire may hide traces of that frontier zone, though there is little to see above ground.

The riding in this part of Cumbria is relaxed and scenic. The coast road from Maryport to Silloth runs along the shore with views across the firth, and inland lanes wind between farms and villages. The roads are narrow and can be muddy, with tractors and livestock, but traffic is light. The Lake District is close, and within half an hour you can be climbing into the fells on roads like the route through Cockermouth to Buttermere. Weather is changeable, with rain and wind from the west, and the light over the Solway can be spectacular in the evening.

Maryport, six kilometres away, is a small harbour town with fuel, shops and cafés, and its Georgian streets and harbour are pleasant for a walk. Aspatria and Dearham are smaller villages with basic services. The local food is hearty: Cumberland sausage, a long coiled pork sausage, and sticky toffee pudding, which claims Cumbrian origins. On a clear evening, standing near the coast and looking across to Criffel and the Scottish hills, it is easy to imagine Roman sentries watching the same view, waiting for boats that never came.
t.wolsty north tower 13a@54.8,-3.4:
Silloth is a small Victorian town on the Solway coast of Cumbria, built in the nineteenth century as a port and a seaside resort, with wide cobbled streets, a green along the seafront and views across the Solway Firth to the hills of Scotland. Just south of the town, at Wolsty, the Romans built a tower as part of the defences that extended Hadrian's Wall down the Cumbrian coast. Tower 13a was one of a chain of small towers and milefortlets, spaced along the shore to watch for raiders crossing the firth from the north.

The Cumbrian coast defences continued for about forty kilometres south from the end of the Wall at Bowness-on-Solway, and they were not a wall but a series of watchposts, with ditches and palisades in places. Most have left little trace above ground, and the site at Wolsty is a field near the coast. The Solway Firth is a wide estuary with huge tides and dangerous quicksands, and its marshes and mudflats are home to large numbers of wading birds and geese in winter. The Solway Coast is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

The riding along the Solway coast is quiet and scenic. The coast road from Silloth south to Maryport runs along the shore, with views across the firth to Criffel, the rounded hill on the Scottish side, and inland lanes wind between farms and villages. The roads are flat and generally narrow, and the wind can be strong off the sea. The Lake District fells rise to the south-east, and within half an hour you can be riding into the mountains. The light over the Solway in the evening, with the sun setting behind the Scottish hills, is spectacular.

Silloth, three kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, and its seafront green is a pleasant place for a break. Aspatria and Maryport are other nearby towns. The local food includes fish and chips, Cumberland sausage and sticky toffee pudding. Grune Point, a shingle spit north of Silloth, is good for birdwatching. On a clear evening, standing on the shore near Wolsty and looking across the firth, it is easy to imagine Roman soldiers keeping watch on these same waters.
t.the english lake district@54.5,-3.1:
Wordsworth wandered lonely as a cloud round here, and anybody who has ridden the Lake District on a wet bank holiday will understand the appeal of being lonely. The English Lake District, listed by UNESCO in 2017 as a cultural landscape, is a compact knot of mountains, lakes and valleys in Cumbria, shaped by glaciers and then by centuries of sheep farming, slate quarrying and, from the late eighteenth century, by poets, painters and tourists who came looking for the sublime. These coordinates sit in the high fells between Grasmere, Ambleside and the Langdales, right in the heart of it.

The riding is legendary, and not for the faint-hearted. The Hardknott and Wrynose passes, west of here, are among the steepest roads in England, with gradients of around one in three, hairpins that need first gear and a surface that can be broken, wet and covered in sheep droppings. Kirkstone Pass, between Ambleside and Ullswater, is the highest road pass in the Lake District, with a famous old inn at the top and a steep descent locals call The Struggle. Honister, between Borrowdale and Buttermere, passes a working slate mine. All of them are narrow, busy in summer and demand total concentration.

Ambleside, Keswick and Windermere are the main towns, with fuel, food and endless outdoor shops. Grasmere has Dove Cottage, where Wordsworth lived, and a famous gingerbread recipe sold from a tiny shop by the churchyard where the poet is buried. Pubs serve hearty food, Cumberland sausage, local lamb and real ale, and tea rooms are everywhere.

The landscape is a mosaic of rough fells, dry stone walls, green valleys and dark lakes, with the hardy Herdwick sheep, grey-fleeced and white-faced, grazing the high ground. Beatrix Potter farmed here and left much of her land to the National Trust. Weather changes in minutes, and rain is part of the experience; the western fells are among the wettest places in England.

Ride early in the morning, out of season if you can, when the passes are empty and the mist lifts off the lakes. Avoid summer weekends on the main routes, when the traffic can be gridlocked. And when you get to the top of Hardknott, stop, breathe and look back at the road you have just climbed; you have earned the view and the smug feeling that comes with it.
t.parton roman fort@54.6,-3.6:
Hadrian's Wall stopped at Bowness-on-Solway, but the Roman frontier did not. Down the Cumbrian coast, the army built a chain of forts, milefortlets and towers to watch the sea and stop raiders slipping round the end of the Wall, and Parton, just north of Whitehaven, was one of them. The fort is known from excavations and records rather than standing remains, and the coastal defences as a whole are included in the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Standing on the cliffs above the sea, you can see why the Romans worried: across the water lie the Isle of Man and, on clear days, the hills of Scotland.

Whitehaven, next door, is a fascinating town in its own right. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries it was one of the busiest ports in Britain, grown rich on coal, tobacco, rum and, uncomfortably, the slave trade. Its Georgian streets were laid out on a grid, one of the first planned towns in post-medieval England, and the harbour is still the heart of the place. In 1778 the American naval commander John Paul Jones raided the harbour, an episode the town remembers with some pride.

The riding on the Cumbrian coast is a mix of fast main road and quieter lanes. The A595 runs along the coast, busy with trucks and commuters, while minor roads head inland into the western fells of the Lake District, toward Ennerdale and Loweswater, with narrow, twisting lanes and wonderful views. Weather here comes straight off the Irish Sea, with wind and rain common, and the light can change dramatically within minutes.

Whitehaven has fuel, shops, cafés and pubs, and the harbour area is a pleasant place to eat. The Beacon Museum tells the story of the town, its mines and its maritime trade. The coast to coast cycle route begins here, so expect cyclists dipping their wheels in the harbour. Local food includes fish, Cumberland sausage and sticky toffee pudding, a dish born in Cumbria.

Visit on a clear day if you can, when the views across the sea are long and the evening light turns the water gold. Then walk the cliff path north of the harbour for half an hour, with fulmars wheeling below and the wind in your face, and finish with fish and chips on the quay.
t.ffestiniog its slate mines and quarries@:
Blaenau Ffestiniog is a town built on, among and out of slate. Great grey tips of waste rock tumble down the mountainsides around it, old quarry inclines climb the slopes, and the houses, chapels and walls are all made of the same dark stone. For a century and more this was one of the slate capitals of the world, roofing houses from London to Melbourne, and since 2021 it has been part of the UNESCO-listed Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales. It is not pretty in the conventional sense, but it is magnificent, and on a day of sun breaking through rain clouds it can look like a lunar landscape lit by spotlights.

The quarrymen worked in dangerous conditions in huge underground caverns and open pits, and the culture they built, of chapels, choirs, Welsh-language newspapers and fierce politics, is part of the story. At Llechwedd you can go underground to see the old workings, and the quarries now also host adventure attractions with zip lines and underground trampolines. The Ffestiniog Railway, a narrow-gauge line built to carry slate down to the harbour at Porthmadog, now carries visitors through the mountains and is one of the most beautiful train rides in Britain.

The riding around Blaenau is superb. The A470 climbs north over the Crimea Pass toward Betws-y-Coed, with fast curves, steep gradients and a bleak, beautiful landscape of rock and moorland. South, the road drops toward Ffestiniog and Trawsfynydd, past the lake and the old nuclear power station, and west toward the Vale of Ffestiniog and the sea. The roads of Snowdonia are popular with motorcyclists, and police patrols and speed checks are frequent. Rain is common, and wet slate dust can make surfaces slippery.

Blaenau Ffestiniog is a town of around four thousand people, with fuel, shops and a few cafés. Porthmadog and Betws-y-Coed, both within reach, have more choice. Local food includes Welsh lamb, cawl, a hearty stew, and bara brith, a spiced fruit loaf perfect with tea.

The weather here is famously wet, so pack waterproofs and patience. But when the clouds lift, the views of the Moelwyn mountains and the slate tips glistening in the sun are unforgettable, and you will understand why so many people love this tough, proud corner of Wales.
t.summer palace@39.9,116.1:
The Empress Dowager Cixi is said to have spent money meant for the Chinese navy on rebuilding the Summer Palace, and the story is captured in stone: a marble boat moored permanently at the edge of Kunming Lake, a ship that will never sail. Whether the tale is entirely fair to her is debated, but the palace itself is beyond argument, a vast imperial garden of lakes, hills, halls, pavilions, bridges and covered walkways on the north-western edge of Beijing, laid out in the eighteenth century under the Qianlong Emperor, burned by British and French troops in 1860, rebuilt and burned again in 1900, and restored once more. It was listed by UNESCO in 1998 as a masterpiece of Chinese landscape garden design.

The Long Corridor, more than seven hundred metres of covered walkway painted with thousands of scenes from history, legend and nature, runs along the lake shore, and Longevity Hill rises above it, crowned by the Tower of Buddhist Incense. The views across the lake to the Seventeen-Arch Bridge and the western hills are among the most famous in China.

These coordinates actually sit a little to the south-west of the palace, in the western hills near Mentougou, where the plain of Beijing gives way to mountains. That is good news for anyone on two wheels: the hills of Mentougou hold ancient temples such as Tanzhe and Jietai, and the Ming-era village of Cuandixia, with winding mountain roads, river valleys and fresh air that feels a world away from the city.

Riding in Beijing itself is complicated. Motorcycle access in the centre is heavily restricted, foreign riders need Chinese permits and licences, and traffic is dense and unpredictable. Outside the city, in the western hills, roads are quieter but can be steep and narrow, with trucks, buses and cyclists on weekends. Fuel, food and every service are plentiful in Mentougou and the surrounding districts.

Food is a joy: Peking duck, jiaozi dumplings, zhajiangmian noodles with bean sauce and street snacks of every kind. Come in autumn, when the skies are often clear and the hills turn red and gold, or in spring, when blossom fills the palace gardens. Summer is hot and humid, winter cold and dry. Arrive at the Summer Palace early, before the crowds, and walk the Long Corridor while the lake is still and quiet.
t.harlech castle@52.9,-4.1:
When Edward I built his castles in Wales, he was not interested in subtlety. Harlech, raised between 1283 and 1289 by the master mason James of St George, sits on a rocky crag above the dunes of Cardigan Bay, with concentric walls, massive gatehouse and round towers that still look ready for a siege. It is one of the castles of Edward I in Gwynedd listed by UNESCO, together with Caernarfon, Conwy and Beaumaris. The sea once came almost to the foot of the rock, and a staircase down the cliff allowed the garrison to be supplied by boat; the coast has since moved, and now there is a broad plain of dunes and a golf course between the castle and the water.

The castle has seen its share of drama. Owain Glyndŵr captured it in 1404 and held his parliament here, and during the Wars of the Roses it endured a long siege that, according to tradition, inspired the song Men of Harlech. The views are huge: across the bay to the Llŷn peninsula and north to the mountains of Snowdonia, which on a clear evening glow in the setting sun.

The town of Harlech is small, a few streets of stone houses clinging to the slope, and it claims one of the steepest streets in the world. The riding along this coast is a pleasure: the A496 runs between mountains and sea, with views opening and closing as you climb and descend, and the roads inland into the Rhinogydd and Snowdonia are narrow, twisting and wild. Expect sheep on the road, gusty winds from the sea and rain that comes in suddenly. Summer brings caravans and tourists; spring and autumn are quieter.

Harlech has a few cafés and shops, but for reliable fuel and a wider choice, Porthmadog, eight kilometres north across the estuary, is the better bet. Welsh food includes excellent lamb, cheese and bara brith, a spiced fruit loaf. Park near the castle, walk the walls and climb a tower for the view. Then imagine the sea at the foot of the rock, the garrison waiting for supplies, and the Welsh hills, full of people who did not want them there.
t.wolsty south tower 13b@54.8,-3.4:
Hadrian's Wall gets the fame, but the Roman frontier did not simply stop at Bowness-on-Solway. Beyond the end of the wall, a chain of milefortlets and towers continued down the Cumbrian coast, watching the Solway Firth for raiders from the north. Wolsty South, tower 13b, was one of them, a small stone watchtower near Silloth on the low, windy coast. There is little to see today, often just a mark in the ground, but the site is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listed by UNESCO, and its position tells a story: from here, Roman soldiers looked across the water to the hills of Scotland.

Silloth is a small Victorian port and seaside resort, built in the nineteenth century as a harbour for Carlisle, with wide cobbled streets, a big green along the seafront and a sense of having been left behind by the railway age. The sunsets over the Solway are famous, with the mountain of Criffel across the water turning purple. Inland, at Abbeytown, the remains of the Cistercian abbey of Holme Cultram recall the monks who once owned much of this land.

The coast here is low and wild, with dunes, salt marshes and shingle beaches, and it is a nature reserve for birds, from waders to wintering geese. The riding is easy and atmospheric: the B5300 runs along the coast from Maryport to Silloth, with views over the firth and very little traffic outside summer weekends. The wind can be ferocious, and rain blows in quickly, but on a clear day the light over the water is magical. Inland, the lanes toward Wigton and the Lake District begin to climb, with the fells rising on the horizon.

Silloth has shops and cafés; for fuel and a wider choice, Maryport, fifteen kilometres down the coast, and Wigton inland are good options. Cumbrian food is hearty: Cumberland sausage, coiled in a long spiral, sticky toffee pudding and local ales. A fish and chip supper on Silloth's seafront, watching the sun set over Scotland, is about as good as it gets. If you go looking for the tower, park carefully and walk the coast path; the sense of standing on the edge of an empire is strong here.
In the 1920s and 1930s, excavations in the limestone caves of Dragon Bone Hill at Zhoukoudian, south-west of Beijing, uncovered the remains of early humans who lived here hundreds of thousands of years ago. They became known as Peking Man, a population of Homo erectus, and in 1929 the Chinese archaeologist Pei Wenzhong found a nearly complete skull. The fossils caused a sensation, offering evidence of early humans in Asia and their use of fire. Then, in 1941, during the Japanese occupation, the original bones were packed for shipment to the United States and vanished; their fate remains one of the great mysteries of archaeology. The site is listed by UNESCO, and a museum displays casts and later finds.

The caves lie in the foothills of the Western Hills, near the town of Fangshan, where the North China Plain meets the mountains. The hills are dry and rocky, with scrub and pine plantations, and the area around has quarries and villages. Motorcycles face restrictions in central Beijing, with bans on certain roads and in the inner districts for motorcycles without local plates, and foreign riders need special permits to ride in China. Air quality can be poor, especially in winter. Summer is hot and humid, autumn is clear and pleasant.

Fangshan sorts out fuel and lunch. Food in the Beijing area includes Peking duck, of course, along with noodles, dumplings and street snacks. For centuries, Beijing depended on grain shipped from the south along the Grand Canal, the longest artificial waterway in the world, and Tongzhou was where the boats arrived. The Tonghui canal connected Tongzhou with the capital, carrying grain, timber and goods to the city's markets and granaries. The Grand Canal, built and rebuilt over more than two thousand years, was listed by UNESCO in 2014, and the Tongzhou section is its northernmost part. The pagoda, an elegant tall brick tower, is a landmark that boatmen used to know they had reached the end of their journey. The new Universal Studios Beijing is also in Tongzhou, a contrast to the history of the canal.

Before there was a Wall, there was a road. The Stanegate, a Roman route running east to west between the Tyne at Corbridge and the Eden at Carlisle, was the first frontier line in northern Britain, guarded by a string of forts decades before Hadrian ordered his great barrier built a little to the north. Near Crosby-on-Eden, a few miles east of Carlisle, the line of the old road passes through gentle farmland on the north bank of the Eden, and while there is little to see of the road itself, the landscape tells the story of how the Romans picked their way across this narrow neck of the country.

This is the Eden valley at its most pastoral: rich red soil, hedgerows, scattered farms, and the river curling in loops through water meadows. The Eden is one of the great salmon rivers of England, and anglers in waders are a common sight. Crosby-on-Eden is a small village with a church and a few houses; nearby is Carlisle's small airport, and you may see light aircraft overhead.

The riding here is rural and relaxed. The A689 runs east towards Brampton, and the minor roads through Crosby, Low Crosby and Irthington are narrow, winding lanes between hedges, with farm traffic, mud on corners and the occasional tractor coming the other way. It is pleasant country for an easy pace, with views north to the Bewcastle Fells and south to the northern Pennines, which rise as a long dark ridge on the horizon. For more challenging roads, the Pennines beckon: the climb from Brampton or Penrith over Hartside towards Alston is one of the classic motorcycle routes of northern England.

The weather in this part of Cumbria is famous for being wet, though the Eden valley is a little drier than the Lake District to the southwest. Rain can arrive with little warning, and wind sweeps across the open country.

Carlisle, just a few miles to the west, is the obvious place for fuel, food and anything else you need. It has a fine castle, a red sandstone cathedral and the Tullie House museum, which tells the story of the Wall and the frontier. Brampton, to the east, is a pleasant market town with cafés and fuel too. Take a moment by the river, listen to the water and the curlews, and imagine the legions marching by.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between the bounda:
Carlisle has been a frontier city for nearly two thousand years, and the vallum that runs across its northern edge is part of the reason. North of the River Eden, in the suburb of Stanwix, stood the largest fort on the whole of Hadrian's Wall, home to a cavalry regiment a thousand strong. The fort lies under the streets and the churchyard now, but the line of the Wall and its rear earthwork, the vallum, can be traced across the fields and gardens to the west, and walkers on the national trail follow it out of the city towards the Solway.

The vallum is one of the odder features of the frontier: a broad, flat-bottomed ditch with a mound on either side, running south of the Wall for most of its length. Archaeologists still argue about its exact purpose, but it seems to have marked a military zone, controlling who could approach the Wall from the south. In this stretch it survives as a faint hollow or a change in the field boundaries, easy to miss unless you know what you are looking for.

Carlisle itself is full of history. The castle, built of red sandstone, has been besieged more times than almost any other in England, including during the Jacobite rising of 1745, when Bonnie Prince Charlie's army took the city before retreating. The cathedral, also red sandstone, is one of the smallest in England. The Tullie House museum is excellent on the Roman period and on the Border Reivers, the raiding families who made life in this region violent for centuries.

Riding around Carlisle is a matter of city roads, roundabouts and the M6. The A7 north towards Longtown and the Scottish border, and the A595 west towards the coast, are quick routes out. Within the city, watch for cyclists, buses and speed cameras. Once you clear the suburbs, the roads into the countryside are quieter and more pleasant, with gentle bends and views of the fells.

Carlisle has every service you could want: fuel, supermarkets, cafés, pubs and restaurants. The old town around the cathedral and the market cross has plenty of places to stop for a coffee or a meal. The weather is famously changeable, so be prepared for rain. Walk along the river and over the bridge to Stanwix, and you will be following in the footsteps of Roman cavalrymen.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between west end@5:
Out on the Solway plain the land flattens, the sky gets enormous, and the sea is never far off even when you cannot see it. The stretch of the vallum near West End lies between Carlisle and the village of Burgh by Sands, on the last run of Hadrian's Wall towards its western end at Bowness-on-Solway. Here the Roman frontier ran along the edge of the marshes and the estuary, where the tide sweeps in across vast sands and salt marsh. Nothing of the Wall stands above ground in this section, but the line is clear on the map, and the country around has a strange, quiet beauty.

Burgh by Sands has a notable piece of English history. In July 1307 King Edward I, the Hammer of the Scots, died on the marsh just outside the village while leading another campaign north. A monument stands on the spot, out on the open grass, and the church in the village, built partly of stones taken from the Roman Wall, has a fortified tower that was used as a refuge during border raids.

The road west to Bowness runs along the edge of the marsh, and at high spring tides it floods; signs and depth markers warn drivers, and it is genuinely dangerous to try to cross when the water is up. Check the tide tables before riding out to the end of the Wall. Cattle and sheep graze on the marsh and wander onto the road, and the surface can be muddy or covered with seaweed after a high tide. The reward is the view across the estuary to the hills of Galloway, the wading birds in their thousands, and the light, which can be extraordinary in the evening.

The riding is flat and easy, with narrow lanes, few bends and little traffic. Wind is the main challenge, blowing in off the Solway with nothing to stop it. Rain often comes with it.

Burgh by Sands has a pub, and Bowness has a small café or two, but opening hours vary with the season. Bring something warm and waterproof, and give yourself time to stop and watch the tide; it comes in faster than you think.
t.hadrian s wall between grinsdale and the:
West of Carlisle the Eden slows and starts to meander, swinging in wide loops through flat meadows on its way to the Solway, and here at Grinsdale Hadrian's Wall ran along the high ground above the river. It is a gentle, almost secret stretch of countryside, only a few miles from the city but feeling much further. The tiny hamlet of Grinsdale has a church dedicated to St Kentigern, an early saint associated with this region, and a scatter of farms. The Wall has gone, robbed for building stone centuries ago, but the line it followed is clear in the field boundaries and the lie of the land.

The Hadrian's Wall Path, a long-distance walking trail that follows the frontier from coast to coast, passes through here, and you will often see walkers with backpacks heading west towards the end of their journey. They are usually tired and happy, and some will tell you they have walked the whole thing. The path follows the riverbank for a while, with views of the water and the meadows, and there is a pleasant stretch through woodland.

The river itself is beautiful, with herons, kingfishers and the odd otter, if you are lucky. In spring and summer the meadows are full of wildflowers, and in winter the floodplain can turn into a lake when the river overflows. The Eden is notorious for flooding; Carlisle suffered badly in 2005 and again in 2015, and the flood defences along the river are a reminder of how quickly things can change.

Riding here is about narrow lanes and quiet countryside. The roads around Grinsdale, Kirkandrews-on-Eden and Beaumont are single-track in places, with passing places, hedges and blind bends. They are pleasant for an easy pace but not for speed, and you will meet tractors, cyclists and the odd walker. The B5307 west towards Kirkbride is a little wider and faster, with long views across the Solway plain.

Carlisle is the place for fuel and supplies; Grinsdale and its neighbours have little in the way of services. There are pubs in some of the nearby villages, but opening hours vary. Weather in this part of Cumbria is changeable, with rain often sweeping in from the west. Find a spot by the river, switch off the engine, and listen to the water; it is a lovely place to pause.

Edward I built Conwy Castle in just four years, from 1283 to 1287, as part of his campaign to subdue the Welsh, and the result is one of the most impressive medieval fortresses in Europe. Designed by the master mason James of St George, it stands on a rock above the estuary of the Conwy river, with eight massive towers and high curtain walls, and the town below is still enclosed by its original walls, with twenty-one towers and three gateways. Walking along the walls gives superb views of the town, the castle, the estuary and the mountains of Snowdonia. The castles and town walls of King Edward in Gwynedd were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1986.

Conwy is a small, charming town, with narrow streets, old houses and a lively quay where fishing boats tie up. On the quay stands what is claimed to be the smallest house in Great Britain, a tiny red-painted building only a few metres wide. The estuary is crossed by a series of bridges, including Thomas Telford's elegant suspension bridge of 1826, designed to blend with the castle, and Robert Stephenson's tubular railway bridge of 1849. The town is proudly Welsh, and you will hear the Welsh language spoken in the streets.

The riding around Conwy is superb. The A55 coast road is fast and busy, but the roads inland are the real attraction. The Sychnant Pass, just west of the town, is a short, narrow climb over the hills with tight bends and great views. The Conwy valley road south toward Betws-y-Coed is a lovely ride, following the river through woods and fields, and from Betws-y-Coed the A5 and the roads into Snowdonia offer some of the best motorcycling in Britain. Weather in North Wales is notoriously changeable, with rain likely at any time, and summer weekends bring heavy traffic.

Conwy has cafés, pubs and restaurants, and Deganwy and Llandudno, nearby, have fuel and more services. Try Welsh dishes such as cawl, a lamb and vegetable stew, or Welsh rarebit, and local mussels from the estuary in season. Leave the bike outside the walls, walk the circuit of the town walls, and visit the castle. Then ride into Snowdonia and let the mountains take over.
t.the slate landscape of northwest wales@5:
Llanberis sits at the foot of Snowdon, Yr Wyddfa in Welsh, beside the lake of Llyn Padarn, and across the water a whole mountainside has been carved into giant terraces. This is the Dinorwic quarry, once one of the largest slate quarries in the world, where thousands of men worked until it closed in 1969, splitting slate for roofs across Britain and beyond. The galleries climb the mountain in steps, with inclines, ruined buildings and waste heaps everywhere, a landscape both scarred and strangely beautiful. In 2021, UNESCO inscribed the Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales, recognising the quarries, villages, railways and harbours that made this region the slate capital of the world.

The National Slate Museum, housed in the quarry's old workshops at Gilfach Ddu, tells the story of the industry, with demonstrations of slate splitting, the giant waterwheel that powered the machinery, and a row of quarrymen's houses furnished from different periods. Inside the mountain next to the quarry, a hydroelectric power station, Dinorwig, was built in the 1970s and 1980s in huge caverns, using water pumped between two lakes. Llanberis is also the starting point of the Snowdon Mountain Railway, which climbs to the summit, and the ruined tower of Dolbadarn Castle stands on a rock above the lake.

The riding here is some of the best in Britain. The Llanberis Pass, the A4086, climbs from the town through a narrow valley between towering crags, with tight bends, steep gradients and spectacular scenery, before descending toward Capel Curig and Betws-y-Coed. The road is busy in summer with tourists, walkers and climbers, and parking is tight, so ride early or late. Other routes through Snowdonia, such as the roads to Beddgelert and Nant Gwynant, are equally beautiful. Weather in the mountains is unpredictable, with rain, wind and low cloud common, so carry waterproofs.

Llanberis has cafés, pubs and shops, and fuel is available in the village or in larger towns like Caernarfon, about eleven kilometres away. Try a hearty Welsh breakfast, a slice of bara brith, a fruit loaf, or a pint in one of the climbers' pubs. Visit the slate museum, look across the lake at the quarry terraces, and then ride the pass. It is a landscape shaped by hard work and natural grandeur, and it is unforgettable.
t.moss side 1 and 2 roman temporary camps@:
Don't expect walls. The two Roman temporary camps at Moss Side are the sort of monument you mostly have to imagine: a pair of rectangles traced in the fields east of Carlisle, known from cropmarks and low earthworks rather than anything that rises above the grass. What you are looking at is a farmed slope of the lower Eden country, hedges and pasture, with Scotby and Wetheral a few kilometres off and the city of Carlisle seven kilometres to the west. The point of stopping is to stand where a Roman army once dug in for the night and to let the landscape do the explaining.

Temporary camps were exactly what the name says. A unit on the march would cut a ditch, throw the spoil up into a rampart, perhaps crown it with stakes, and pitch its leather tents inside in neat rows. Next morning they might march on and leave the earthwork to slump. Northern England is dotted with them because this was a frontier in motion for decades before and after Hadrian's Wall went up in the 120s. Carlisle was Luguvalium, a fort and then a town, and the Stanegate road ran east from here towards Corbridge long before the Wall itself was planned.

The riding around here is gentle and green rather than dramatic. The lanes between Scotby, Wetheral and the Carlisle outskirts are narrow, hedged and often muddy where tractors have crossed, with blind farm entrances and the odd cattle grid. They link up nicely with the quieter roads that run west along the Solway towards Burgh by Sands and Drumburgh, where the Wall met the estuary. Expect wind off the Irish Sea, sudden showers that clear as fast as they arrive, and long summer evenings when the light goes golden over the Scottish hills across the firth.

Wetheral is worth the short detour for its village green, the surviving gatehouse of a Benedictine priory, and the railway viaduct striding over the River Eden, whose wooded gorge makes a fine short walk if you want to get off the bike. For fuel, food and anything mechanical, Carlisle is the obvious base: it has all the services of a city, plus a red sandstone castle that withstood sieges in the border wars and Tullie House, whose Roman galleries make far more sense of fields like these than any signboard could.
t.the luxulyan valley@50.4,-4.7:
Granite boulders furred with moss, beech and oak closing overhead, and somewhere below you the sound of water running in a stone channel built by people who wanted it to work, not to look pretty. The Luxulyan Valley, tucked between Par, Lostwithiel and St Austell in mid Cornwall, is one of those places where industrial history and woodland have grown into each other so completely that it is hard to tell where one ends.

Most of what you see was the work of Joseph Treffry, a mine owner and entrepreneur who in the 1830s and 1840s set about connecting his mines and the china clay country above to his new harbour at Par. He built leats to carry water, an inclined plane to haul wagons up the steep side, and the great Treffry Viaduct, a long granite bridge that carried both a tramway and a water channel across the valley on the same arches. It is now part of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape World Heritage Site, and the railway from Par to Newquay still threads through the bottom of the valley.

On a motorcycle this is lane country, and Cornish lanes deserve respect. They are single track for long stretches, sunk between high earth hedges topped with gorse and foxgloves, with grass and gravel up the middle and tractors appearing round blind corners at exactly the wrong moment. Go slowly, use the passing places, and keep a finger on the brake. The reward is a sequence of shaded dips and climbs where the air turns cool and smells of wet stone and wild garlic in spring. Parking near Ponts Mill at the lower end lets you walk up beside the canal and the river to the viaduct.

Nature has done well out of industrial neglect. Ferns, liverworts and lichens love the humid air, and the old inclines and leats are now green tunnels. Buzzards hang over the clay country above, where the spoil heaps around St Austell earned the nickname of the Cornish Alps. The Eden Project sits in a former clay pit only a few kilometres away if you want to see what became of one of them.

Par and St Austell both have fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and Lostwithiel, the old stannary town on the River Fowey with Restormel Castle above it, is a nicer place to stop for a pasty and a pot of tea. In summer the main roads around St Austell clog with holiday traffic, so mornings and late afternoons are kinder.
t.blenheim palace@51.8,-1.4:
Blenheim is what happens when a nation decides to say thank you with stone. After John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, beat the French and Bavarians at the Battle of Blenheim in 1704, Queen Anne granted him the royal manor of Woodstock, and Parliament voted funds for a palace to go on it. Sir John Vanbrugh designed it, with Nicholas Hawksmoor at his side, and the result is so theatrical, so heavy with towers, trophies and courtyards, that it still divides opinion three centuries later. Funding rows, a famous falling out between Vanbrugh and the Duchess Sarah, and decades of building followed.

The park is arguably the finer work. Capability Brown reshaped it in the 1760s, damming the little River Glyme into a lake that drowns the lower storey of Vanbrugh's enormous Grand Bridge and turning formal avenues into rolling pasture with clumps of trees. On an autumn morning with mist on the water it looks effortless, which was exactly the illusion Brown was selling.

Blenheim's most famous resident arrived by accident: Winston Churchill was born here in 1874, during a visit by his parents. He is buried in the churchyard at Bladon, just outside the park's southern edge, under a plain stone that surprises people expecting something grander. Woodstock, at the gates, was a royal hunting ground long before the palace, and its streets of honey coloured stone, old coaching inns and antique shops make a pleasant place to park and wander.

As a starting point for a ride, Blenheim puts you on the doorstep of the Cotswolds. The A44 north-west towards Chipping Norton is fast and open, while the B-roads towards Charlbury and the Evenlode valley wind through stone villages, dry walls and beech woods. Watch for horses, cyclists in groups on weekends, and tractors dragging mud onto the bends after rain. The A34 and the Oxford ring road to the south are busy and best treated as a transit.

The palace and park charge for entry, and the house has its own cafés. Kidlington, five kilometres south-east, is the nearest sizeable place with straightforward fuel and supermarkets, and Oxford is close enough to pull you in if you have the afternoon free.
t.silloth golf course tower 12b@54.9,-3.4:
Most people think Hadrian's Wall ends at Bowness-on-Solway, where the stone curtain reached the sea. It did, but the frontier did not. From there, the Romans continued their defences down the Cumbrian coast for many miles, with a chain of milefortlets and towers watching the Solway Firth for raiders crossing from what is now Scotland. Tower 12b stood near Silloth, on ground now occupied by the town's golf course. Nothing much is visible, but the location makes sense as soon as you stand on the shore: the firth is wide and shallow, and across the water rises the hill of Criffel in Galloway.

Silloth itself is a Victorian creation, built as a port and seaside resort when the railway arrived from Carlisle in the 1850s. It has a broad, grassy seafront, the Green, wide cobbled streets laid out on a grid, and a quiet, slightly faded charm. The docks still handle some cargo, including flour for a mill in the town. The sunsets over the Solway are famous, and on summer evenings the Green fills with people watching the sun sink behind the Scottish hills.

The Solway coast is an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and its salt marshes, mudflats and dunes are rich in wildlife. In winter, tens of thousands of geese, particularly barnacle geese from Svalbard, arrive to feed on the marshes, and the sound of them overhead is unforgettable. Natterjack toads breed in the dunes, and wading birds work the tideline.

The B5300 coast road runs south from Silloth to Allonby and Maryport, flat and open along the shore, with the sea on one side and fields on the other. It is not a road for curves, but it is lovely in good weather, with the Lake District fells rising on the eastern horizon. Inland, the roads through the villages towards Wigton and Abbeytown are narrow lanes between hedges, where tractors and livestock are common. The wind off the firth can be relentless.

Silloth has shops, cafés and fish and chips; Wigton and Maryport are the nearest larger towns if you need more. Have an ice cream on the Green and watch the tide, which comes in fast across the flats.
t.dubmill point milefortlet 17@54.8,-3.4:
Dubmill Point is where the Solway coast road comes closest to the sea, and on stormy days with a high tide, waves break right over the B5300 and the road can be closed. The point is a low spit of shingle and grass between Allonby and Silloth, and here the Romans built milefortlet 17, part of the coastal defences that extended the frontier of Hadrian's Wall down the Cumbrian shore. A small garrison watched the firth for boats crossing from the north, and signals passed from post to post along the coast. Little remains today, but the site is exposed and evocative, with the sea on one side and the flat fields of the coastal plain on the other.

Allonby, a little south, is a village of whitewashed cottages strung along the shore, with a wide beach and a reputation for horses: you will often see riders galloping on the sand. It was a fashionable bathing spot in the eighteenth century, and Charles Dickens and Wilkie Collins stayed here in 1857 on a walking tour. A famous ice cream shop on the front draws people from miles around on summer days.

Further south, Maryport was a Roman fort and naval base called Alauna, and the Senhouse Roman Museum on the clifftop holds one of the finest collections of Roman altars in Britain, many dedicated to Jupiter, found buried near the fort. The town itself is a Georgian port with a harbour and a maritime museum.

The ride along the B5300 between Maryport and Silloth is easy, flat and open, with constant views across the Solway to the hills of Galloway and, inland, to the fells of the Lake District. The road surface is generally good, but sand and seaweed can be blown onto it, and crosswinds are frequent. It is a calm road for a sunny afternoon or a spectacular one in a gale, when spray flies across and the sea turns white. Check the tide times if the weather is rough.

For fuel and food, Maryport is the nearest town with full services, about ten kilometres south, and Silloth has shops and cafés to the north. A coffee in Allonby, watching the tide, is a fine pause on this exposed edge of England.
t.beaumaris castle@53.3,-4.1:
Beaumaris is often called the most perfect castle never finished. Edward I began it in 1295 on the shore of Anglesey, at the northern entrance to the Menai Strait, as the last of his great chain of fortresses built to hold down Wales after his conquest. His architect, Master James of St George, designed it as a perfectly symmetrical concentric castle: an inner ring of high walls and towers, an outer ring of lower walls, and a moat linked to the sea so that supply ships could sail up to a dock at the gate. Money ran out, the Scottish wars took priority, and the towers never reached their planned height. Even so, it is a masterpiece of military design, and with the castles of Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech it is listed by UNESCO.

The town of Beaumaris, built at the same time for English settlers, is a handsome place of Georgian and Victorian houses, with a seafront green looking across the strait to the mountains of Snowdonia. The old courthouse and the Victorian jail are open to visitors, and the jail, with its treadwheel and condemned cell, is grimly fascinating.

The ride in is a pleasure. From Bangor, you cross the Menai Strait by Thomas Telford's suspension bridge, opened in 1826, a graceful structure that was one of the first of its kind in the world. Then the A545 runs along the shore to Beaumaris, a narrow, twisting road with the water on one side and woods on the other, and views of the mountains across the strait. Beyond Beaumaris, the lane continues to Penmon Point, where there is a ruined priory, a holy well, a lighthouse and a view of Puffin Island, a toll road for the last stretch.

Anglesey's weather comes straight off the Irish Sea. Rain and wind are common, but the light after a shower is wonderful, and the mountains across the strait change colour constantly. The island's roads are mostly quiet, rolling across farmland with long views; the coast is lined with small coves and sandy beaches.

Beaumaris has cafés, pubs and shops; for fuel, Menai Bridge or Bangor are the reliable choices. Eat local seafood if you can; the Menai Strait is famous for its mussels. Then sit on the green and watch the boats in the strait.
t.stonehenge@51.2,-1.8:
Nobody quite knows why Stonehenge was built, and that is part of its power. Begun around 3000 BC as a circular ditch and bank, it was remodelled over the following thousand years, and the great sarsen stones, some weighing more than twenty tonnes, were raised around 2500 BC. The sarsens came from the Marlborough Downs, about twenty-five kilometres north; the smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in west Wales, more than two hundred kilometres away, and how they were moved remains one of the great puzzles of prehistory. The monument is aligned with the sunrise at the summer solstice and the sunset at the winter solstice, and thousands gather here at those times. With Avebury and the surrounding landscape, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The visitor centre is about two kilometres from the stones, with a museum and reconstructions of Neolithic houses; a shuttle bus or a walk across the downs takes you to the circle. You cannot normally walk among the stones themselves, but the path around them gives good views from every side. Book ahead in summer, when it gets very busy.

The surrounding Salisbury Plain is a vast chalk upland, much of it used by the army for training, with tank crossings and red flags warning of live firing. The landscape is open and rolling, with huge skies, skylarks singing over the grassland, and burial mounds scattered across the downs. Larkhill and Bulford are army garrison towns.

The A303 runs right past the stones and is notoriously congested, especially on summer weekends, as it is a main route to the West Country; there have been long-running plans and controversy over a tunnel to bury the road near the monument. The smaller roads around the plain, through the valleys of the Avon and the Wylye, are much nicer, with thatched villages and gentle curves. To the south, Salisbury has a cathedral with the tallest spire in Britain.

Amesbury, three kilometres east, has fuel, shops and pubs, and claims to be the oldest continuously inhabited settlement in Britain. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the low sun casts long shadows and the crowds are thinner.
t.temple of heaven an imperial sacrificial:
The Temple of Heaven was where the emperor of China, as Son of Heaven, performed the annual ceremonies of prayer for a good harvest. It was built in the early fifteenth century under the Yongle emperor, the same ruler who raised the Forbidden City, and its layout expresses a view of the cosmos: the altar is round, for heaven, set within a square park, for earth. The great Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, with its triple blue-tiled roof and wooden pillars, rests on a marble terrace and was built without nails.

The park around the buildings is as interesting as the architecture. Ancient cypress trees, some hundreds of years old, stand in rows, and in the early morning the grounds fill with locals practising tai chi, playing cards, singing, flying kites and dancing. The Circular Mound Altar is a set of three marble terraces where the emperor stood at the winter solstice, and the nearby Echo Wall is said to carry whispers around its curved surface. Walk along the harbour and look at the museum before going on, since the light in the evening is soft and the sea is calm.
t.temple and cemetery of confucius and the:
Confucius was born in 551 BC in the small state of Lu, in what is now Shandong province, and Qufu was his home town. When he died in 479 BC, his disciples buried him on the banks of the Si river, and a small shrine was built to his memory. Over two thousand years, that modest shrine grew into a huge temple complex, rebuilt and enlarged by emperors who wanted to link themselves to the sage whose teachings underpinned the Chinese state. The temple, the Kong family mansion and the Kong Lin, the family cemetery, were listed together by UNESCO in 1994.

The temple, laid out along a long north-south axis with a series of courtyards, gates and cypress groves, resembles an imperial palace in miniature. The Dacheng Hall, the Hall of Great Accomplishment, stands at its centre, raised on a terrace and supported by carved stone dragons, with yellow roof tiles in the imperial colour. Ancient trees, some said to be more than two thousand years old, shade the courtyards, and stone tablets recording imperial visits stand in neat rows. The Kong Family Mansion beside it housed the descendants of Confucius, who held titles for generations, and it is a maze of halls and gardens.

The Kong Lin is the quietest part. It is a forest of old trees, among which lie tens of thousands of tombs, of Confucius and his descendants, with the oldest graves more than two thousand years old. Stone statues of animals and officials line the paths, and the place has a feeling of calm and continuity. Every year, on 28 September, the birthday of Confucius is celebrated in the town with a ceremony of music, dance and offerings.

As for riding, it is worth being realistic. Foreign visitors cannot normally ride their own motorbike in China without special permits, local plates and a guide, so most people come by train or bus, or on a rented scooter where it is legal. Qufu has a high-speed rail station and is about a day trip from Mount Tai. Qufu has fuel, restaurants and hotels, and nearby Yanzhou and Zoucheng, the home town of the philosopher Mencius, add more to see. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and summer is hot and humid.
t.the imperial palace of the ming and qing:
The Forbidden City is the largest palace complex in the world, and from 1420 to 1912, it was the home of twenty-four emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties. It was built by the Yongle emperor, who moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, and who used tens of thousands of craftsmen and hundreds of thousands of labourers to finish it in about fourteen years. It covers about seventy-two hectares, with some nine hundred buildings, surrounded by a moat and a high wall. The name comes from the fact that ordinary people were forbidden to enter without permission, on pain of punishment.

The layout is a lesson in power. A long central axis runs from the Meridian Gate, through courtyards and halls, to the imperial garden at the back, with the great Hall of Supreme Harmony at the heart, where emperors held court and ceremonies. The roof tiles are yellow, the colour of the emperor, and the walls are red, and the decoration is full of dragons and phoenixes. Behind the public halls lie the private quarters, with the small, dark rooms where concubines and eunuchs lived. The last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in 1912 as a child, and lived in the palace until 1924. Since 1925, it has been a museum.

Practical points matter. Tickets must be booked in advance through the official channels, a passport is needed to enter, and the palace is usually closed on Mondays. It gets very crowded, so arriving at opening time is wise. From the top of Jingshan, the hill north of the palace, you get a good view of the golden roofs. The Western Qing Tombs, in Hebei province to the south-west, are the burial grounds of several emperors, and one of the day trips from the city on the ride list.

Riding in Beijing is difficult for visitors. Foreign riders normally cannot bring their own motorcycles or hire them freely, and many restrictions apply in the city centre, so the subway, taxis and bicycles are far more practical. Beijing has fuel and services everywhere, and the food, from roast duck to hand-pulled noodles, is part of the pleasure. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear skies and mild temperatures, and summer is hot and humid, while winter is cold and dry.
t.old beijing city section of tonghui cana:
The Grand Canal of China is the longest man-made waterway in the world, and for centuries it carried the grain, silk and taxes of the south to the capital in the north. The Tonghui section, built in 1292 by the engineer Guo Shoujing under the Yuan dynasty, brought water from springs in the hills to the north-west of Beijing and gave the canal its final link to the city, running from the capital to Tongzhou, where barges unloaded. The old Beijing section follows the line of the river through the city, passing lakes, bridges and old neighbourhoods, and it forms part of the UNESCO listing of the Grand Canal, listed in 2014.

The same water explains two of the great sights of the ride. The Summer Palace, in the north-west, is a vast imperial garden of lakes, hills and pavilions, centred on Kunming Lake and Longevity Hill. It was rebuilt in the 1880s by the Empress Dowager Cixi, and a long covered corridor, painted with thousands of scenes, runs along the shore. The Temple of Heaven, in the south of the city, is where the emperors made offerings for good harvests, and its circular Hall of Prayer, with a triple blue roof and no nails in its structure, is one of the most recognisable buildings in China. Both are parks as much as monuments, filled in the mornings with elderly people doing tai chi, playing cards and singing.

The Beijing waterways are best seen on foot or by bicycle. The lakes of Shichahai, around which old courtyard houses and lanes called hutongs cluster, are lively in the evening, with bars and cafes, and the water in winter is covered with skaters. The canal has been restored in parts, with paths along the banks.

Riding a motorbike in Beijing is, for foreign visitors, effectively impossible, since licences, plates and restrictions make it difficult, so plan on the subway and taxis. Fuel and services are everywhere in the city, and the local food is wonderful, from Peking duck to dumplings and hot pot. The best seasons are spring and autumn, and the summer is hot, wet and busy.
t.cliff of bandiagara@14.3,-3.4:
A sandstone wall some 150 kilometres long and in places 500 metres high runs across the Sahel of central Mali, and clinging to its face are houses, granaries and shrines that have been there for a thousand years. The Cliff of Bandiagara is the home of the Dogon, a people famous for their masks, their dances and their cosmology, which is among the most elaborate in Africa. The first inhabitants of the cliff were the Tellem, small people who built granaries in caves high up on the rock, and the Dogon who arrived from about the fifteenth century built their villages below, in the cracks and at the foot, linked by paths, stone steps and ladders. The area was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1989.

Dogon villages are a world of mud and stone. Square houses with flat roofs are crowded together, with granaries topped with thatched, pointed caps that look like witches' hats, and in the centre of a village stands the toguna, a low, open shelter with a thick thatched roof, where the men meet to discuss affairs. The roof is held up by pillars carved with symbols, and is deliberately low so that no one stands up in anger. Masked dances, performed at funerals and festivals, are the most famous expression of Dogon culture, with tall, swaying masks representing animals, ancestors and spirits.

I have to be honest about the present. Central Mali, including the Bandiagara area, has seen serious violence and insecurity for more than a decade, with attacks by armed groups and intercommunal conflicts, and most governments advise against all travel to the region. Tourism has largely collapsed. Anyone who is thinking of visiting should consult current official advice and local contacts, and treat any plan with great caution.

In better times, visitors came via Mopti and Sevare, where fuel and supplies were available, and then followed the tarred road to Bandiagara, about twenty kilometres from here, before leaving the road for the sandy tracks leading to villages on the plateau and at the foot of the escarpment. The dry months from November to February are the most comfortable, with warm days and cool nights, while the hot season from March to June is oppressive.
t.hadrian s wall between apple garth@54.9,:
The Solway Firth is a strange piece of sea. It is wide and shallow and has some of the biggest tidal ranges in Britain, and at low water it empties into a landscape of sand, mud and channels where the tide can return faster than a walker can run. On its northern shore, the Scottish side, the land around Eastriggs and Annan is flat salt marsh and farmland, backed by low green hills, and across the water you can see the Cumbrian fells rising bluish and far off. The Roman frontier ended on the other side, at Bowness, but the Romans watched this shore too, and the wall's western run along the English edge is the reason the area is on the heritage map.

The tides have always shaped life here. Old fishing communities used haaf nets, a method where men wade into the shallows holding huge frames, and a few still do it. The saltmarsh feeds geese, great flocks of barnacle geese that come down from Svalbard each autumn and fill the sky with noise. On a still evening the light lingers on the water and the outline of Criffel, the big granite hill to the west, turns purple.

The roads along this coast are quiet, flat and rather straight, with the occasional gentle bend between hedges and farm gateways. Tractors, cattle crossing and mud are the usual hazards, and the verges can be soft. In winter the wind comes straight up the firth, damp and sharp, and sea mist can turn a clear morning into a cold one in minutes. Spring and early autumn are the best times, when the sky is big and the marsh is full of birds.

Eastriggs is a small village, and Annan, eight kilometres away, is the nearest proper town, with fuel, supermarkets and cafes. Gretna and its famous wedding history are a short way east, and the border with England lies just beyond. Bring a windproof layer even in summer, and keep an eye on the tide tables if you plan to wander on the shore, because the tide really can catch you out.
t.stonehenge and associated monuments@51.2:
Stonehenge looks smaller than people expect and stranger than the photographs, a ring of grey stones standing alone on a swell of chalk grassland with the sky pressing down. It sits on Salisbury Plain, a high, open expanse of downland that was a holy landscape long before the stones. The monument went through phases from about 3000 BC, with the great sarsen blocks raised around 2500 BC, hauled, it seems, from the Marlborough Downs some thirty kilometres to the north. The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in west Wales, about two hundred kilometres away, which remains one of the most astonishing facts in European prehistory.

The stones are only the centre of a much bigger landscape. Burial mounds line the ridges, the Avenue runs off towards the river Avon, and nearby are Woodhenge and the vast ditch-and-bank ring at Durrington Walls, where the builders probably lived and feasted. At the summer solstice the sun rises in line with the Heel Stone, and thousands gather to watch it, while at the winter solstice the sun sets in the same axis.

The riding here is mostly about the roads that frame it. The A303 passes right by the monument and has been a famous bottleneck for holiday traffic bound for the west, with long queues on summer Fridays. Better to approach on quieter roads from Amesbury or along the Avon valley, where thatched villages and water meadows lie in the folds. The plain itself is open, windy and fast, with big views and little shelter, and military ranges cover large parts of it, so you will see red flags and warning signs.

The visitor centre lies a couple of kilometres from the stones, with a shuttle, and there is a charge to enter the managed site, so booking ahead is sensible. You can also see the stones from the public byway. Amesbury, with about ten thousand people, has petrol and cafes, and Salisbury, with its cathedral spire, is not far south. Go early or late; in the low light the stones glow, and the crowds vanish.
t.herd hill@54.9,-3.3:
Herd Hill is a modest rise in the flat country near Annan, the sort of landmark that appears on a map without much fanfare. What matters is where it lies: on the Scottish shore of the Solway, in Annandale, a broad farming valley that runs up to the Southern Uplands. Annan sits on its river, once a port with tobacco and timber trade, and has a long history as a border town where English and Scottish armies fought over a place that changed hands many times.

The country is full of small, surprising stories. At Ruthwell, a few kilometres west, the church holds the Ruthwell Cross, an Anglo-Saxon stone cross from the eighth century covered in carvings and runic verse, one of the earliest pieces of English poetry. Thomas Carlyle was born at Ecclefechan, a short drive inland, and Robert Burns spent his last years in Dumfries, along the coast. The Solway estuary beyond is wide, silty and teeming with birds, and the tide runs in across the sands with remarkable speed.

The riding is calm, a succession of small B-roads between pastures and woods, over low rises like this one, with gates and cattle grids and the occasional farm lorry. Surfaces are variable, mud on the corners near farms is common, and in wet seasons roads flood in low spots. It is a good area for a lazy day at a measured pace, stopping where the view or the sun suggests. Winds from the west can be fierce, and sea fog sometimes rolls in.

Annan is close with fuel, a supermarket, bakeries and cafes. Dumfries, a bit further, has more, and the M74 corridor is near if you want a quicker route south to Carlisle. The best months are May and June, with long evenings and flowering gorse, or September, when the sky turns a clear pale blue.
t.hadrian s wall between tarraby and beech:
Carlisle has been a border city for two thousand years, and the Romans were the first to make it one. On the eastern edge, around Tarraby, the line of Hadrian's Wall passes beneath modern housing, and for much of its length here there is nothing to see above ground except the occasional dip in a field or a bend in a lane that follows the old ditch. The great fort of Uxelodunum, now buried beneath Stanwix, was the largest on the whole wall, home to a thousand cavalrymen, which tells you how much weight the Romans put on this crossing of the river Eden.

Carlisle's later history is just as bloody. The castle, a red sandstone fortress, held Mary Queen of Scots for a time, and the city was fought over by Scots and English for centuries, and again in the Jacobite rising of 1745. The cathedral, one of the smallest in England, has a fine painted ceiling of stars, and the Tullie House museum tells the Roman and border stories well. The railway arrived in Victorian times, and the Settle to Carlisle line, one of the great scenic routes of Britain, ends in the station here.

For a rider, Carlisle is a gateway rather than a destination. From here you can go west along the Solway, east along the wall country toward Brampton and Haltwhistle, or south into the Eden valley and the Pennines.
