The city has a ring road that works well, but town traffic is heavy at peak times and the A69 east is busy with lorries heading for the Tyne. Quiet roads south-east of town climb into the north Pennines, with long views and clean curves.

With nearly eighty thousand people, Carlisle has plenty of fuel and food, and the old centre has the usual range of pubs and cafes. Allow time to walk the walls of the castle and find a local cumberland sausage. The wall path, a national trail, is within reach, and wet weather brings the fells into sharp, damp focus.
t.sea brows@54.7,-3.5:
Maryport is a small harbour town on the Cumbrian coast, built in the eighteenth century by the Senhouse family, who named it after Mary, the wife of Humphrey Senhouse. Long before that it was a Roman fort called Alauna, part of the coastal defences that continued south along the shore from the end of Hadrian's Wall. The Senhouse Roman Museum, set in a former Victorian naval battery on the cliffs, has a remarkable collection of altars found nearby, many of them dedicated by the commanders of the cohorts stationed here.

Sea Brows is the high ground on this seaward edge, and from it you can see the Solway Firth and, on a clear day, the hills of Scotland and the shape of the Isle of Man. The harbour at the foot has fishing boats and yachts, and the town has a Georgian grid of streets laid out in a plan. Thomas Henry Ismay, founder of the White Star Line, whose ships included the Titanic, was born in Maryport. The mix of Roman, Georgian and industrial history is surprisingly dense for a town of this size.

On a bike the coast road is the pleasure, with the sea on one side and the fells on the other, and a landscape that turns from sunny to stormy in an hour. The surface is generally good, with gentle bends and long straights, though the sea wind can be very strong and salt mist makes the road greasy. Traffic builds in summer around Allonby and the holiday spots. Look out for a stretch of beach where the tide runs in rapidly.

Maryport has fuel, shops and cafes, and the harbour has a few places for fish and chips by the quay. Cockermouth, a short ride inland, is a good market town with Wordsworth's birthplace. Come on a bright evening when the sun sets over the Solway and the whole sky turns orange, and carry a windproof layer because the breeze is persistent.
t.tower of london@51.5,-0.1:
The Tower of London is the oldest and most layered fortress in the capital. William the Conqueror began the White Tower in the 1070s, a massive keep of Caen stone meant to show the English who was in charge. Over nine centuries it was a palace, a mint, an armoury, a menagerie and a prison, and some of the people who went in did not come out: Anne Boleyn and Lady Jane Grey were executed here, and the two young princes of the fifteenth century vanished within its walls. Today the Crown Jewels sit in the Waterloo Block and the Yeoman Warders, known as Beefeaters, lead tours with a mix of grim history and well-polished jokes.

Ravens live on the green, and an old tradition says that if they leave, the kingdom will fall, so the keepers clip their wings and look after them well. Beyond the walls lies the Thames, with Tower Bridge looming above and the glass towers of the City on the other side, an almost comic juxtaposition of ancient and modern.

You will not ride into the Tower, and central London is not a place for pleasure riding. Motorbikes are free from the congestion charge, but the capital's low-emission zone rules may affect older machines, so check before you go. Parking is the main concern: there are motorcycle bays in the City, and some are free, but they fill early on weekdays. Cobbles and tramlines are rare, but wet manhole covers and painted road markings are slippery, and buses and cyclists weave around you.

The best time is early on a Sunday morning, when the streets are almost empty and the stone glows. There is no shortage of fuel or food in London, but petrol stations in the very centre are scarce, so fill up on the way in. Entry to the Tower is ticketed, with a charge, and queues are long in summer. Allow at least two or three hours, and wear comfortable shoes, because the inside is full of stairs.
t.swarthy hill milefortlet 21@54.7,-3.5:
Milefortlets are the small, easily overlooked members of the Roman frontier family. On Hadrian's Wall itself they stood every Roman mile, with a gate through the wall and a tiny garrison, and when the Romans extended the system along the Cumbrian coast, to guard against landings from across the Solway, they built milefortlets and watchtowers all the way down the shore. Number 21 stood at Swarthy Hill, on a low rise by the sea north of Maryport, and excavations here showed a small rectangular fortlet with timber buildings inside and a ditch around.

Little can be seen above ground today, and that is part of the point. The frontier here was a line of attention rather than a line of stone, and you have to imagine a soldier on a tower looking out over the same grey water as you. On a clear day the view over the Solway takes in the Scottish hills and the long silhouette of the Galloway coast, and in the evening the sun drops behind them in a long gold streak. Fields behind the cliff are grazed by sheep and cattle, and skylarks sing over the grass in spring.

The roads here are minor, narrow and exposed. The coastal route is gentle, without hills, and in good weather it is a relaxed ride, but wind pushes hard across the open fields, and farm traffic is common. Mud on the road near field gates is a hazard, and the roads often have soft edges. Keep the speed low and watch for walkers on the coast path, which runs near the site.

Dearham is a village of under two thousand people, with a small shop and a pub, and Maryport, five kilometres away, has the fuel, bakeries and cafes. It is worth combining this stop with the Roman fort and museum in Maryport itself, which tells the wider story. Go in late afternoon in spring or autumn, when the low sun picks out the shape of the ground and the whole coast feels very quiet.
t.nanwang complex@35.7,116.4:
China's Grand Canal has a trick at its summit. The canal runs north to south for nearly two thousand kilometres, but in Shandong the land rises to a ridge between the Yellow River and the Huai, and boats cannot cross a hill. At Nanwang, near Wenshang, Ming dynasty engineers solved the problem in the early fifteenth century. The overseer Song Li and the water expert Bai Ying built a dam across the Wen River to divert its water to the summit of the canal, where it split, sending a share north and a share south. The idea was to feed both slopes from one high point.

The complex included the diversion channel, a sluice, a dam and a temple to the Dragon King, the water god, and some of these survive. The Nanwang hub made the canal work for centuries, and it carried grain, silk and soldiers between the rich south and the capital in the north. The canal's scale is hard to grasp, but here, at the summit, you can see how the engineers shaped water to their purposes. UNESCO listed the Grand Canal in 2014.

The land around is flat farmland on the North China Plain, with wheat, corn and cotton, and small villages built of brick. Wenshang, about seven kilometres away, has about sixty thousand people, and Zhoucheng, a bit further, is a larger town. The roads are straight and busy with trucks, and a motorbike here is a rare sight. In summer, heat and humidity are heavy, and thunderstorms come in the afternoon. Winter is dry and cold, and spring can bring dust from the north.

Please note that riding rules in China are strict. Foreign visitors generally cannot ride a motorcycle without local registration and a Chinese licence, so check what you can do before you plan anything. Fuel and food are easy to find in the towns, and local dishes in Shandong include noodles, steamed buns and braised meat. Early morning, when the farmers are out and the light is soft, is the best time to look at the water. It is a place for thought.
t.beijing central axis a building ensemble:
A line runs through Beijing, and you can ride beside it for nearly eight kilometres, from the Yongding Gate in the south to the Bell and Drum Towers in the north. It is the central axis of the old city, and everything of importance in imperial Beijing was arranged along it or symmetrically on either side. The Forbidden City sits at its heart, with the great halls of the emperors, and the axis passes through Tiananmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace, the artificial hill of Jingshan Park, and the old temple precincts. UNESCO listed the axis in 2024.

The axis shows how the city was meant to be understood. Visitors approached from the south, through a sequence of gates and courtyards that increased in grandeur, and the emperor sat at the centre, facing south. The design dates back to the Yuan dynasty in the thirteenth century, and was refined under the Ming and Qing. The Temple of Heaven and the Temple of Agriculture flank the southern part, and the Drum Tower and Bell Tower mark the northern end, where officials once announced the hours.

For motorcyclists, central Beijing is a complicated place. The city has more than eleven million people, traffic is heavy and motorcycles are subject to strict local controls, so foreign riders will generally find it simplest to explore on foot, by bicycle or by metro. The streets around the Forbidden City are among the busiest in the world, and security checks are common near the major sites. Fuel and everything else is plentiful, but rules change, so check before you plan.

The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the sky is clear and the temperature is mild. Summer is hot and humid, and winter is dry and cold, with pollution at times. Climb Jingshan Park at dawn if you can, because the view south along the axis, over the golden roofs, is one of the great sights of the capital. The neighbourhoods of narrow lanes, called hutong, to the north of the axis are a good place for a quiet walk and a bowl of noodles.
t.cardurnock marsh turret 4a@54.9,-3.3:
The Solway Firth is a long, shallow estuary where the tide rushes in faster than a man can run, and at Cardurnock the land finishes in a flat, grassy peninsula that pokes into it. Hadrian's Wall once ran this way along the coast, and the line of the frontier continued along the shore with a series of milecastles and turrets watching the water. Turret 4a is one of those small signal towers, set about every third of a Roman mile, and nothing much remains of it above ground. What there is, instead, is a landscape that explains why the Romans put a tower here: wide, open and exposed, with a clear view over the sea to Scotland.

Across the water lie the hills of Dumfriesshire, and the great hump of Criffel stands against the sky. The saltmarsh and mudflats in the foreground are rich in birds. In winter thousands of barnacle geese arrive from Svalbard to feed on the grass, and the noise of them rising at dusk is one of the great sounds of the British countryside. Curlews, oystercatchers and wheeling flocks of knot are common, and the whole area is protected as part of the Solway Coast landscape.

The lanes that lead to the peninsula are narrow, flat and quiet. They run between hedges and fields, with sudden bends where a farm track meets the road, and in places the tarmac is crumbling at the edges. The wind is a constant companion, and in a westerly gale it can be strong enough to push a bike across the lane. Sheep and cattle graze on the roadside marshes, and signs warn of floods at high spring tides.

The nearest bigger town is Annan, but that lies across the water, and by road it is a long way round. On the English side, Silloth, a Victorian seaside town with a wide green and about three thousand people, is the nearest place for fuel and a bite to eat. Carlisle is the sensible alternative.

The light on the Solway at sunset is memorable. Come in autumn or winter for the geese, though take warm clothing, as the wind off the water is bitter.
t.blaenavon industrial landscape@51.8,-3.1:
Blaenavon is a town on a hill that ought to be a mountain, with a shape and a story that suit the mountain. It stands high at the head of a valley in south Wales, at the edge of the Brecon Beacons, and in the late eighteenth century it became one of the great ironmaking centres of the world. The ironworks, built in 1789 and now preserved, shows how the furnaces, the casting house and the workers' cottages fitted together, and Stack Square, where the ironworkers lived, is still a place you can walk through. The whole landscape, with its quarries, tramroads, reservoirs and spoil heaps, was listed by UNESCO in 2000.

Nearby Big Pit is the best-known part. It is a real coal mine that closed in 1980 and now runs as a national museum, with free entry, and the tour takes you roughly ninety metres underground in a cage with a helmet and a lamp. The guides are former miners, and they know how to tell a story. It is cold and damp down there, whatever the weather outside, and the experience is a good deal more affecting than a display case.

For motorcyclists, the roads around Blaenavon are some of the best in south Wales. The mountain road to Abergavenny climbs over open moorland, with huge views, sheep on the verge and quick, flowing bends. The ridge of the Blorenge, a mountain of about five hundred and sixty metres, stands over the town, and the road along its flank is a favourite. Surfaces are variable, with potholes after the winter, and cattle grids and unfenced animals demand care. Wind and cloud can come from nowhere, so a waterproof is a sensible companion.

Blaenavon has five and a half thousand people and a petrol station, with more choice at Pontypool and Abergavenny. The town has a few cafes and pubs, and the famous Welsh cakes are on sale at the bakery. In Sidney Gilchrist Thomas, whose process for making steel from phosphoric iron was first tried here, the town has a local hero who changed world industry.

Spring and autumn offer the best of the light. Summer weekends are busy with riders, and winter brings snow and ice.
t.hadrian s wall vallum between drawdykes:
There is an old joke that Hadrian's Wall is easiest to find where it has gone. In the western suburbs of Carlisle it has, for the most part, vanished under houses, roads and fields, and what remains is a faint line of ditch and bank that only becomes obvious when you stand in the right place. The vallum, the great earthwork that ran south of the Wall, is one of those traces. It was a flat-bottomed ditch with a mound on either side, a sort of military boundary zone that kept civilians, and raiders, from the soldiers' side of the frontier. It was dug on the orders of the emperor Hadrian, who came to Britain in AD 122, and it is one of the more puzzling pieces of Roman engineering.

Drawdykes Castle, a name on this ride, is a small tower house on the line of the Wall, a reminder that medieval and later builders reused the Roman stone when they could. Much of Hadrian's Wall disappeared this way, carried off to build farms, churches and bridges, and what remains is partly an accident of survival.

For a rider it is mostly a suburban stop, but the setting is a pleasant one. The River Eden runs close by, with wooded banks and water meadows, and the roads towards Stanwix and the old fort cross it in gentle curves. The surface is good, and the traffic is steady, with commuters and school runs at the usual hours. The ride out to the countryside is quick, and within minutes you are in a quieter land of hedged fields and low hills.

Carlisle, with seventy-eight thousand people, has everything: fuel at the edge of town, plenty of cafes, and the castle and cathedral in the middle. The border country around it was fought over for centuries by the English and the Scots, and the reivers, who raided across the frontier in the Middle Ages and later, left a mark on the language. The word blackmail may well come from this region.

Cumbrian weather is wet and changeable, and the best days are in late spring and early autumn.
t.hadrian s wall between houghton road and:
Where does the Wall go when it reaches a city? In Carlisle, it takes a quiet route under the pavement. The Roman fort of Luguvalium stood here, on the south bank of the River Eden, to guard a crossing, and the line of the frontier ran north of the town, through what is now the suburb of Stanwix. Along the road between Houghton Road and the river, you are following a stretch where the Wall once stood, though you would need a map and a good imagination to see it. A small plaque, a piece of ditch or a slightly raised bank is all that remains.

Building began in AD 122, in the time of the governor Aulus Platorius Nepos, and the western section, which includes this stretch, was at first made of turf rather than stone. It was later rebuilt in stone, and the whole thing ran for eighty Roman miles, from the Tyne to the Solway. It was not a barrier in the sense of a Berlin Wall, since soldiers could march through the gates, but it controlled movement and marked the edge of the empire. Today it is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The riding here is a modest thing. The road into Carlisle from the north runs through hedged farmland and low hills, then joins streets of brick houses and shops, with traffic lights and roundabouts. Surfaces are good and speeds are low. At the northern edge, you can turn onto quiet country lanes, where the light is soft and the fields are full of sheep. At the end of the day, a visit to the Tullie House museum in the centre of the city explains the Roman story, with finds from forts all along the Wall, including leather shoes and writing tablets.

The Parton Roman fort, which sits on the west coast of Cumbria, was part of a chain of coastal defences that continued the Wall's idea south along the sea. It is another site where the evidence lies under the ground.

Fuel is plentiful in Carlisle, and the cafes near the station are good. Wind and rain are the norm, so pack your waterproofs. The end of spring and September offer the best weather.
t.the vallum between the road to laversdal:
When the Romans abandoned their Wall, local builders found it a splendid quarry. Lanercost Priory, a few kilometres east of Brampton, was begun in the twelfth century by Augustinian canons, and its red sandstone includes dressed stones that were once part of the Wall and its forts, still marked with the tool lines of Roman masons. Naworth Castle, close by, was built from the same stone. In that sense, the Wall never really went away: it turned into churches, castles and farm walls across the north of England.

The vallum on this stretch lies between the road to Laversdale and the countryside around Irthington, east of Carlisle, and its ditch and banks can still be traced in the fields. It runs parallel to the line of the Wall, a short way to the south, and its purpose has been argued over for generations. The most common view is that it marked a military zone, with crossings only at the forts. Whatever its purpose, it was a huge piece of work, dug by hand in a few years.

The countryside here is gentle and green. The Eden plain gives way to the low hills of the Pennine edge, with oaks, hedges and red sandstone farmhouses. The B roads that run between Brampton, Irthington and Wetheral are narrow and winding, with sudden dips to cross streams. They are best ridden at a measured pace, since gravel and mud on the bends are common after rain and farm traffic can appear at any moment. The A69, the main road from Carlisle to Newcastle, is faster but less interesting.

Brampton has four thousand people, a market square and a couple of petrol options, while Wetheral, with a famous railway viaduct over the river, is smaller. For a big shop or a repair, Carlisle is only nine kilometres away. A market day at Brampton, on Wednesday, brings stalls into the square and a lot of local colour.

Birdoswald, a bit farther east, is a Roman fort with a fine stretch of Wall and a visitor centre, and makes a worthwhile extension. Early morning mist on the Eden is beautiful in autumn. Winter rain can turn the lanes into streams.
t.cardurnock@54.9,-3.3:
From Cardurnock the whole Solway coast opens out, and on a clear day you can see Criffel and the Scottish shore, the Lake District fells to the south and the long line of the tide marking out the sand. The peninsula is a lonely place, flat and breezy, with a few farms, a lot of birds and the remains of an old railway viaduct at Bowness a few kilometres away. That structure, a long iron bridge across the firth, linked Cumberland with Dumfriesshire from 1869 until it closed in the 1920s and was taken down in the 1930s. It carried iron ore from Cumbria to the Scottish furnaces and, according to the stories, thirsty Scots across to Bowness on the days when their pubs were closed.

The Wall lay here, too, though it has largely disappeared. The Roman line followed the coast, with milecastles and turrets, to Bowness-on-Solway. The path that now follows it is a popular walk, and the tops of the dunes give clear views of the water. In a west wind the surf and the cries of birds make an unforgettable noise.

Riding to Cardurnock requires care. The roads are narrow, straight and level, with little protection from the weather. Gusts can be fierce, and the low sun in the evening is dazzling. The tide has a habit of flooding the coastal road at the highest spring tides, so look for signs. In winter the geese on the marsh are thick, and in spring the lapwings and skylarks fill the sky.

The ride is part of a longer journey to the English Lake District, which lies to the south and east, with its lakes, fells and passes. To get there from here you ride through quiet farmland, with the rounded shape of Skiddaw growing on the horizon. Silloth, three thousand strong, has fuel and chip shops, and Annan, over the water, is only a long drive away by way of Carlisle.

Come on a bright, windy day, and bring a layer you do not need. The landscape is big and bare and does not forgive anyone dressed for the town.
t.derwent valley mills@53.0,-1.5:
The first factory in the modern sense stood at Cromford, in a narrow valley in Derbyshire, and the man who built it was a barber from Preston. Richard Arkwright's cotton mill of 1771 was the first to spin cotton with water power on a large scale, and it set a pattern that spread to the Midlands, Lancashire and across the world. The Derwent Valley Mills, the series of mills and villages that stretch from Cromford down to Derby, were listed by UNESCO in 2001 as the birthplace of the factory system.

Belper, on the river a little below, was the domain of the Strutt family, who built mills, houses, chapels and a school for their workers. North Mill, rebuilt after a fire, is one of the oldest surviving iron-framed buildings in the world, and the rows of workers' houses on the hillside still stand. Cromford has the best-preserved village, with a street of three-storey cottages built by Arkwright, with long upstairs windows for the weavers' looms, and a canal wharf nearby.

The valley is also one of the great motorcycling places in England. The A6 winds through the gorge between Matlock and Cromford, and Matlock Bath, a little spa town of Victorian villas under steep wooded cliffs, is a famous meeting place for bikers, who fill the promenade on fine Sundays. The road is fast and flowing, but the corners are tight and unforgiving in places, the surface can be slippery, and police keep a watch on speed. For a quieter ride, the lanes up onto the Peak District plateau offer open moors, stone walls and long views.

Belper, with twenty-three thousand people, has fuel, a good selection of cafes and bakeries, and a market. Matlock, a few kilometres north, is the other main town, and Heage, a village on the hill, is smaller. A Bakewell pudding is a local speciality, as is the Derbyshire oatcake, a soft pancake filled with cheese and bacon.

The weather in the Peak District is changeable, with cloud and drizzle on the tops. Autumn, when the woods along the river turn colour, is the best season for the Derwent Valley.
t.palace of westminster and westminster ab:
Few views in the world are photographed more often, and few are harder to enjoy from the saddle. The Palace of Westminster, rebuilt after the fire of 1834 by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin in a Gothic style that deliberately looked backward, stands on the north bank of the Thames, with its famous clock tower at one end. The tower is properly called the Elizabeth Tower, and Big Ben is the name of the great bell inside it. Across the road is Westminster Abbey, where English and British monarchs have been crowned since William the Conqueror in 1066, and where many of them are buried, along with poets, scientists and the Unknown Warrior.

The abbey was consecrated in 1065 under Edward the Confessor, and the surviving building is largely thirteenth-century, with a later chapel built by Henry VII. Poets' Corner holds memorials to Chaucer, Dickens and many others, and the Coronation Chair, which has been used since 1308, stands in a side chapel. Westminster Hall, part of the palace, is far older than the rest, dating from the late eleventh century, and its great timber roof is a masterpiece of medieval carpentry.

Riding in central London is a matter of preparation. The city has a congestion charge and an ultra-low emission zone, and the rules can apply to motorbikes depending on their age and engine, so check before you arrive. Traffic is heavy and slow, with buses, taxis, cyclists and tourists crossing at random, and tram lines and metal covers are slippery in the wet. Parking for motorcycles is available in designated bays around Westminster, but they fill early and you should read the signs carefully.

You will find fuel on the edges of the centre rather than in it, and cafes and sandwich bars are on every corner. For a quieter coffee, walk across Westminster Bridge and sit on the south bank, with the whole palace spread out in front of you.

Come early on a Sunday morning to see the streets almost empty and the stonework lit by low sun. Weekday afternoons are packed and slow.
t.hadrian s wall between the m6 motorway a:
The M6 motorway comes up the length of England and ends at Carlisle, only a few kilometres from the line of Hadrian's Wall, a fair joke for a road that also moves people from one side of a border to the other. The stretch of Wall between the motorway and the suburbs of Stanwix is a quiet one, where the line has to be guessed at from low earthworks and a few modern signs. Junction 43 sits just east of the city and serves the A69 towards Newcastle and the Roman Wall country, while the last junctions carry on to the north of the city and the road to Scotland.

What lies underfoot is the unusual thing. The Wall here was first built in turf, with timber gates, and replaced in stone. Beside it was the vallum, a broad ditch with banks, and a military road ran along the line, linking the forts. The system was designed to be walked, patrolled and controlled, with gates at the forts and milecastles and small turrets between. It lasted, with some interruptions, for around three hundred years.

For the rider, the M6 is a way to cover distance rather than a pleasure in itself. It runs through the Eden valley, with the Pennines on the east and the fells of the Lake District to the west, and on a clear day the views are fine. Traffic is heavy, with lorries in the nearside lane, and at weekends and holidays the holiday traffic slows things. Rain and spray are the real hazards, and the exposed section north of Penrith can be bitterly cold and windy. Leave the motorway at junction 43 and the roads become quiet again, with small lanes through red sandstone villages and an easy run into the heart of Carlisle.

The city has fuel on all the main roads, and a number of services at the motorway junctions. Scotby, a village with fifteen hundred people on the eastern edge, is a quiet place for a stop. The old market hall in the city centre is a good place for a pie and a coffee.

Spring is lovely, with lambs in the fields. Winter fog can linger on the plain.
t.hadrian s wall north of kirkland house@5:
The Wall does not end where most people think. It runs, in fact, right out to the Solway Firth, and the Roman fort of Maia stood at Bowness-on-Solway, where the frontier met the tidal water, and the coordinates here are within sight of the firth, across the water from the Scottish town of Annan. Kirkland House is a name on the map; the point is the flat, open country around it, where the line of the Wall survives as a low, faint bank in places and a footpath on the line of the old ditch. The nearest listed towns, Annan and Eastriggs, are in Scotland across the water, so for a practical stop you want to look east and south instead, to Carlisle.

The Solway Firth is one of the great tidal estuaries of Britain, with a huge range between high and low water, and its salt marshes are a feeding ground for geese and waders in winter. Barnacle geese arrive in tens of thousands from Svalbard, and on a still October evening the sound is memorable. The tide can come in fast over the sands, so keep off the flats unless you know what you are doing. Nearby Burgh by Sands is the place where Edward I, the Hammer of the Scots, died in 1307 on his way north, and a monument stands on the marsh.

The riding is a quiet, slow business. The B5307 runs along the shore through villages with long views across the water to the Galloway hills, with the road flat and the corners gentle. A strong westerly can make it a fight, and the hedgerows funnel the wind. In summer the long light lasts for hours, and the sunsets across the firth are some of the best in the north. In winter, spray and flooding sometimes close the lower roads.

Fuel and shops are scarce on this coast, so fill up in Carlisle before heading out, or check the village shops, which may not open when you need them. The Hadrian's Wall Path ends at Bowness, and there is a pub, so you can have a pint beside walkers who have just completed the whole walk. Be ready to share the lanes with them, and with the odd tractor, and keep your speed low around blind bends.
t.dinorwig slate quarry mountain landscape:
Above Llanberis, on the slopes of Elidir Fawr, the mountain has been cut into giant steps. This was Dinorwig, one of the largest slate quarries in the world, which employed thousands of men and closed in 1969, leaving galleries, inclines, barracks and rusting machinery on the hillside. In 2021 the slate landscape of north-west Wales was added to the UNESCO list, and Dinorwig is a central piece, with Penrhyn quarry at Bethesda. Their slates roofed Victorian cities across Britain and beyond, and the Welsh-speaking communities around the quarries built chapels, choirs and a tradition of fierce independence.

The story is not purely romantic. Quarrymen worked at heights on ropes, breathed slate dust, and many died young. The great Penrhyn lockout and strike of 1900 to 1903 was one of the longest industrial disputes in British history. Beneath Elidir, in the 1970s and 1980s, a vast cavern was blasted out to house the Dinorwig power station, a pumped storage plant known as Electric Mountain, which stores water in a lake high on the hill and releases it to generate power when the grid needs it. The visitor centre in Llanberis runs tours into the mountain.

The riding here is good in a stern way. The A4086 climbs from Llanberis through the Llanberis Pass, a classic glacial valley with huge boulders and cliffs on either side, and sheep on the road, with Snowdon above. The road is narrow, quick to change from sunshine to drizzle, and busy with walkers' cars in summer. Take it early or late. Llyn Padarn beside the town is a handsome lake, and the narrow-gauge Llanberis Lake Railway runs along it from the old quarry workshops. The mountain air is clean and cold, and clouds sit low on the tops.

Llanberis has fuel only sparingly, if at all, and it is a small village of under two thousand people, so check before relying on it; Caernarfon, eleven kilometres away, is the town with larger shops, with its great castle built by Edward I. The village has cafes, outdoor gear shops and pubs, all busy with climbers. For something to eat, a bowl of cawl, Welsh lamb broth, is the right dish after a wet ride. Visit in spring or early autumn, when the tourist crowds thin and the light on the slate is silver.
t.temple of heaven an imperial sacrificial:
The Temple of Heaven was where the emperors of China spoke to the sky. Built in the early fifteenth century under the Yongle emperor, the same ruler who ordered the Forbidden City, it was the stage for a ritual that the Ming and Qing emperors performed each year, at the winter solstice, to pray for good harvests and report to Heaven on the state of the empire. Heaven was imagined as round and Earth as square, and the geometry of the complex follows that idea: round buildings and altars on a square ground.

The most famous structure is the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, a circular, triple-roofed hall covered in deep blue tiles, held up by great wooden pillars and built, tradition says, without a single nail. Nearby, the Circular Mound Altar is a three-tiered marble platform where the emperor stood at the centre and the sounds of his voice seemed to rise from the stone. A short distance away, the Echo Wall, a curved enclosure, carries whispers around its circumference. UNESCO inscribed the temple in 1998.

The park is also a living part of Beijing. At dawn, locals gather under the old cypress trees to do tai chi, sing, play cards, practise calligraphy with water on the pavement and dance. It is one of the best places in the city to watch ordinary life. Come early, in the cool air, when the tour groups have not yet arrived, and plan on a couple of hours of walking.

For a rider, Beijing is more a place to visit than to ride in. Traffic is dense, and rules on motorcycles and on foreign vehicles are strict, with restrictions in the central city, so check what applies before bringing a bike. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear skies, while summer is hot and humid and winter is cold and dry. Fuel, food and lodging are everywhere in a city of this size, and the nearest areas of countryside lie in the hills to the north and west, where the Ming Tombs and the Great Wall can be reached.
t.yanggu section of huitong canal@36.1,116:
The Grand Canal is the world's longest artificial waterway, and in Shandong, near Yanggu, you can still see why it was a fiendish piece of engineering. The Huitong Canal was dug in the Yuan dynasty, at the end of the thirteenth century, to link the Yellow River region with the Wei River and carry grain north to the capital at Beijing, and it crossed ground that rises and falls, so that boats had to be lifted by locks over a high ridge. The Ming dynasty reopened and improved it in the early fifteenth century, after the canal silted up, with the engineer Song Li often credited with the repair.

What survives here is a stretch of the old channel, with earth embankments, remnants of locks and the sites of landing places where boats loaded and unloaded. The canal formed part of the UNESCO listing of the Grand Canal in 2014. It is not a showy monument: you will see a long ditch, now partly dry, among fields of wheat and maize, with village roads running alongside. The interest lies in imagining the traffic of grain barges, official boats and merchants that once passed this way, and the labourers who kept the channel clear.

Riding here means flat, straight roads across the North China Plain, where the horizon is wide and the skies are often hazy. The roads are generally paved and busy with trucks and farm vehicles, and the villages are modest. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with summer hot, humid and stormy, and winter cold and dry. Early mornings are the best time for clear light. Foreigners riding motorcycles in mainland China need to check licensing and permit rules carefully before travel.

Yanggu is a county town of about seventy-five thousand people, twenty-odd kilometres away, and has fuel stations, restaurants and simple hotels. Try the local wheat-based foods, such as steamed buns, noodles and flatbreads, which are staples of Shandong cooking. Carry water, and expect little signposting in English at the site, so a map or translation app helps.
t.mount taishan@36.3,117.1:
Mount Taishan is the greatest of China's five sacred mountains, rising from the Shandong plain to 1,545 metres, and for about three thousand years it has been a place of pilgrimage and imperial ritual. Emperors climbed it to perform the feng and shan sacrifices, ceremonies reporting their success to Heaven and Earth, and Confucius is said to have climbed it too and remarked that the world seemed small. UNESCO listed it in 1987 for both natural and cultural value, one of the first sites in China to be recognised.

The mountain is covered in carved stone: inscriptions by emperors and poets are cut into cliffs and boulders along the way, with temples, pavilions and gates marking the route. The main path starts at the Dai Temple in the town of Tai'an, where emperors prepared for the ascent, and climbs thousands of stone steps, through pine forests, to the South Gate of Heaven and the summit. Many pilgrims climb at night to watch the sunrise from the top, a great sight when the sky is clear, and the mountain also has a cable car for those who prefer to save their knees.

The nature is lovely: ancient cypresses, some said to be over two thousand years old, grow near the temples, and mist often clings to the ridges. The weather at the top is colder and windier than at the base, even in summer, so bring a warm layer. Spring and autumn offer the clearest views, though they also bring crowds, and national holidays can be extremely busy.

For riders, Tai'an is the base, with the roads in the area flat and busy. Tai'an has fuel, restaurants and hotels, as does Feicheng, further away, and local cooking includes Tai'an tofu dishes and wheat pancakes. Plan to spend most of a day on the mountain, wear good shoes and carry water. Rules for foreign motorcyclists in China are strict, so confirm licensing and permits in advance, and consider using local transport for the town and mountain.
t.enumclaw@47.2,-122.0:
Enumclaw sits on the plateau east of Seattle where the suburbs thin out into horse paddocks, hay fields and dairy farms, with Mount Rainier standing on the horizon on any clear day. The mountain, at about 4,390 metres, is an active volcano and the highest in the Cascade range, covered in more glacier ice than any other peak in the lower forty-eight states. It looks very close from here, and it is, which is a large part of why so many riders begin the day in this town.

The road from Enumclaw to the mountain is State Route 410, which follows the White River upstream into the national forest, through tall Douglas fir and cedar. After the village of Greenwater the road climbs, the corners get longer and the trees come right to the verge. Crystal Mountain ski area lies to one side, and beyond it the road rises to Chinook Pass, at roughly 1,650 metres, where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the highway. The pass is closed by snow through the winter, usually from November until late spring, so check the state transportation website before setting out. From the pass the road drops toward Yakima country, and the forest gives way to dry pine and rock.

In summer the Sunrise road, which climbs from the northeast entrance of Mount Rainier National Park to the highest point reachable by road on the mountain, is the usual objective, and a park entry fee applies. The weather on Rainier makes its own rules. A clear dawn can be shut in with cloud by midday, and it can be cold and wet at the top even in July. Traffic is heavy on weekends in summer, so aim for an early start. Deer and the occasional bear cross the roads, especially at dusk.

For practical reasons, Enumclaw is the last sizeable place for fuel, groceries and repairs before the mountains, and nearby Buckley has more. The town also has bakeries and diners that suit riders heading out early. Once you pass Greenwater, services are scarce, so top up the tank and carry water, snacks and a warm layer.
t.aberystwyth@52.4,-4.1:
Aberystwyth is Welsh to the core and slightly eccentric with it. The town sits where the rivers Rheidol and Ystwyth meet Cardigan Bay, with a sweeping Victorian seafront, a pier, a ruined thirteenth century castle left by Edward I, and a university that was founded in 1872 as the first in Wales. The university's old building on the seafront, a Gothic fantasy that began life as a hotel, tells you something about the ambitions of the founders, who raised the money from small donations from ordinary Welsh people. The National Library of Wales stands on a hill above the town and holds some of the country's greatest manuscripts.

The town has the energy of students and the pace of a fishing resort. In winter, thousands of starlings swirl and roost under the pier at dusk, a spectacle that draws crowds. Beyond the harbour, Constitution Hill rises at the northern end of the promenade, and an old cliff railway, one of the oldest of its kind, carries visitors up to a camera obscura and a view over the bay. The Vale of Rheidol Railway, a narrow-gauge steam line, still runs up the valley to Devil's Bridge, where three bridges are stacked on top of one another over a waterfall.

The riding from Aberystwyth heads into the Cambrian Mountains, sometimes called the green desert of Wales for its emptiness. Roads such as the A44 and the minor routes over to Rhayader and the Elan Valley offer long, open climbs across moorland, with sheep, red kites and very little else. Surfaces vary, some of it excellent, some of it patched and potholed, and weather can be harsh, with wind and rain sweeping in from the sea. The red kite, once almost extinct in Britain, has been brought back from a tiny population in mid Wales, and you will see it often.

Fuel, food and repairs are all available in town, and the chip shops along the front are generous. Summer weekends bring caravans and holiday traffic on the main routes, so a weekday is kinder. Expect a mix of Welsh and English on signs and in conversation. After the day's ride, a walk along the promenade is a good way to finish, particularly when the sunset turns the bay a rich orange.
t.keswick@54.6,-3.1:
Keswick is a slate-grey market town at the northern end of Derwentwater, and everything about it is shaped by the fells. Skiddaw rises to the north in a vast smooth dome, Blencathra's ridges lie to the east, and the lake spreads out to the south toward the jaws of Borrowdale, with small wooded islands scattered across it. About four thousand people live here, but the numbers multiply in summer, and the main street is full of walkers in damp coats peering into the windows of outdoor shops.

The town has two curious claims to fame. Graphite was found in the hills of Borrowdale in the sixteenth century, and the pencil industry that grew from it gave Keswick the Pencil Museum, which proudly displays a very long pencil. Just east of town is Castlerigg Stone Circle, a ring of about forty stones laid out roughly five thousand years ago on a plateau ringed by mountains, and one of the most atmospheric sites in Britain. Visit early or late, when mist hangs between the stones and there are few people.

For riders, the roads around Keswick are glorious and a little frustrating. The route over Honister Pass, from Borrowdale to Buttermere, climbs steeply between slate crags with gradients that flirt with twenty-five percent, and the surface is narrow and sometimes broken. Whinlatter Pass is gentler, rising through forest toward Cockermouth. Hedged and walled lanes mean blind corners and sheep, and in summer tourists in cars block the way, so be patient. Rain is frequent, and the Lake District has among the highest rainfall in England, so take waterproofs and expect the road to be wet. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the bracken turns rusty and the crowds thin.

Fuel is available in town, with the nearest larger centre at Cockermouth, about sixteen kilometres west. Keswick has a wide choice of cafés, pubs and tea rooms serving Cumberland sausage, sticky toffee pudding and local ale. Parking is tight in summer, so arrive early or use the larger car parks on the edge of town. Look up at Skiddaw when you leave, and decide whether you have the energy for the walk.
t.exeter@50.7,-3.5:
Exeter's cathedral has the longest unbroken medieval vault in the world, a stone ceiling that runs for about ninety-six metres without interruption, and it looks like a stand of enormous palm trees sprouting from the pillars. The building is mostly fourteenth century, and its west front is crowded with weathered statues of kings and saints. It stands in a grassy close just a few streets from the centre of the city, which for a settlement of this age is quite normal. The Romans founded the town as Isca Dumnoniorum around AD 50, and parts of their wall still stand beside the cathedral and under the pavements.

The city has had a hard time. During the Second World War, in the Baedeker raids of 1942, German bombers destroyed much of the old centre, and the shopping streets around the cathedral were rebuilt in the plain style of the postwar years. Enough survived to make it interesting, though. The Quay on the river Exe has cafés in old warehouses, and beneath the High Street a network of medieval vaulted passages that once carried water to the city can be explored on guided tours. A strong student population from the University of Exeter keeps the town lively.

Exeter is the gateway to Devon, and for riders that means moors and coast. To the west, the A30 and B roads climb toward Dartmoor, with its granite tors and ponies, and the high roads across the moor offer open views and tight bends. To the east lie the lanes of the Axe valley and the Jurassic Coast, where cliffs expose layers of rock from the Triassic to the Cretaceous. Devon lanes are famously narrow, sunk between high hedges, with blind corners, tractors, and mud and gravel at field entrances, so keep speed modest. Rain and sea fog come easily.

Everything a rider needs is in the city. Fuel stations and bike shops are on the ring road, and there are plenty of places to eat, from pubs to cafés that serve cream teas. Devon pours cream first, then jam, which Cornwall disputes. The city is a big one, with traffic, so avoid the rush hour on the main routes. Late spring is perhaps the best time, when hedges are in flower.
t.squamish@49.7,-123.2:
Squamish sits at the head of Howe Sound, where the fjord ends against a wall of granite, and the first thing it shows you is the Stawamus Chief, a monolith of rock rising some seven hundred metres straight out of the forest. It is one of the largest free-standing granite faces in the world, and on any good day the white specks on its walls are climbers, which has turned this small town into a minor capital of the sport. Beside it Shannon Falls drops in a long white thread, easily seen from the highway.

For riders, Squamish is the honest start or finish of the Sea to Sky Highway, the road between Vancouver and Whistler. The southern section from West Vancouver hugs the fjord, a series of fast, flowing bends cut into the cliff above the water, with views across to Anvil Island and the Britannia Beach mining museum on the way. The road was thoroughly rebuilt before the 2010 Winter Olympics, so the surface is generally excellent and passing lanes are frequent, but weekends in summer bring heavy traffic and speed enforcement, and you should assume the limits are watched. North of Squamish the road lifts toward Whistler through forested valleys beneath the glaciers of Garibaldi Provincial Park.

The town has a population of around seventeen thousand, which means everything you need: fuel on the highway, coffee shops, breweries, gear shops and a gondola that carries you up into the high country. The wind is the other defining thing. In summer a reliable afternoon breeze blows up the sound, and kiteboarders and windsurfers line up on the Spit to use it. Riders get a bit of it too, as a sideways push on exposed sections.

Squamish takes its name from the Skwxwú7mesh people, whose territory it is. In winter there is something else worth seeing: thousands of bald eagles come to feed on spawning salmon in the Brackendale area, a few kilometres north, from about December to February. It is a different season for riding, with ice at altitude, but anyone who happens to be here then should pull over and see them.
t.dawenliu@37.7,119.2:
Where the Yellow River meets the sea, the land is made of mud. The river carries an immense burden of silt, scoured from the loess plateau thousands of kilometres upstream, and at its mouth on the Bohai Gulf it drops it, building new land year by year. The Dawenliu area, in the Yellow River Delta, lies in the southern part of the national nature reserve and is one of the best places to see how fresh the ground is: reed beds, tamarisk, salt marsh and shallow channels, all flat and glittering under a huge sky.

The delta is a stopover on the East Asian flyway, one of the world's great bird migration routes, and in spring and autumn hundreds of thousands of birds pass through, including cranes, storks, gulls and a long list of waders. Some of the rarest, such as the oriental stork and the red-crowned crane, are protected here, and Saunders's gull breeds on the salt flats. In autumn, a low plant called seepweed turns the shore bright red, a carpet of colour along the water, and photographers go there for the evening light. The delta has been recognised for its role as a stepping stone for migratory birds, and the coastal wetlands of this part of China are part of a UNESCO listing.

The town of Dongying, the nearest large city, owes its modern growth to oil, found in the 1960s in the Shengli field, and the nodding pump jacks in the fields are as much a part of the landscape as the reeds. Riding here is simple, on straight, flat roads that cross the marshes on raised embankments, with little traffic and long views. There are few bends and little shade, and the wind can be strong. In summer mosquitoes are fierce, and in winter the temperature drops well below freezing with a bitter wind off the sea.

The pin lists no town in the data, so plan on fuel and food from Dongying. Local seafood, including crab and prawns, is cheap and fresh, and the region is known for its salt-cured fish. Bring binoculars, water and sun protection, because there is no shade. Foreign riders in China face strict rules about licences and permits, so arrange everything beforehand. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for birds, and the reserve rules and access points are set by the authorities, so check before you go.
t.north part of the yellow river estuary@3:
The Yellow River has never stayed in one place. In 1855 it burst its banks in Henan and abandoned the course it had followed for centuries to reach the sea south of the Shandong peninsula, and instead found a new route north-east into the Bohai Gulf. The mouth of that new course is here, in the northern part of the Yellow River Delta, and it is a place of geological theatre: a young landscape of mudflats and reed beds, growing seaward by some metres a year in good times, a map being redrawn as you watch.

The silt makes the colour. The river gets its name from the fine yellow loess it carries, and where it enters the sea, a plume of ochre spreads across the green-blue water, so that you can see the line between river and sea from the shore. The northern reserve is wilder and emptier than the southern, with tamarisk thickets, tidal creeks, wide marsh and a boardwalk or two. Several million migratory birds pass through the Yellow Sea coast each year, and the delta is one of their main refuelling stations, so in the right season the sky is full.

A visit is about atmosphere. The land is utterly flat and the horizon is far away, with an enormous sky that changes with the weather, and the sound is of reeds, wind and birds. Roads on the embankments are narrow and straight, sometimes unsurfaced, and after rain they turn to mud. A bike with road tyres will struggle on the worst sections, so ask locally before you commit to a track. Mosquitoes are a plague in warm weather, and the winter is cold and windy. Late April to May and September to October are the best times for birds and weather.

The nearest large city is Dongying, a place of oil wells and wide new boulevards, and it has fuel, hotels and restaurants. Local seafood is very good, with crab, shrimp and fish fresh from the Bohai. Foreign riders in China need local permits and often a guide, so check the rules well ahead, and bring a good map, because signage in English is scarce. Water, sun cream and binoculars are the essentials.
t.western qing tombs@39.3,115.2:
Ninety minutes from Beijing, where the North China Plain runs into the Taihang mountains, a line of tombs lies in a landscape of old pines. These are the Western Qing Tombs, in Yi County of Hebei province, the burial ground of four Qing emperors, including Yongzheng, Jiaqing, Daoguang and Guangxu, along with a crowd of empresses, concubines and princes. The Qing had a second great cemetery, the Eastern Tombs, on the other side of Beijing, and the two were laid out according to feng shui principles with hills behind and open ground in front.

You approach along a long sacred way, an avenue lined with stone guardians, and the dark pines, which were planted in their thousands, give the whole place a hush. Each tomb has a gate, a hall for sacrifices, a stone pavilion with an inscription and a burial mound at the back, and the main buildings have yellow glazed roof tiles, reserved for the emperor. The last emperor to be buried here, Guangxu, died in 1908 under mysterious circumstances, and modern analysis of his remains found a huge quantity of arsenic, which suggests poison. The very last emperor of China, Puyi, did not rest in the imperial cemetery, though his ashes were eventually placed in a private cemetery nearby in the 1990s.

The riding in this area is pleasant, if you can arrange the paperwork. The roads climb gently from the plain into folded hills, with orchards, persimmon trees and small villages, and they offer some of the quieter riding within reach of the capital. Traffic is fairly light away from the main road, though lorries can be a nuisance, and the weather is clear and dry for much of the year. Spring brings blossom, and in autumn the persimmons hang like lanterns on bare branches.

The pin has no town in the data, so plan on supplies from Yi County, which has fuel, restaurants and hotels, or from Beijing itself. Foreign riders in China need permits and often a guide, so check the regulations before you plan a trip. Local food includes noodles, dumplings and roast duck, and simple restaurants near the entrance serve hearty plates. Summer can be hot and thundery, winter is cold and dry with clear skies, and spring and autumn are best. A morning visit, when the mist is in the trees, is the finest.
t.north cascades highway@48.3,-122.5:
Stanwood is a quiet farm town at the head of Port Susan, on the flat delta lands north of Everett in Washington state, with the low shoulder of Camano Island across a slough to the west. The North Cascades Highway is the reason you are on a motorcycle in this part of the world, but it is more than a hundred miles east of here, so this stop is the early breakfast before the long run up the Skagit valley, or the heavy meal on the way home.

The delta is bird country. In winter, snow geese gather by the tens of thousands on the Skagit and Stanwood flats after flying down from Wrangel Island in the Russian Arctic, and trumpeter swans feed in the fields, so a grey winter day out here can be noisier and more spectacular than you would think. In April the tulip fields of the Skagit Valley burst into stripes of red, yellow and pink, which brings a lot of traffic on the back roads. Stanwood was settled by Scandinavians, mostly Norwegians, who farmed and logged here in the late nineteenth century, and a few of their barns and the town's Nordic style still show.

The riding between here and the mountains is the introduction. Highway 20 runs flat and straight across the farms, then follows the Skagit River upstream through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete and Marblemount, and begins to climb in earnest after Newhalem, with the green glacial lakes of Diablo and Ross beside the road. Beyond them it climbs to Rainy and Washington Passes, with the sharp spires of the Liberty Bell group above the hairpins. Washington Pass stands at roughly 5,500 feet and the road is closed in winter by snow and avalanche danger, usually from late autumn until spring, so check the state transportation department before you go.

Fuel is easy here in Stanwood and the larger spots on Camano Island, but the mountain stretch has few stations, with services at Marblemount the last reliable ones before the pass, so fill the tank there. Early mornings are cool and often wet on this side of the Cascades, and the sun is worth waiting for.
t.olympic peninsula hood canal photo pull:
Home is the unlikely name of a small community on the Key Peninsula, on the western side of Puget Sound south-west of Tacoma, and the story behind it is one of the more quirky bits of Washington history. It began in 1896 as a utopian settlement, the Home Colony, founded by anarchists and free-thinkers who wanted to live without a government, and over the following years it became known for its radical newspaper, its free-love reputation, and a long quarrel with the authorities. It never became much of a town, and the colony dissolved in the early twentieth century, but a few buildings and a name remain.

The Key Peninsula is a hand of land with deep inlets, forested slopes and muddy tidal flats. Key Center, the slightly larger place nearby with a few thousand people, has a grocery, a petrol station and a small selection of places to eat, and that is the sensible stop. For a bigger choice, head to Gig Harbor across the Narrows, or to Tacoma itself, where the original Narrows Bridge, nicknamed Galloping Gertie, famously twisted itself to pieces in a wind in 1940, a story you can read about at several viewpoints.

The reason it appears on the list is Hood Canal, the fjord to the north-west, and the Olympic Peninsula beyond it, where a long ride on 101 circles the Olympic Mountains. This point is the way in, from the south, with roads through second-growth forest and past water inlets, with sunlight flickering through firs. The surface can be rough and patched in the wet months, and the bends are smooth rather than technical. Deer wander across without warning, especially at dawn and dusk.

On a clear day Mount Rainier shows its great white dome to the south-east above the water, an unforgettable sight that tends to appear unexpectedly at a gap in the trees, and there are a few pull-offs near the shores. The weather is often damp and grey, but summer is dry and bright, with long evenings, and cool enough for a jacket even in August.
t.vancouver@49.3,-123.1:
Vancouver is a city that sits between mountains and sea, so closely that you can ski in the morning and sail in the afternoon, as the local line goes. Glass towers crowd a peninsula with the North Shore peaks rising directly behind, and Stanley Park, a huge, forested park on the tip of the peninsula, wraps around the downtown with a seawall path and old-growth cedar. Gastown, the historic quarter, takes its name from a talkative saloon keeper, Gassy Jack Deighton, whose statue stands in the square.

The Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 99, leaves from the Lions Gate Bridge, a graceful suspension span opened in 1938, and rises along the edge of Howe Sound, a deep fjord with mountains tumbling straight into the water. The road is one of the best in Canada, with smooth tarmac, curves that follow the cliff edge and views across to the islands. It was widened and improved for the 2010 Winter Olympics, and it is now safer, though traffic is heavy on summer weekends. Squamish, about an hour north, lies at the foot of the Stawamus Chief, a huge granite dome beloved by rock climbers, and nearby Shannon Falls drops more than three hundred metres. Further on is Whistler, the ski resort, and Pemberton beyond.

The road continues beyond Pemberton as the Duffey Lake Road, which crosses the Coast Mountains in a wilder fashion, with tight bends, steep grades and a great view of glaciers and turquoise lakes. It is less forgiving than the first part, and the surface can be damp and patchy, so ride carefully. Rain is the great theme of Vancouver's weather, particularly from October to March, when grey skies can persist for weeks, but in summer the days are long, dry and warm. In late spring and early autumn, the mountains offer clear air and fewer visitors. Snow can linger on the high passes until early summer.

In the city itself, practicalities are no problem, with fuel stations, motorcycle dealers and repair shops. Eat well before leaving: Vancouver has superb sushi, dim sum and fresh salmon, and its coffee culture is serious. Parking downtown is expensive, so find a secure lot in advance. Bring waterproofs, whatever the forecast, because weather on the coast can turn within an hour, and wildlife, including bears, appears on some of the northern sections.
t.sunshine coast ferry ride@49.9,-123.3:
Squamish is a mountain town of seventeen thousand at the head of Howe Sound, an hour's ride north of Vancouver on the Sea to Sky Highway, and with its shops, bakeries and brewpubs it is the natural place to eat before or after the long run to Whistler or onwards. The big thing in town is the Stawamus Chief, a vast granite dome rising more than 600 metres above the water, which climbers have scaled for decades, and which you will see from almost every corner of the town.

The Squamish people have lived here for thousands of years, and the Chief carries a name from their tradition. In winter, bald eagles gather along the river near Brackendale, with hundreds of them arriving for the salmon run, and the town holds an annual count that has recorded some of the largest numbers in North America. Shannon Falls, just south of town, drops about 330 metres in a stream down the cliff, and is easily reached from the highway. The area has also become a centre for mountain biking, kiteboarding on the Squamish estuary, and rock climbing.

The ride itself is a joy. Highway 99, widened and improved before the 2010 Winter Olympics, runs along the side of the sound beneath steep, forested walls, with long fast curves and views over the water, and it is busy at weekends, with traffic heavy on Fridays and Sundays. Beyond Squamish it climbs through Garibaldi Provincial Park country towards Whistler, with glacier peaks overhead, and the road continues towards Pemberton and the Duffy Lake Road. The ferry to the Sunshine Coast leaves from Horseshoe Bay, some forty minutes back to the south.

Fuel is available in Squamish and Whistler, and the stretch between has little, so top up. Rain is common on the coast, and winter can bring snow and rockfall onto the highway, so check conditions before you go. A sunny morning here is hard to beat, and the cafés open early.
t.duffy lake road loop@49.3,-123.8:
Sechelt sits on a narrow neck of land between the open water of the Strait of Georgia and the long, fjord-like Sechelt Inlet, on what Vancouverites call the Sunshine Coast, though the name reflects the drier climate rather than any guarantee. It is a town of about nine thousand, the home of the shishalh Nation, whose name for themselves is the origin of the town's, and a practical food and fuel stop on the coast highway, with a handful of bakeries, a farmers' market in summer, and a cluster of galleries.

You reach the coast by ferry. From Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver, the boat to Langdale takes about forty minutes, and then Highway 101 runs north along the shore through Gibsons, Roberts Creek, Sechelt and onward to Earls Cove, where another ferry crosses the Jervis Inlet to Saltery Bay. Welcome Beach, the little community next on the list, has a historic community hall and a quiet pebble shore, a spot for a short stroll along the water. Booking the ferry in summer is wise, since long queues build on sunny weekends.

The Duffy Lake Road, which gives this ride its name, lies on the far side of the water, a long way inland, and it is the high, dramatic road from Pemberton to Lillooet. This part of the day is the gentle, sociable part, with the highway rolling over forested rises and curving beside small bays, passing driftwood beaches and boat sheds, and the speed limits are reasonable and enforced. Seals loll on rocks, eagles perch on snags, and on clear days the mountains of Vancouver Island stand on the western horizon.

Fuel is easy in Sechelt and Gibsons, while the long stretch to Earls Cove has fewer places, so check your gauge. The air smells of salt, cedar and seaweed. Rain is likely in the cooler months, and the best weather is from June to September. Plan your loop around the ferries rather than the road.
t.london motorcycle escapes@51.5,-1.1:
Where the Thames squeezes between the Chiltern Hills and the Berkshire Downs, the river has had to cut a passage through a chalk ridge, and the result is the Goring Gap. The pin sits on the Oxfordshire bank just upstream, a few kilometres from Goring, with Wallingford to the north and Pangbourne across the water. It is the sort of place that looks very English from a distance and even better up close: willows, pastures, narrow locks and a weir, with the brick railway bridge at Moulsford that Brunel built crossing the water.

The river is the reason this stop is marked for a swim. On a warm day the banks upstream of the locks fill up with picnic blankets, paddleboards and children in the water, and the Thames here is clean enough that the small swimming spots by the meadows are well used. Take care near weirs, where the current is stronger than it looks, and remember the river is also a busy navigation channel.

There is a good deal of quiet history in the neighbourhood. The Ridgeway, said to be Britain's oldest road, crosses the river here between Goring and Streatley, and walkers have been using it for thousands of years. Pangbourne is where Kenneth Grahame, the author of The Wind in the Willows, lived in his later years, and the riverside scenery has more than a little of the book about it. Nearby Cholsey is where Agatha Christie is buried. At Whitchurch-on-Thames, a small toll bridge still takes your coins to cross the river, which is a fine thing to do on two wheels.

The roads here run along both sides of the valley, with a mix of fast A roads and winding lanes. Climb out of the river onto the Downs and the lanes become narrower, with wide views over the Vale of the White Horse and old beechwoods, and traffic drops away. Weekends in summer are crowded near the river, so go early or late.

For practical matters, Wallingford, with ten thousand people, has fuel, a market square and plenty of cafés, and Goring has a couple of good pubs and a railway station. The way home to London is either the quiet road along the Thames or a faster run on the M4, depending on how much daylight you have left.
t.cambridge fen edge and ely scenic road@5:
Luton has an unfair reputation, but it has one great advantage for riders: it sits right at the foot of the Chiltern Hills, so within a few minutes of the airport and the car factories you are climbing onto chalk downland. The pin lies on the northern edge of the town, a few kilometres from the airport, in the strip of land between Luton and the Hertfordshire villages of Kimpton and Hitchin. Hitchin, with thirty-six thousand people, is the charming market town in the area, with an old church, a market square and a long history as a centre for lavender growing, which scented the fields around it until the twentieth century.

The geography is distinctive. The Chiltern scarp runs northeast to southwest in a line of open, grassy hills, and the old roads follow the gaps through it, climbing steadily to a pass before dropping to the Bedfordshire plain. Close to the airport, Someries Castle stands as a ruined brick gatehouse in a field, a fifteenth-century fragment that most travellers never notice. Luton Hoo, once one of the great country houses of England, is just south, now a hotel and golf course.

The riding is mixed. The A6 and the A505 are fast, busy roads with a lot of lorries, and the town's ring roads are heavily signalled. But the lanes toward Kimpton and the small valleys north of Harpenden are narrow, hedged and surprisingly quiet, with lovely light in the evenings. The surface is generally good, though rural lanes accumulate mud and gravel in wet weather. Watch for cyclists, who flock to the Chilterns at weekends.

For fuel, coffee and food, Luton and Hitchin both have everything you need, and Kimpton has a small shop and a couple of pubs. The label mentions the Cambridge fens and Ely, which lie to the east and north, and the route is likely to use this stop as the start or end of the day's ride.

If you have an extra half-hour, Dunstable Downs, a short ride west, has a wide view over the Bedfordshire plain, with kites flying and gliders circling over the slope. It is one of the best simple viewpoints within reach of London, and it sits right where the Chilterns meet the open country.
