Odiham is a small town with an enormous sound. It lies on the Hampshire plateau between Farnham and Basingstoke, and the RAF base just outside is home to the Chinook helicopters, whose twin rotors thud across the whole district whenever they train. The pin sits just west of the town, near Hook and Long Sutton, in a neat patchwork of fields, hedges and little woods. It is a quiet, comfortable stretch of rural Hampshire that most people drive through on the way to somewhere else.

The town itself is a delight, with a wide High Street lined with Georgian brick houses, a good old church and several pubs. A short walk away the ruins of Odiham Castle, an octagonal keep built for King John in the early thirteenth century, stand beside the Basingstoke Canal. John is said to have stayed here before riding out to Runnymede to seal Magna Carta. The canal itself is a peaceful, mostly disused waterway with a towpath popular with walkers, and the Greywell Tunnel nearby is home to one of the largest bat colonies in Britain.

The riding is a mix of A roads and meandering lanes. The A287 and the A30 are the main arteries, quick and busy, while the lanes toward Long Sutton and Upton Grey twist between hedges with the occasional short rise. Surfaces are generally good, but they carry a lot of rural traffic, and the sudden junctions can catch you out. Early mornings in spring are the best, with mist lying in the fields and blossom in the hedges.

For fuel, food and coffee, Hook, three kilometres away, has everything you need, with supermarkets, a station and cafés, and Odiham has several pubs and tea rooms along the High Street that open for lunch. Long Sutton, in the Hampshire countryside, has a small golf club and an old church.

The label refers to the Cambridge fens and Ely, which are far to the north-east, but this stop works well as a starting point for riders coming out of southwest London, and the route eventually crosses over to Kent and the White Cliffs. If you hear the Chinooks overhead, stop and look up: they fly low, and they are an impressive sight.
Marlow's suspension bridge is the first thing to look at, and it is worth the detour on its own. William Tierney Clark, who also designed the original Hammersmith Bridge, built it in the 1830s, and it still carries traffic across the Thames in a slim, elegant span beside the church spire and the weir. The pin sits a few kilometres downstream, between Marlow and Henley, on the Buckinghamshire side of a stretch of river that rowers and sailors treat as a sacred place.

Henley's Royal Regatta, held each summer since 1839, is the famous event, and Marlow holds its own regatta, but the river is busy with boats most of the year, and the towpath is a pleasant walk. Between the two towns, near Medmenham, the ruins of an abbey were used in the eighteenth century by Sir Francis Dashwood's Hellfire Club for gatherings that were rumoured to be more debauched than they probably were. To the north the Chiltern beechwoods begin at once, and the Hambleden valley, with its flint and brick cottages, is the sort of village you recognise from television even if you cannot name it.

The riding is a glorious tangle of narrow lanes, steep wooded hills and sudden river views. The road from Marlow to Hambleden, and onward through Turville and Fingest, is a favourite among local riders, with short climbs, tight bends and a lot of tree cover, so shade, damp and fallen leaves are constant companions. Surface quality is mixed. The main roads along the Thames, the A4155 and A4130, are busier and slower, especially at weekends.

Marlow is the place to eat, with thirteen thousand people more or less, a high street of independent cafés, bakeries and some very good pubs, plus fuel at the edge of town. Henley is larger and has more of everything, although parking on a summer weekend can be a battle. For a quick lunch, Marlow's riverside has benches near the bridge.

The label says Surrey Hills and Box Hill, which are on the other side of London, and the truth is that this stop is the natural start for a loop through the Chilterns. If you arrive on a Sunday morning, you will see the first scullers on the water and the coffee shops opening, and the day is yours.
Cowdray House at Midhurst is one of the finest ruins in southern England, a Tudor mansion that burned to a shell in 1793 and has stood open to the weather ever since. It is the best-known sight in this part of West Sussex, and it sets the tone for the area: old stone, old money, polo ponies and lots of beech woods. The pin sits a few kilometres south-east of the town, where the land begins to rise toward the escarpment of the South Downs, with Petworth and Fernhurst not far away.

Midhurst, with six and a half thousand people, is the natural halt: it has fuel, cafés, a market square and a good scatter of pubs, many of them in old coaching inns with big fireplaces. The River Rother flows nearby, and the town has a long literary connection: H. G. Wells worked here as a young man, and the nearby villages have been home to many writers and artists. Petworth, a short ride east, has an enormous house and park, once home to the painter J. M. W. Turner's patron, and Turner made many of his glowing, hazy landscapes here. The park's herd of deer and the old lake are a good reason to take a slow walk.

The riding is of the lovely, narrow, hedged kind, with sunken lanes, steep little hills and tight bends where the road dips under the beech trees. The South Downs offer wide, open views over the Weald, and the quiet roads that cross them are good for a long, slow ride, but they are narrow, patched and often covered in leaves in autumn. Expect horses, cyclists and farm vehicles. The best times are early morning in spring, when the bluebells are out, and clear autumn afternoons, when the light turns the beech woods copper.

Food is easy. Midhurst has bakeries, delis and a few good tea rooms, and the pubs on the Downs serve generous lunches, though they fill up on Sundays. Fernhurst, to the north, is smaller but has a village green and a shop.

The ride is the Essex saltmarsh and Suffolk villages, which are on the other side of London, so this stop is mostly useful as a start or a halt on a day out in West Sussex. It is a classic place to refuel body and bike before the climb onto the Downs.
t.chilterns ridge and thames valley photo:
Frensham Ponds, Thursley Common and the Devil's Punch Bowl are the big names of this corner of Surrey, but the pin sits quietly among them, near Elstead and Milford, where the heathland meets the sandstone hills. It is an area of pines, birches, sandy tracks and acid soils, quite unlike the chalk of the North Downs, and it has a character of its own, with open heather, hidden ponds and old oak woods. Thursley Common, a short ride away, is a national nature reserve famous for its dragonflies, Dartford warblers and rare reptiles, and the wooden boardwalk that crosses the boggy heart of the common is a pleasant short walk.

Elstead is a small village centred on a green and an old mill, with a medieval bridge over the River Wey, and it is the sort of place where cricket is still played on summer afternoons. Milford and Witley are larger villages close to Godalming, with shops, pubs and a railway line. Hindhead, further south, has the Devil's Punch Bowl, a huge natural hollow in the sandstone, and since the A3 tunnel opened the old road along its edge has become much quieter, which is good news for riders who want the views.

The riding is lovely. The lanes between Elstead, Thursley and Churt are narrow and winding, with sandy verges, steep banks and tall hedges, and the surface can be uneven. Gravel and sand on the apex of bends is a hazard, especially after dry spells, when the heather dries out and horses and walkers appear on the roads. The Hog's Back, a high ridge of chalk to the north, has a good road with long views, and it is a few minutes away.

For practical matters, Milford and Witley have small shops and a couple of pubs, and Godalming, a short ride north, has fuel, supermarkets and a good market town. The photo stop is a place to enjoy the heathland light, and the best moments come early in the morning and again in the evening, when the sun sets low behind the pines.

The ride is the Chilterns and Thames valley, which are some way north, but the Surrey Hills make a gentle introduction to a longer day out of London.
t.peak district overnight escape@51.2,-1.3:
Overton owes its existence to the River Test, one of the most famous chalk streams in the world, which rises nearby among the downs and runs south toward Southampton. The pin sits on the quiet road between Overton and Basingstoke, in the north Hampshire countryside, with the old paper-making village of Laverstoke just beside it. Laverstoke Mill is where the paper for Bank of England banknotes has been made since the early eighteenth century, and the water of the Test was the reason.

The landscape is long, smooth chalk downland, with big arable fields, beech hangers on the ridges and thatched villages in the valleys. A few miles north, near Kingsclere, lies the high down that inspired Richard Adams's Watership Down, and the book's world of warrens, hedges and sky is very recognisable on a bright day. Highclere Castle, the setting of Downton Abbey, is a short ride further north. Whitchurch, a little way south, has a working silk mill beside the river, which is well worth a visit.

The riding is a gentle delight. The B and unclassified roads of north Hampshire run in long straight lines and gentle curves over the downs, with wide views and little traffic, and the smooth surface is a pleasure after the potholes of the clay lowlands. The A303, a few miles south, is the main route to the West Country and carries heavy traffic, but the lanes around Overton, Ashe and Steventon are very quiet. Early mornings are best in summer, when the mist lies in the valleys, and in autumn the beech hangers turn bright orange.

For food, fuel and a coffee, Basingstoke, thirteen kilometres away, has a lot of chain restaurants and petrol stations, and Overton has several pubs, a bakery and a small supermarket. The pub gardens beside the Test are a good place for lunch, with the stream running clear over the gravel and trout lying in the current.

The ride is the Peak District Overnight Escape, which is far to the north, but this stop is the first part of a long journey out of London to the west and north. If you are heading for the Peak, you will reach the M40 or M1 within an hour, but you will remember the Test valley, and you may well prefer it.
t.north cascades highway@47.5,-121.8:
Snoqualmie and North Bend sit where the Cascade foothills meet the valley of the Snoqualmie River, about forty kilometres east of Seattle, and the great peaks are suddenly close. Mount Si, a steep, rocky bluff of about 1,260 metres, rises above North Bend and is one of the most popular hikes in the state, while the Interstate 90 corridor runs through the valley toward Snoqualmie Pass. The label mentions the North Cascades Highway, which lies far to the north, but this is the real beginning of Washington's mountain country.

Snoqualmie Falls, about seven kilometres from here, drops nearly eighty-three metres, higher than Niagara, and the roar of the water and the cloud of mist are impressive, particularly in spring when the river is high. A lodge sits at the top of the falls, and a viewing platform and a short trail lead to the base. The falls are sacred to the Snoqualmie people, who believe that the mist rising from the base connects the earth and the sky.

North Bend is also known for another reason: the television series Twin Peaks was filmed here in the early nineties, and a cafe in town, Twede's, is still recognisable as the diner in the show, serving cherry pie and coffee. Fans come from all over the world to see it, and the town leans into the connection with good humour.

Snoqualmie, with over thirteen thousand people, and North Bend, with about six and a half thousand, have fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a good range of restaurants. This is the last place to stock up before the mountains, and a good place to start a ride. The roads into the Cascades are smooth, with long bends and forest views, and in winter can be icy or closed by snow. In summer, traffic on weekends can be heavy, so start early.
t.north cascades highway photo pull off@47:
West of Hood Canal, on the edge of the Olympic National Forest, the roads run through a patchwork of working woods, logging roads and small valleys, and the whole area smells of fir and cut timber. This stop lies between Belfair and Shelton, in Mason County, where the economy has always depended on trees. Shelton, a town of nearly ten thousand people, proudly calls itself the Christmas tree capital of the nation, and thousands of conifers are shipped from its farms every December. The lumber mills and tree farms give the countryside a tidy, managed look.

Shelton also sits on Oakland Bay, an arm of Puget Sound that is famous for shellfish. Oysters, clams and mussels are cultivated in the clean, cold waters, and you can buy them fresh at stands and restaurants along the road. It has drawn artists and back-to-the-landers since the sixties, which is why a Saturday market in Ganges sells cheese, bread and pottery through the warmer months. In July and August the ferries fill, so book if you can or plan to wait, and carry whatever you need for the day because the smaller islands have little in the way of fuel. Winter is mild, wet and nearly empty.
t.duffy lake road loop@49.4,-122.9:
The pin for this stop lands in the mountains north of Port Moody and Coquitlam, in the rugged country above Indian Arm, well away from any road you would choose for a pleasure ride. Much of this land belongs to the Metro Vancouver water supply and parks system, and the Coquitlam watershed in particular is closed to the public to keep the reservoir clean. That is worth knowing before you start poking down side tracks, because gates here are locked and meant seriously. What you actually need is the gas station and the motorway on the valley floor, where the day begins.

Port Moody, at the head of Burrard Inlet, is the nearest sizeable town, with Coquitlam and Anmore close by. It is a good place for fuel, coffee and a last check of the bike before you head out. Port Moody was the original western end of the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1886 before the line was extended on to Vancouver, and the old railway history still shows in the waterfront and the heritage buildings around Rocky Point Park. A short ride east brings you to the Trans-Canada Highway and the Fraser Valley.

The ride that begins here heads for Duffy Lake Road, the stretch of Highway 99 from Pemberton to Lillooet. It is a mountain crossing of real character: a steep, winding climb through Cayoosh Pass with hairpins, glacier views and the turquoise Joffre Lakes beside the road. The summit is well above one thousand metres, so it can be cold and can see snow outside high summer. Services are very sparse, so fill up before you start. The road is a narrow two-lane highway, with logging trucks and campervans sharing the bends, and the surface is mostly good but patched here and there.

Nearer to this pin, the landscape is dense with cedar, hemlock and Douglas fir, and black bears are common in the hills. The air smells of resin after rain, and the creeks run clear and cold from the high peaks. If you want to ride the area above the Fraser, Mount Seymour and Cypress to the west offer short, steep road climbs with views over the city. Fuel is plentiful in Coquitlam and Port Moody, though prices in Metro Vancouver run high, so check your options before the long haul north.

Howe Sound is Canada's southernmost fjord, a long finger of deep green water pushing north from the Strait of Georgia into the Coast Mountains, and this pin is out in the high country on its western side, above the water and far from any street. The nearest town of any size is Squamish, twenty-odd kilometres to the north-east, and Lions Bay, a small village clinging to the opposite shore, is more than thirty kilometres away. What lies between is steep forested slope, small lakes and rock, with the Tantalus Range showing its white shoulders to the east.

What you can ride is the Sea to Sky Highway, number 99, along the far shore of the sound. It begins at Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver and runs north past Lions Bay, Porteau Cove, Britannia Beach and Shannon Falls, with the road sometimes only a few metres above the water and the mountains plunging straight down on the other side. It is the sort of road that makes people slow down simply to look, and that is the main hazard: drivers braking for views, and the odd rock fall on the cliff sections. The surface was widened and improved for the 2010 Winter Olympics, and the passing lanes are generous.

Porteau Cove is worth a stop. The old rail line runs along the shore, and the cove is a provincial park with a pebbled beach and a shipwreck that scuba divers visit. The sound itself was once badly polluted by the mine at Britannia, but in recent decades the water has recovered, and you can now see dolphins and even humpback whales some summers. The Gambier, Bowen and Anvil islands sit offshore, and BC Ferries run from Horseshoe Bay to Bowen, a short crossing with its own small, wooded loop of roads.

Fuel is available at Horseshoe Bay and at Squamish, but the long stretch between them has limited services, so start with a full tank. For a good day, begin early to beat the commuter crowd, and ride the highway northbound in the morning light, when the sound is still and the mountains are sharp.
t.linqing section of huitong canal@36.8,11:
Linqing is where the Grand Canal still carries the memory of an empire, and its bricks may be the best evidence. The town lies in western Shandong, on the flat plain of north China, at the meeting of the Wei river and the Huitong Canal, a stretch of the great waterway dug in 1411 under the Ming emperor Yongle to carry grain from the Yangtze south to the new capital at Beijing. It was one of the busiest places on the route, a customs post and transfer point where goods changed boats, and for centuries it was one of the richest towns on the plain.

The bricks are special. Linqing was a major producer of the huge, fine-grained grey bricks that built the walls and halls of the Forbidden City, and each was stamped with the name of the kiln, the supervisor and the year, so that any faulty brick could be traced. Piles of old stamped bricks have been found along the canal, and the Ming granary buildings nearby were built of the same material. Walk along the water at dusk, with the old bridge and the quiet embankment, and imagine the thousands of barges that once jammed it.

The land here is as flat as a table. The plain is a patchwork of wheat, maize and cotton fields, with poplar windbreaks and brick villages, and the sky is wide and often hazy. Roads run straight and long through the fields, and the pace is slow, with tractors and three-wheelers sharing the lane. Summer is hot and humid, and spring winds can bring dust from the north, so autumn is the best time, when the air clears and the fields are golden. UNESCO added the Grand Canal to the World Heritage list in 2014.

For practical purposes, this is a big, busy region of cities and highways, and riding in China as a visitor involves rules on licences, vehicles and permits that are strict and change from time to time, so check them carefully before planning anything. Fuel is easy to find in the larger towns, including Qingnian, which is the nearest, and food is plentiful and cheap. Look for the noodle dishes and flatbreads typical of Shandong, and in the evening local people gather by the canal to walk and talk.
t.weishan section of huitong canal@35.1,11:
Weishan sits on the eastern shore of a very big lake, and the lake changes everything about the place. Weishan Lake is the southernmost of a chain of shallow lakes in south-west Shandong, forming a long strip of water that links the Huitong Canal with the Grand Canal further south. In summer the shallows are covered with lotus flowers, in pink and white, and reed beds stretch for kilometres along the shore. Fishing boats move through the channels, and the air smells of water and mud.

The canal here is one of the great engineering stories of the Ming dynasty. In the early fifteenth century, the emperor wanted to bring grain to Beijing along an extended Grand Canal, and the difficulty was the high ground in western Shandong, where the water had to be shared between north and south. The engineer Bai Ying solved it at Nanwang, well north of the lake, by building a dam and diverting the Wen river into a channel that split the water, sending about thirty percent south and seventy percent north, a ratio memorised by later generations. The clever hydraulic hub at Nanwang, along with the Huitong stretch, is part of the UNESCO site.

Weishan was also a theatre of the Second World War, when railway workers and local guerrillas fought the Japanese army along the Tianjin-Pukou line, an episode that inspired a popular film. A small memorial to the Railway Guerrillas stands on the lake. In the countryside, the farmland is flat and rich, with fields of wheat, corn and vegetables, brick villages and long straight roads between rows of poplars.

Riding conditions are straightforward but the paperwork is not: foreign visitors who want to ride in China must follow strict rules on licences and permits, which change often, so check before you go. The nearest town with services is Yucheng, about twenty-seven kilometres away, and the larger city of Jining, nearly forty kilometres, has fuel stations, hotels and restaurants. For a meal, try fresh lake fish, boiled and spiced, or a plate of lotus root. The best months are May to October, when the lotus is in flower and the weather is warm.
t.south part of the yellow river estuary@3:
Few rivers move so much earth as the Yellow, and here, at its mouth in Shandong, you can watch the land being made. The Huang He carries more silt than any other major river, a load picked up from the loess plateau, and where it slows at the sea, it drops it, building a delta that grows by many square kilometres in some years. The river has often changed course here. It has flooded, shifted and found new channels, and its mouth has moved hundreds of kilometres over the centuries, which is why the Chinese call it China's Sorrow.

The result is a flat, wet, shining country of mudflats, tidal creeks, reed beds and salt marsh, in the area near Dongying. The wetlands here are among the largest young wetlands in the world, and they are a vital stopover on the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, the route that carries millions of migratory birds each year between Siberia, China and Australia. In spring and autumn the flats fill with sandpipers, plovers, geese and cranes, and rare species such as the oriental stork and the red-crowned crane use the reeds for nesting and wintering. Tens of thousands of birds in the air at once is a sound as well as a sight.

The delta is also an oil field. The Shengli field, one of the biggest in China, pumps from beneath the marsh, and its nodding donkeys, pipelines and roads share the landscape with the reeds. The two worlds are oddly interleaved, with pumpjacks beside bird hides, and the flat horizon is broken by gas flares and wind turbines.

Riding on the delta means long, flat, straight roads, with wide skies and strong winds off the sea. The surfaces are generally good on main roads and poor on the farm tracks, and trucks serving the oil field share the road. Visitors who want to ride in China should check the rules on licences and permits well ahead, since they are strict. Fuel is easy to find in Dongying, the nearest city, and the reserve has few facilities, so bring water. Autumn is the best season for birds, and the sunrise over the flats is a good reason to stay overnight.

Capel lies on the Surrey side of the Weald, in the low, wooded country south of Dorking, and it is one of those places where the soft clay country begins to rise toward the hills. To the north-east stands Leith Hill, which at about three hundred metres is the highest point in south-east England, topped by a Gothic tower built in the eighteenth century so that the summit would reach the three hundred metre mark. On a clear day, the view from it takes in the sea at Brighton and the towers of London.

Holmwood, a village on the common, and Warnham, a few kilometres south in Sussex, are the nearest places. Warnham has a large millpond, now a nature reserve, and was the birthplace of the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley in 1792 at Field Place, a house nearby. Horsham, a bit further south, is the main town. The roads between are a pleasure, lined with oak and hazel, with high banks and sudden dips, and the whole area has a sense of age.

The photo stop might offer you the green quilt of the Weald, with ridges of woodland rolling off into haze. The light is best in the early morning and the late afternoon, when the haze brings out the layers of the landscape and the sun picks out church towers. The surface of the lanes is mixed, with patched tarmac and loose gravel on the bends, and you will share the road with cyclists, who love these hills, and with horse riders.

Services are sparse, so fill up before you come. Dorking and Horsham have the nearest stations, and Holmwood has a pub and a shop. Spring is the best time, when the bluebells carpet the woods and the beeches are in fresh leaf. In winter, the roads can be icy under the trees, and fallen branches may block the lanes after a storm. A quiet pause here is a good way to remember that Surrey has a wild side.
t.hastings cliffs and high weald photo pul:
Bicester is a market town in north Oxfordshire that has outgrown its old boundaries, and its new estates spread across the Cherwell valley, but it still has a sleepy centre of limestone buildings and a good market square. With nearly thirty-four thousand people, it has plenty of fuel and food, and the villages of Ambrosden and Somerton are quiet places a few kilometres away. The town is best known for its outlet shopping village, which brings coachloads of visitors, and the old RAF airfield, now preserved as a heritage site where vintage cars and aircraft are restored.

Roman history lies close by. Alchester, a large Roman fort and town a short distance south-west of Bicester, was a major military base in the first century, and though little of it can be seen above ground, its position on a Roman road from Verulamium explains the district's long importance, and the whole area has been settled since prehistoric times.

The photo stop is a pull-off in flat arable country, and the view is of wide fields, hedges and the occasional church tower. The Cherwell, a gentle river that winds south toward Oxford, has meadows and willows, and the villages along it have stone houses with thatched or slate roofs. The roads here are good and fast, with long gentle bends and little to slow you apart from the villages, and traffic is light away from the A34 and the M40.

The ride begins and ends at this point, and Bicester is a good place to do so, with easy access from the motorway and a ring road that bypasses the centre. Fuel stations are numerous, and the supermarkets open early. The label speaks of Hastings and the High Weald, which are a long way to the south-east, so be sure of your plans before you set off. A good breakfast in the town square is an easy way to start.
t.dorset jurassic coast long day photo pul:
Silverstone is a name that means one thing to most people: the home of the British Grand Prix. The first world championship race was held on the old airfield here in 1950, and the circuit has hosted the race almost every year since. The village itself is small, with just under two thousand people, and for most of the year it is quiet, but on race weekends the roads for miles around fill with traffic. Buckingham, six kilometres away, has nearly thirteen thousand people and fuel, shops and cafés, and it is a handsome market town on the River Great Ouse.

Near Buckingham lies Stowe, one of the great landscape gardens of England, laid out in the eighteenth century with temples, lakes and bridges by some of the best designers of the age, including Capability Brown, who began his career as head gardener here. It is now a National Trust property and well worth a visit, with its Palladian bridge and Temple of Ancient Virtue. The school that now occupies the house is one of the more famous in the country.

For a rider, the area offers pleasant if undramatic country, with rolling farmland, hedgerows and small stone villages. The roads are generally good, though near the circuit, traffic can be heavy during events, and the signs and diversions can be confusing. On a quiet day, you can sometimes hear the sound of engines drifting over the fields, a distant roar that carries a sense of speed.

The photo stop is a place to look back across the fields to the airfield and perhaps to catch a glimpse of cars testing on the circuit. Tingewick, a village a few kilometres away, has a green and a pub, and the other villages have a handful of shops. A good time for a ride here is on a weekday in spring, when the blossom is out and the roads are empty. If a race is on, avoid the area entirely.
t.london motorcycle escapes@52.1,-0.2:
The Greensand Ridge runs across Bedfordshire like a low spine, and Potton and Gamlingay lie on its eastern edge, a pair of small towns of brick and clay tile that once made their living from the soil. Potton, with nearly five thousand people, was famous for its market gardens, and Gamlingay, with about thirty-two hundred, has an old heath and woodland, the Gamlingay Wood, which has been managed for nearly a thousand years and is one of the oldest in the county. Everton, a tiny village nearby, sits on the ridge with views over the Ivel valley.

Biggleswade, six kilometres away with over sixteen thousand people, is the nearest large place, and it has fuel, shops and cafés on the River Ivel. Not far off, Old Warden is home to the Shuttleworth Collection, a remarkable museum of historic aircraft and vehicles, many of them still flown on summer weekends, and the sight of a biplane over the fields is one of the pleasures of the district. The RSPB reserve at The Lodge, near Sandy, has heathland, woodland and birds.

The label calls this a swim stop, but the local waters are small and mostly private, so treat it as a rest. The riding is gentle, with lanes among arable fields and hedgerows, and the Greensand Ridge gives enough relief for bends and short climbs. The soil is sandy, and the roads can be gritty on corners, particularly after dry weather. Traffic is light apart from the A1 and the A603, and the cyclists are many.

t.chilterns ridge and thames valley@51.9,-:
Wing and Stewkley are villages on the edge of the Vale of Aylesbury, and each has a church that would be famous in a less crowded country. Wing's All Saints has an Anglo-Saxon nave and apse, with a crypt dating from perhaps the eighth century, one of the finest early churches in England. Stewkley's St Michael's, built around 1150, is regarded as one of the best Norman parish churches in the country, with a massive tower, carved arches and a zigzag decoration that has survived intact. Both are worth a short stop, even if you know nothing of church architecture.

Wingrave, a village nearby, has a green and a pub, and Leighton Buzzard, eight kilometres to the north-east with nearly thirty-seven thousand people, is the main town, with fuel, shops and cafés. The town has a narrow gauge railway, built to carry sand from the local quarries and now run by volunteers, and the sand from this district, a fine pale silica, has been used in glassmaking and building. Ascott House, near Wing, belongs to the Rothschild family and has a notable collection of art and a lovely garden.

The roads here are flat and straight across the clay vale, with a few gentle bends and the occasional hump bridge. The surface is generally good, but heavy farm vehicles and lorries serving the quarries use some lanes, and the edges are broken. A coffee at a farm shop or a slice of cake at a village tearoom is a pleasant pause. t.hampshire test valley roads photo pull o:
Blewbury is a pretty village at the foot of the Berkshire Downs, with thatched cottages, chalk streams and a wide green, and it was the home of Kenneth Grahame, author of The Wind in the Willows, who lived here for several years in the early twentieth century. The chalk stream that runs through the village is the sort of water that inspired the book's riverbank. Cholsey, a few kilometres away, is where Agatha Christie is buried, in the churchyard of St Mary's, and her grave is a quiet place under a tree. Compton is a smaller village on the Downs.

Didcot, seven kilometres away with nearly thirty thousand people, has the fuel and shops. It was once dominated by the cooling towers of its power station, which were demolished in stages between 2014 and 2019, and it is also the home of the Didcot Railway Centre, a museum of Great Western Railway locomotives and carriages, where steam days are held through the year. Wallingford, across the Thames, has a Saxon street plan and the ruins of a castle.

Motor vehicles cannot use most of it, but the quiet lanes beside it are a good substitute. The country is rolling chalk, with big fields, beech clumps and wide views, and the sound of skylarks on a warm day is unmistakable.

Riding here is gentle, with long flowing bends and a good surface, though the lanes are narrow and sometimes muddy near farms. The light across the downs in the early morning is lovely, and the mist in the valley adds to the atmosphere. As the start and finish of a ride, it is an easy place to meet, with parking near the green and a pub within a short walk. Time your photo stop for the golden hour and you will not be disappointed.
t.peak district overnight escape@51.8,-0.5:
Dunstable lies at the foot of the Chiltern escarpment on Watling Street, the old Roman road, and its streets and shops carry the weight of the long-distance traffic that has passed through for two millennia. With nearly fifty-two thousand people, it has fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and Kensworth, Markyate and Caddington, smaller villages in the surrounding hills, are strung along the chalk. Markyate was the home of a twelfth-century holy woman called Christina, who hid from an unwanted marriage in a cell and eventually founded a priory.

Above the town, the Dunstable Downs rise to the highest point in Bedfordshire, a steep chalk slope covered with wild flowers that is popular for kite flying, with a visitor centre and a gliding club whose planes circle silently on the updraught. On a clear day, the view across the Vale of Aylesbury to the Cotswolds is wide. A few kilometres west, near Whipsnade, the chalk figure of a lion, cut into the hillside in 1933, is visible from the road, and the zoo there is one of the largest in Britain.

The ride starts here with a short, steep climb up the escarpment, and the road winds up through beech and hawthorn to the ridge. The bends are tight enough to give pleasure, and the surface is good. Once on top, the lanes run between hedges and fields, with fine views, and the traffic is much lighter than on the main roads below. The wind on the ridge can be strong, and the weather often differs from that in the valley.

Fill the tank here before heading into the Chilterns, and eat a decent breakfast in one of the cafés on the high street. The ride to the Peak District will be long, and the early miles go by on motorways, so take care to use the quiet hours. A walk on the downs in the morning, if time allows, is a good way to blow away sleep.
Amersham on the Hill grew up around the railway. In 1892 the Metropolitan Railway extended its line from London to Amersham, and the new station on the hilltop became the centre of a settlement that would later be called Metro-land, a name coined by the railway company to advertise the green suburbs beyond the city. The poet John Betjeman made it a subject of affection in his television film Metro-land, celebrating the semi-detached houses and tree-lined roads. With the old town, Amersham has nearly forty thousand people, and Seer Green and Chalfont are leafy villages nearby.

Fuel and food are easy to find, with stations on the A413 and the roads toward Chesham, and plenty of cafés along the high street. The Chess valley, a chalk stream that runs through the hills toward Rickmansworth, is a lovely place to ride, with watercress beds, mills and wooded slopes. The beech woods of the Chilterns are at their best in autumn, when the leaves turn copper and gold, and the lanes are carpeted with mast.
