The food stop is in Maple Ridge, in the flat farmland and suburbs where the Fraser Valley begins to open out east of Vancouver. It is a place to eat well rather than to ride well, and that is fine after a day on mountain roads, because there is a lot of choice: a town of seventy thousand people supports a mix of diners, Asian restaurants, bakeries and the sort of coffee shop where locals read the paper at ten in the morning.

Mountains rise to the north, and on days when the cloud lifts you can see the dark, steep face of the Golden Ears range above the rooftops. Where the Fraser River's south arm meets the sea, the land stops in a sprawl of mudflats and marsh, and this pin sits just off that edge, on Sturgeon Bank, a broad tidal flat west of Richmond's dyke. It is a landscape that looks empty and is not: each tide carries it from shining water to glistening mud and back, and every square metre is grazed by birds.

Western sandpipers arrive in huge flocks in April and May, feeding on the biofilm that coats the mud, and at certain times of year the whole shore seems to ripple with their flight. It was once one of the busiest salmon canning centres in the world, home to dozens of canneries and a large Japanese Canadian fishing community, which was forcibly removed in 1942. The Gulf of Georgia Cannery, now a national historic site, preserves the machinery and stories of that period. The boardwalk along the working harbour is lined with fish stalls where you can buy prawns or salmon straight off the boat, and the fish and chips are widely praised.

The ride along the river dyke from Steveston to Garry Point is flat and quiet, with a path used by cyclists and walkers, and the main roads of Richmond are straight and busy. A day starting at the Kootenays, in the high interior, is a long way from here, but the Fraser Valley freeway brings you down to the sea in a few hours.

Old Windsor does not shout about itself, and the stop is better for that. It is a quiet riverside village beside the Thames, in the shadow of Windsor Great Park, a few miles upstream from where the river becomes the London river. Datchet sits across the water, with its green and its pubs. The place is the start of the day's ride west and south, and what it offers is a clean set of practical things: fuel, a coffee and a chance to check the bike in the quiet before the road begins.

The surrounding landscape is surprisingly historic. A short way along the river at Runnymede, in 1215, King John sealed Magna Carta, and the meadows there are now owned by the National Trust and are free to walk. The Great Park behind Windsor, a vast royal hunting ground of oak, bracken and grass, spreads across the hills to the south, with the Long Walk and the castle on its eastern edge. It all sits very close to Heathrow, and the planes come low overhead, a noisy reminder of how close you are to the capital.

Riding out of here is a slow warm-up. The roads around Windsor are busy with commuters and day-trippers, with roundabouts and cameras, and the best approach is to leave early, when the Great Park is quiet and the light is soft. Once you are through the first few villages and into the Berkshire lanes, the pace improves and the corners start to appear. Weekends are heavy with traffic around the castle, so a Sunday-morning start works best.

Old Windsor has about seven thousand residents and Datchet nearly five thousand, so fuel and basic supplies are not a problem. Windsor itself, a short ride away, has the larger supermarkets and a wide choice of cafés, though parking for a motorcycle in the centre can be awkward on a busy day. The Thames Path is easy to walk from the village if you want to see the river before you go, and the water meadows are a good place to check your kit.

High point is a generous phrase for this part of Berkshire, and it helps to be honest about it. The land here, between Bracknell and Hurst, is a rolling mix of heath, pine and oak woodland, at only around a hundred metres above the sea, and what passes for a summit is a modest rise in the gravel and sand country that stretches south toward Surrey. What it does offer is a break from the traffic of the Thames Valley and a first taste of trees and quiet lanes.

This was once the edge of Windsor Forest, a royal hunting district, and the soils are poor and sandy, which is why so much of the ground is still heathland and conifer plantation rather than farmland. Birch, Scots pine and bracken cover the verges, and in summer the heather turns the open ground purple. Nearby Crowthorne and Sandhurst carry the military and educational history of the area, with the Royal Military Academy and Wellington College among the names. Bracknell itself was designated a new town in 1949, and the contrast between its modern streets and the older villages around it is stark.

The riding is gentle and varied rather than dramatic. The lanes wind between hedges and woods, with occasional fast sections on open roads and then short, tight bends through villages. Surfaces are generally good but can be patchy where trees overhang, and after rain the sandy margins wash onto the road. Early morning is the best time, before the commuter traffic builds, and in autumn the leaves turn the lane tunnels gold and bronze, though they also make the surface slick.

For fuel and food, Bracknell, a few kilometres away, is a large town with a long list of stations, supermarkets and cafés, and it is the sensible place to fill up. Hurst is a small village of just over a thousand people, with a pub or two but little else. If you want a quiet stop, look for one of the nearby heathland car parks, where you can take your helmet off, listen to the birds and enjoy a short break before the next set of lanes.
t.hastings cliffs@51.1,-0.2:
This pin falls in West Sussex, in the quiet country around Balcombe and Handcross, on the high ground of the Weald south of Crawley. The land here rolls in long ridges of sandstone, with deep ghylls, the local word for a wooded stream valley, cut between them. It is pretty, in an unshowy way: small fields, oak woods, white-painted weatherboard on the farm buildings, and every junction signed for somewhere with an unlikely name.

The thing that most people notice is the Ouse Valley Viaduct near Balcombe, which carries the London to Brighton railway across the river on thirty-seven arches of pale brick. It was opened in the early 1840s, and its stone balustrades and pavilions were designed to make it look less like an industrial thing and more like a feature in a park. You can see it from a footpath and a couple of lanes, and it is worth a minute even if you do not care about railways. Nearby, Nymans garden at Handcross is a National Trust property with a ruined house and a very good collection of plants, and it makes a decent excuse for a stop if the rain starts.

The riding is fun in the old, unsophisticated way. The B2036 and the lanes between Balcombe, Staplefield and Cuckfield offer tight bends, patchy surfaces and a lot of mud after rain, so keep your speed honest and watch for horse riders. The A23 runs close to the east and carries the main London to Brighton traffic, which is a reminder of how near the capital is, and on a Sunday afternoon its southbound lanes can be solid. The nearest big shops and fuel stations are at Maidenbower and Crawley a few miles north, and Handcross has a village pub and a garage within reach. If you plan to run low, do not trust a village.

As a place on a route home, this is a good one to have at the end: gentle, wooded, close to the motorway but far enough from it to keep a sense of the countryside for a little longer.
t.burford stone street@51.8,-1.6:
Burford's High Street drops down a hill so steeply that you can see the roofs below you before you see the street, and it ends in a medieval stone bridge over the River Windrush. That one view is the whole reason to stop. The town grew rich on Cotswold wool in the Middle Ages, and the honey-coloured limestone houses with their tilted stone-tiled roofs, the big church and the arched doorways all date from that prosperity. Later it became a coaching stop between Oxford and the west, and some of the old inns still serve travellers.

History comes in a harder form too. In 1649, at the height of the Civil War's political chaos, Cromwell's troops crushed a mutiny of Levellers, the radical soldiers who wanted a wider vote and fairer laws, and locked several hundred of them in Burford church. Three leaders were shot against its wall the next morning, and the town still marks the day each May. Nothing in the quiet street prepares you for it. A few miles east, the ruins of Minster Lovell Hall stand on the riverbank, and the village of Swinbrook, where the Mitford sisters grew up, is also nearby.

The riding around here is gentle and good for a slow day. The A361 and the lanes along the Windrush valley run through small stone villages, past fields bounded by dry-stone walls and sheep in neat blocks. Surfaces are generally fine, though a lot of lorries use the A40 close by. Traffic in the street itself is slow on weekends, with coaches and visitors on foot, and parking a bike on the High Street is easy if you tuck it in among the cars. Go early and the town is almost empty, with the smell of baking drifting out of the bakery doors.

Burford is a small place of barely twelve hundred people, so for fuel, plan on Carterton, about six kilometres away, which is a proper town of sixteen thousand with supermarkets and filling stations. For food you are well served. There are tea rooms, pubs with log fires and a couple of delis, all of which cater to the sort of walkers and riders who arrive tired and wet in autumn.
t.broadway tower ridge@52.0,-1.8:
A Cotswold escarpment does not announce itself from the Vale of Evesham side; you simply turn a corner at Broadway and the road tilts upward, steeply, toward a tower on the skyline. Broadway Tower is a folly, built in 1798 for the Earl of Coventry on one of the highest points of the Cotswolds, at about three hundred and twelve metres. It was designed to look like a small castle and to be seen from the earl's estate far to the west, and the legend says that on a clear day you can see sixteen counties from the top.

The climb up Fish Hill is a proper test for a loaded bike, with a steady gradient, a couple of hairpin-like bends and a wide view back over the vale as you gain height. At the top, the tower sits in a country park, with grass, sheep and a car park, and the wind is nearly always blowing. Autumn and winter mornings can bring mist in the vale below while the ridge stays clear, and the sunrises are memorable. Weekends bring crowds, so if you want the view with some peace, go early on a weekday.

The story of the tower includes an interesting piece of Victorian history. William Morris, the designer and founder of the Arts and Crafts movement, rented the tower as a retreat in the 1880s, and it became a gathering place for artists and writers. The honey-coloured Cotswold limestone, formed in warm seas about a hundred and seventy million years ago, is the material of the villages below, and it glows gold in low sun, especially in Broadway and Chipping Campden.

Broadway, about two and a half kilometres away, has a good choice of tea rooms, pubs and shops along a wide green-lined high street, and it makes a handsome place for a break, though it is busy in summer. Chipping Campden is smaller but just as lovely. Fuel is not abundant in the villages, so plan around Evesham, about eleven kilometres away, which is a proper town of over twenty thousand people. Bring a windproof layer, since the ridge always seems to be colder than the valley.
Waltham Cross takes its name from the Eleanor cross that still stands in the middle of the town, one of the monuments Edward I had built to mark the resting places of his queen's funeral procession in 1290, and it is a handsome surprise among the shops. The fuel stop is on the northern edge of London, where the Lea Valley meets the rise of Enfield, and the place feels like a suburban crossroads with a long memory.

The district is stuffed with unexpected histories. Enfield Lock, a short distance south, was the home of the Royal Small Arms Factory, which produced the Lee-Enfield rifle that served the British army through two world wars. Nearby Theobalds Park was the site of a great Tudor and Jacobean palace, where James I died in 1625, and the New River, a seventeenth-century channel built to bring fresh water to London, still runs through the area. It is an odd place for a petrol stop, but the layers of history are easy to find.

For riding, this is a launching pad. The M25 and A10 are close, and the roads north and east into Hertfordshire and Essex are quick, while those south lead back into the city. A smart rider will plan an early start, since the junction at Waltham Cross is a regular bottleneck, and avoid the rush hours. Heading out, you can slip into the lanes of Epping Forest or the quiet fields around Cheshunt and Hertford, where the corners are gentle and the scenery changes fast.

Fuel and food are straightforward. Waltham Cross has about ten thousand people and Enfield Town more than a hundred thousand, so supermarkets, stations and cafés are everywhere, and many stay open late. If you have time, walk to the cross itself for a minute, because it is easy to drive past without noticing. Take care with the multi-lane roundabouts and bus lanes in the area, where the signs are dense and the cameras many. A full tank here makes the run south feel easy.
Chobham is a Surrey village at the edge of one of the biggest areas of open heath left near London. Chobham Common, a national nature reserve of several hundred hectares, is a broad mixture of heather, gorse, birch scrub and boggy hollows, and it is home to rare birds such as the Dartford warbler and nightjar, as well as adders and lizards. The village sits beside it, with a long high street, a church and a handful of pubs and cafés, and the whole place has the feel of a small country town that London has not quite swallowed.

The common has an unexpected claim to fame. The armour called Chobham armour, a composite material developed for tanks in the 1960s, takes its name from the research establishment near here, where trials on tank technology were carried out. It is a strange thought as you listen to the skylarks above the heather. Nearby are Brookwood Cemetery, one of the largest in the country, and the town of Woking, which has a long link to the early Muslim presence in Britain, with the Shah Jahan Mosque dating from the 1880s.

As a food stop, Chobham is easy and pleasant. The high street has bakeries, delis, a pub or two and a few cafés, and there is room to park a motorcycle on the roadside. Knaphill, a short distance away, is larger and has more shops and cafés, and a handful of petrol stations. The sandy soil drains fast, so the roads are rarely wet for long.

The riding around here is gentle and easy, with straight roads through pine and heath and short winding sections through villages. The land is flat, so the views are limited, but the open common gives a pleasant sense of space, and the light in early morning is soft and golden. Be careful on summer weekends, when dog walkers and horse riders are on the lanes, and in dry weather heath fires are a real risk, so there are sometimes closures. In autumn the bracken turns a deep orange, and the whole common glows.
t.south downs@51.7,-0.1:
Waltham Cross takes its name from one of the most moving things a medieval king ever built. When Queen Eleanor of Castile died in 1290, her husband Edward I had her body carried from Lincolnshire to London, and at each place the funeral procession stopped overnight he put up a stone cross. Only three of the twelve survive, and the one at Waltham Cross, with its carved figures of the queen and its pinnacles, is the most complete. It stands in the middle of the high street, among bus stops and cafés, and most people walk past it.

The town sits on the River Lea and the old Roman road, Ermine Street, on the line where Hertfordshire meets Essex and Greater London. Close by, in Waltham Abbey, are the ruins of a church said to have been where King Harold was buried after Hastings, and the Royal Gunpowder Mills, which for centuries produced explosives for the Navy and the army and are now open as a museum and nature reserve. The M25 crosses overhead at a busy junction, so the noise is constant. Further north the Lea Valley has reservoirs and wide marshes, with herons and kingfishers.

For a rider this is an edge place. It is where the suburbs finish and you can head north into the Hertfordshire lanes or east into the quiet Essex farmland around Epping, and equally the point where the fast roads, the A10 and the M25, take over for the journey home. The streets in the centre are mostly one-way, often congested, and not much fun. The reward is behind you: the cut-through lanes toward Cheshunt, Goffs Oak and Theobalds Park are short and shady, and on a weekday morning they are good practice for a slow, steady pace.

A couple of kilometres away you are in Enfield, with about a hundred thousand people, so fuel and food are everywhere. In Waltham Cross itself there are a number of cafés, takeaways and a big supermarket with a fuel station, and the pubs along the high street serve a Sunday lunch to bikers and cyclists alike. It is not a place for contemplation, but the cross is worth thirty seconds and a photo.
t.bude@50.8,-4.5:
Bude is where the long Atlantic Highway comes to a stop against the sea. The town sits at the top of north Cornwall, on a coast of black, folded cliffs and long sandy beaches, with big Atlantic swells rolling in and surfers in the water at almost every hour of daylight. It is not a pretty harbour town in the manner of south Cornwall; it is a windy, bright, slightly salty place, with a canal, a sea pool and a handful of old streets behind the beach.

The sea pool at Summerleaze beach is a good example of the town's character. It is a large tidal pool built in the 1930s into the rocks and filled by the sea at high tide, giving a place for safe swimming in clear water, and it is free. The old Bude Canal, which was built in the early nineteenth century to carry sea sand inland for farmers, ends at the sea lock beside the beach, and it is a handsome piece of industrial heritage. Be careful on those lanes: they are narrow, with high Cornish hedges and blind bends, and sand and gravel often lie on the surface after a storm.

Parking near the beach can be tight in summer, but the town has pay car parks within a short walk. The weather changes fast on this coast, with fog, wind and sudden showers, so carry waterproofs, and enjoy the end of the road with a cup of tea facing the waves.
t.box hill rider@51.3,-0.3:
Box Hill is the Surrey Hills' best-known bump, and it earns its fame. The hill rises sharply from the valley of the River Mole to a crest of chalk grassland and ancient box trees, from which the land falls away in a wide view toward the South Downs. It is a National Trust property, and it has been a favourite day out for Londoners since the railway came to Dorking in the nineteenth century. The poet John Keats finished part of Endymion in the inn below the hill, and Jane Austen set a famous picnic scene on its slopes in Emma.

The road up is the Zig Zag, a series of well-graded hairpins that climb the north face, and it is well known among riders and even more among cyclists, who test themselves against it all year round. It was part of the road race route at the 2012 Olympics, which brought a new wave of visitors. The corners are wide and the surface generally good, but they are busy at weekends, with groups of riders and cyclists, so ride carefully and do not overtake on the bends. The cafe at the top is a well-known meeting point.

The nature here is distinctive. Box Hill is one of the few places in Britain where native box grows wild, along with yew and juniper, and the chalk grassland supports orchids and butterflies in early summer. The air is clean and the light on the slopes is soft in the morning. In autumn the beech woods turn gold, and the view over the Weald is at its best after rain, when the haze lifts.

Dorking, about two and a half kilometres away, has about seventeen thousand people and has stations, supermarkets and a good range of cafés, so that is where to fuel. Great Bookham is another option. At the hill itself, the National Trust has a visitor centre and a cafe, but the car park fills early on fine days. If you plan to start here, arrive before nine o'clock on a weekend, when the road is quiet and the riders are only beginning to appear.
t.ditchling beacon@50.9,-0.1:
Ditchling Beacon is the highest point on the South Downs in East Sussex, at 248 metres, and the way up from the north is steep enough to make a loaded bike grumble. The lane leaves the village of Ditchling and climbs the scarp in a series of narrow bends, with a gradient that is a serious test for cyclists, who treat it as a rite of passage, since the London to Brighton charity ride famously ends with this climb. A motorcycle takes it in its stride, but there is little room to pass, so patience is needed.

At the top, the land opens into a wide, open grass hilltop with a view that justifies the climb. To the north lies the Weald, a green, wooded plain stretching away to the horizon, and to the south the Downs roll toward Brighton and the sea, a pale glimmer on clear days. The summit carries the earthworks of an Iron Age hill fort, a ring of banks and ditches built more than two thousand years ago, and the whole hilltop is a nature reserve of chalk grassland, rich in wild flowers and butterflies in summer.

The wind is the thing to watch. The Beacon is exposed, and a stiff breeze coming off the Channel can be strong and cold, even in summer, so bring a windproof layer and keep a firm grip when getting on and off the bike at the car park. Weekends are busy with walkers, cyclists and dog owners, and the car park fills early on fine days. Mornings are quieter, and sunsets from the top are worth waiting for.

Nearby Ditchling is a village of about fifteen hundred people, with old flint cottages, a museum and a couple of pubs, and it was once home to a community of artists and craftspeople. It is a good place for coffee or a bite, but fuel is limited. Hassocks, about five kilometres away, is a small town with a station and shops, while Brighton, a short ride south, offers everything. Fill up in one of those before you tackle the Downs, because the roads beyond are quiet and the pumps are far apart.
t.box@51.3,-0.3:
Box Hill is the great chalk lump south of Leatherhead, where the River Mole cuts through the North Downs and leaves a steep slope of box trees, yews and wildflower grassland on one side. The box trees give the hill its name, and it is one of the few places in Britain where they grow wild. The National Trust looks after much of it. Down by the river at Burford Bridge, the poet John Keats finished his poem Endymion in 1817, and Jane Austen set the famously awkward picnic in Emma on the hill.

Riders know it for the zig-zag road, a set of nine or so hairpins that climbs the northern slope in a long series of bends. It was a part of the 2012 Olympic cycling road race, and ever since it has been busy with cyclists, especially at weekends, so ride it with respect. The road is smooth and well graded, the bends are open enough to see through, and the view from the top car park over the Weald is wide and calm. It is a good road to ride slowly and well, and it rewards a smooth line more than speed.

The café at the top has been a meeting place for bikers for decades, and on Sunday mornings dozens of machines line up there, from vintage Triumphs to modern sports bikes. It is a good place to look at other people's bikes, drink tea and trade stories. Police patrols and speed checks are common, and noise complaints from residents have led to a firmer line on loud exhausts, so keep it civil. Wet leaves in autumn can make the bends greasy.

Dorking, about three kilometres away, has fuel stations, supermarkets and pubs, and Great Bookham has a few more. If you want a quiet visit, come on a weekday or at dawn, when the mist lies in the valley below and the box trees smell sharp and green. Put your bike on its stand, walk a few hundred yards on the path along the ridge, and you will feel a long way from London.
Ewell does not look like a place with a deep past, but it has one. Beneath the suburban streets, springs rise from the foot of the North Downs and feed the Hogsmill river, and the village that grew around them was already old when the Romans built a road past it. The old centre has a pond, a church tower and a few Georgian houses, and Bourne Hall, an unusual 1970s building, now serves as a library and museum. Cheam, next door, has its own long history, including a school that once educated royal princes.

Between the two lies Nonsuch Park, a large stretch of open parkland that was once the site of one of the strangest buildings in Tudor England. Henry VIII began a palace here in 1538, to be so splendid that no other could match it, which is where its name comes from. It was pulled down in the seventeenth century, and today only the foundations remain, but the park is a good place for a walk and a rest, with big old trees and open meadows.

For a rider, this is a fuel and food stop at the beginning of a day's ride, and it does the job without ceremony. The roads around are busy suburban routes, with traffic lights, bus lanes and the usual speed cameras, so leave early and avoid the rush. Ewell has about forty thousand people and Cheam about eleven thousand, so stations, supermarkets and cafés are plentiful, and many open early. A coffee and a pastry in the village are a fine way to wake up before heading south.

From here, the route usually drops south onto the Downs, where the roads begin to climb and wind, and the Surrey Hills open out around Epsom, Walton on the Hill and Headley. The change is fast: in ten minutes you go from semi-detached streets to chalk slopes, beech woods and open views. Early autumn mornings, when mist lies in the valleys, are especially lovely. Be gentle on the first few bends, because leaf litter and damp patches can be slippery in the shade.
t.new forest and solent easy ride high poi:
There is a long way to go before this is mountain country. The land here, around Cobham in Surrey, is gently rolling, a mix of sandy heath, pine woods and the wooded valley of the River Mole, and the high point is only a modest rise above the surrounding fields. What it offers is something different, a pleasant, green landscape of big gardens, commons and country lanes, so close to London that it is easy to forget the city is there.

The district has a good deal of history and some surprises. Cobham is home to Painshill Park, an eighteenth-century landscape garden with a lake, a Gothic temple and a crystal grotto, designed by Charles Hamilton and restored in recent decades. Just to the south, Bookham Common is a large area of oak woodland and scrub, managed by the National Trust, where nightingales sing in spring. The Mole winds through water meadows, and the old mill at Cobham still stands beside the river.

The riding is relaxed and varied. The lanes between Cobham, Stoke d'Abernon and Great Bookham are narrow, with bends and dips, and there are stretches of pleasing, fast road across the open heath. Traffic is a problem, because the area is close to the M25 and a favourite of commuters, so a weekend morning or midweek ride is best. In autumn, the woods turn gold and the lanes fill with leaves, which are slippery, and in winter frost often lingers in the shade.

Cobham has about sixteen thousand people, so there are stations, shops and cafés in the village and along the main road, and Great Bookham has about eleven thousand with a good range of services. The high street in Cobham has several pubs and cafés and a few interesting shops, and it is a pleasant place to rest. The motorway services near the junction also have fuel and food, though they are a poor substitute for the village.
t.new forest and solent easy ride scenic r:
Watford is not usually described as scenic, and the label on this stop is more of an ambition than a description. The town sits on the River Colne in Hertfordshire, just north of the M25, and the land around it is a patchwork of suburbs, parks and fragments of old countryside. Bushey, next door, was once a village favoured by artists, and the Victorian painter Hubert von Herkomer set up a famous art school there, so the town has more culture than it first appears.

What the place does offer is a gateway to better roads. North of Watford, the land begins to rise toward the Chiltern fringe, and the lanes around Bushey Heath and toward Radlett and Elstree wind through trees and fields, with a pleasing mix of open bends and short climbs. Close to the town is Leavesden, where the Harry Potter films were made, and the studio tour there draws crowds, while the football club at Vicarage Road is in the middle of town, and has a long history of its own.

The riding in the area is mostly a matter of choosing the quiet lanes. The main roads, including the A41 and the M1, are heavy with traffic, and the town centre is congested at peak times. Early mornings and Sunday afternoons are much better. Take care at the many roundabouts and watch for speed cameras, particularly on the approach roads. The Colne valley has some pleasant riverside stretches, with water meadows, lakes and woodland, and they give a green break before the next village.

Watford has more than a hundred thousand people, so petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés are everywhere, and it is the best place for fuel before heading north. Bushey has a high street with a good number of small cafés and shops, and it is easier to park a bike there than in the big town centre. After the busy roads, the first quiet lane feels like a release, and the day starts to feel like a ride rather than a commute.
t.new forest and solent easy ride photo pu:
Two very different kinds of Hertfordshire sit on either side of this spot. To the west is Wheathampstead, an old village in the valley of the River Lea, a place of flint walls, a medieval church and a handful of pubs, with a large Iron Age earthwork called Devil's Dyke running through the fields beside it. Many historians think this was the stronghold of the British chieftain Cassivellaunus, whom Julius Caesar fought in 54 BC. To the east lies Hatfield, a bigger town with a much grander house.

Hatfield House is the great Jacobean mansion built by Robert Cecil in the early seventeenth century, beside an older royal palace where the young Elizabeth I was living when she learned she had become queen in 1558. The park and gardens are open to the public, and the old brick palace beside the house is one of the few surviving Tudor royal buildings. In the twentieth century, Hatfield was also a centre of aircraft building, and the de Havilland company produced the Mosquito and the Comet jet airliner here.

The countryside between the two is a gentle chalk landscape of big arable fields and low hills, cut by the Lea and its tributaries. It is attractive but unspectacular, and the riding is relaxed, with open roads and moderate bends. The A1 and the old Great North Road are nearby and carry heavy traffic, but the smaller roads are quiet, particularly in the early morning. In summer, the fields are golden, and in winter the bare trees show the shape of the hills.

Hatfield has more than forty thousand people, so fuel, food and parking are straightforward, and it is the better choice for supplies. Wheathampstead has about four thousand people, with a small high street and a few pubs, and it is a pleasant place for a pause. If you want a quiet spot for a photograph, find a gateway on one of the lanes in the evening, when the light turns the fields warm and the shadows lengthen.
t.new@51.3,-0.2:
Ewell and Cheam are two of the old villages that London swallowed in the twentieth century, on the border between Surrey and the capital, with Nonsuch Park between them. That park holds the secret. In 1538 Henry VIII began building a palace here, meant to be so grand there would be none like it, and he named it Nonsuch. It was never finished in his lifetime and was demolished in the 1680s after Charles II gave it to a mistress who sold the materials to pay her gambling debts. The site was lost for centuries and was found again by archaeologists in the 1950s, and the park remains as a wide expanse of grass and trees, with the old mansion house of a later era at its edge.

Ewell itself is older. The Hogsmill river rises from springs in the village, and its clear water was enough to power mills for centuries. The village has a few timbered cottages and a pond, and the parish church tower is a medieval survivor. Nearby is the great racecourse on Epsom Downs, where the Derby has been run since 1780, and its grandstand is visible from the surrounding roads.

For a rider, this is the last leg. The A24 and A217 lead north through a long run of suburban streets to the city, and the lanes toward Banstead and Tadworth offer a little more interest, with brief runs of hedgerow and open downs. Crowds appear on Derby day in early June, when the roads are closed or heavily congested around the racecourse, so check first. Otherwise it is steady, calm riding with little excitement.

With forty thousand people in Ewell alone, plus Cheam and Sutton close by, everything is easy. Filling stations stand along the A240 and the Ewell bypass, and there are plenty of cafés in the village and in the big shopping streets. A bike can be parked in Nonsuch Park for a modest fee, and a short walk across the grass is a decent way to loosen up before the final push home.
t.manchester@53.5,-2.2:
Manchester invented a good part of the modern world and then spent a century being too busy to brag about it. The first passenger railway station anywhere, Liverpool Road, opened here in 1830, the Bridgewater Canal brought coal into the city, and the mills of Cottonopolis spun and wove so much cloth that the damp red-brick warehouses became the model for industrial cities from Osaka to Massachusetts. The Cooperative movement began a few miles north in Rochdale, and the splitting of the atom was first achieved at the university here. Karl Marx's friend Friedrich Engels ran a mill in the city and wrote about its slums.

It is a tough, funny, welcoming place, and the old mills along the canals now hold flats, bars and offices. The Northern Quarter has independent record shops and the kind of cafés where the barista also plays in a band. The rain is real, but the stereotype is a little unfair; a fine Sunday morning here, with sunlight on the canal basins at Castlefield, is as good as anywhere. Football is a religion, with two enormous clubs on the east and west sides, so do not talk about it unless you mean it.

For a rider, though, the point of Manchester is what lies east. Within forty minutes you can be on the Pennines. The A57 Snake Pass climbs from Glossop to about 500 metres across wild moorland and drops into the Derwent valley, and the A537 over the Cat and Fiddle is another famous, exposed road with a long record of crashes and a firm speed limit. Beyond them lie Buxton, Castleton and the Peak District, with limestone dales, reservoirs and a thousand sheep. Moorland weather changes in minutes, and ice can linger on the high roads into April, so dress for a different season than the city's.

Leaving the city takes patience, because the M60 ring road and the radial roads fill at rush hour. The sensible plan is to go early on a weekend. Fuel and food are everywhere, with filling stations on every main road and more cafés than you could try in a year. Look for secure bike parking near the centre; the city has designated motorcycle bays, and many hotels will let you leave a bike inside a gated yard.
t.bath@51.4,-2.4:
The Romans came to Bath because of the water. Hot springs rise here at roughly forty-six degrees, and the legions built a sacred pool and a bathing complex around them in the first century, dedicating the place to a local goddess whom they merged with Minerva and calling it Aquae Sulis. The great bath is still there, green and steaming, below a Victorian terrace of statues. Over a thousand years later the Georgians remade the city in pale golden stone, the architect John Wood and his son building the Circus and the sweeping Royal Crescent, so that the place looks like a stage set for a Jane Austen novel. Austen herself lived here for several years and was not entirely happy about it.

Bath sits in the steep valley of the Avon, with hills rising on all sides, and the stone itself is dug from the local limestone, which glows in low sun. Pulteney Bridge, with shops built along both sides like Florence's Ponte Vecchio, crosses the river by the weir. The city is small and very walkable, but it is a magnet for visitors, so the centre is crowded and slow most days.

As a place to ride from, it is wonderful. Within a few minutes you are out onto the Cotswold edge or south through the Limpley Stoke valley, a deep wooded gorge where the canal and the railway run beside the river. Bradford on Avon is a few miles away, with its tiny Saxon church, and beyond lie the Mendip Hills, Cheddar Gorge and the Somerset Levels. The A36 along the valley is a good road, but it is busy with lorries. The better riding is on the B-roads that climb the hills and run along the ridge tops, with lovely views down into the valley and a mix of tight bends and fast, open sections.

Traffic inside the city is a headache. The ring road is clogged at rush hour, and parking in the centre is expensive, though motorcycles are often better treated than cars. Fuel stations stand on the outskirts, around Lower Weston and along the A4, and the centre has plenty of cafés, bakeries and the famous Sally Lunn buns, which are a decent way to start a ride.
t.troutdale@45.5,-122.4:
Samuel Lancaster, the engineer who built the Historic Columbia River Highway between 1913 and 1922, wanted a road that would show off the gorge instead of conquering it, and Troutdale is where it begins. The town sits where the Sandy River meets the Columbia, on the eastern edge of the Portland area, with a tidy main street, an old railroad depot and a hotel that began life as a poor farm. For a rider the gateway is easy: you leave the suburban edges, cross the river, and within a few miles the road starts to climb.

The highway was the first planned scenic road in the country, designed with stone guardrails, arched bridges and viaducts that fit the cliffs. At Crown Point, about 700 feet above the Columbia, Vista House, an octagonal stone building from 1918, serves as an observatory and rest stop, with a view up the gorge that explains why people drive here from across the world. Beyond it, the road threads past waterfalls, among them Latourell, Bridal Veil, Wahkeena and the biggest of all, Multnomah Falls, which drops 620 feet in two tiers and attracts huge crowds. During busy seasons, access to the waterfall corridor can require timed permits, so check before you go.

The road is narrow, curvy and quite slow, with tight bends under the rock and damp patches in the shade, and the sections in the woods can be covered with moss and leaves. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends, so a weekday morning is much better. Mist and fog hang in the gorge in spring and autumn, and the wind that whips through the gorge can surprise you at exposed viewpoints. The Columbia River Gorge is a transition zone, with wet, mossy forest in the west and dry grassland in the east, and the change over a short distance is remarkable.

Troutdale has around sixteen thousand people, with fuel, cafes and bakeries, and the nearby Gresham and Portland have everything else. Pick up supplies before you go, since there are limited stops along the old road, and stop for a pastry in one of the villages. Spring, with waterfalls at full flow, and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.hood river@45.7,-121.5:
Wind is the reason Hood River became what it is. Where the Columbia River Gorge narrows between the cool, wet west and the dry eastern plateau, the air funnels through with such force that windsurfers and kiteboarders gather by the hundreds, and the town has grown into a capital of outdoor sports. On a summer afternoon the river is dotted with colourful sails, and the bridge across to Washington State hums in the wind. Behind the town, Mount Hood rises to 11,249 feet, snow-covered through most of the year, and in front of it lies a valley full of orchards.

The Hood River Valley is one of the major fruit-growing areas of the Pacific Northwest, famous for its pears and apples, and in spring the blossom covers the slopes in white. A loop of farm stands, cideries and wineries, usually called the Fruit Loop, takes you along small roads through the orchards with Mount Hood hanging over the scene. The valley has a gentle rhythm, with undulating road, small bridges, packed farm stands and signs for u-pick cherries in June. In autumn the harvest brings pumpkins and fresh cider.

The Historic Columbia River Highway ends here after climbing out of Troutdale, and some of its most beautiful stretches lie east of the town, including a section of restored road between Hood River and Mosier, with two old tunnels cut through the cliffs that now carry bikes and walkers instead of cars. For motorcycles, the better route east follows the road along the cliffs, with long views and strong winds. Take care of crosswinds, particularly on the bridge and in the open sections.

Hood River has about seven thousand people, so fuel, repairs and good food are easy. Local breweries are plentiful, and the downtown, set on a steep hill above the river, has coffee shops and bakeries. Late April has blossom, summer has the sails and the heat, and September is warm and quieter. Highway 35 runs south toward Mount Hood, with pine forest, snow-covered peaks and, in winter, ice, so check conditions.
t.chinook pass@46.9,-121.5:
At 1,656 metres, Chinook Pass is a gate into Mount Rainier country, and the mountain makes itself known well before you arrive. State Route 410 climbs from the Enumclaw plateau through dark Douglas fir and hemlock, past the little settlements of Greenwater and the access road to Crystal Mountain, and then breaks out into subalpine meadows where the great white cone appears over the shoulder of the road. Rainier stands 14,410 feet, and on a clear morning it looks close enough to touch.

The pass was a trade and travel route long before cars, used by Native peoples crossing the Cascades between the coast and the interior, and the modern road was carved out in the 1930s. At the summit the Pacific Crest Trail crosses over the highway on a planted land bridge, so you may see backpackers in the middle of their months-long walk from Mexico to Canada, blinking at the traffic. Tipsoo Lake, just beside the road, is a small, still tarn framed by firs and flowers, and has the best easy photograph of the whole crossing.

The riding is lovely, with long, easy bends rather than hairpins, wide enough for a relaxed rhythm and with a smooth surface. Weather swings fast. A sunny afternoon in Enumclaw can turn to cold drizzle at the pass, and in spring and autumn snow comes down onto the tarmac. The road is shut in winter once snow builds up, usually from late autumn until late spring, so check the state transport page before planning. Late July to September is the safe window, and early autumn adds red huckleberry and mountain ash on the slopes.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. Nothing on the pass sells it, and the last dependable stations are in Enumclaw to the west or in Naches and Yakima to the east. Bring water, expect cool air, and treat the summit as the place to pull over and listen. You will hear marmots whistle among the rocks, and ravens, and perhaps nothing at all.
t.victoria@48.4,-123.4:
Victoria sits at the southern tip of Vancouver Island, the capital of British Columbia and the very British city that nobody expects on the Pacific coast. The Inner Harbour is the center of it, with the Parliament Buildings outlined in lights at night and the grand old Fairmont Empress hotel facing across the water, and ferries, seaplanes and little harbor taxis crowd the dock. The Hudson's Bay Company built a fort here in 1843, and the town grew from it, with a Chinatown that is among the oldest in Canada.

The weather is mild, the mildest in Canada, with flowers blooming early in the year and Beacon Hill Park a mass of color in spring. The city is known for afternoon tea, pubs, bookshops and a gentle pace of life, and it has a lively, walkable downtown. Mile Zero of the Trans-Canada Highway lies at the edge of the park, where the road begins its long way east across the country. Butchart Gardens, a spectacular garden in a former quarry, is a short drive north.

The Pacific Marine Circle Route starts here. The loop follows Highway 14 west through Sooke, along a coast of rocky coves and driftwood beaches, to Port Renfrew, then crosses the island through Lake Cowichan and returns south on the Trans-Canada over the Malahat, a steep, winding highway with big views over Saanich Inlet. Along the way, the forest is huge, with old cedar and Douglas fir, and the rain, when it comes, is persistent. The roads have gentle curves with some tight bends, and the surface is generally good, though logging trucks and tourist traffic are common.

Victoria has all the services: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, though downtown parking is tight. The ferry terminal at Swartz Bay, about thirty kilometers north, links to the mainland. The best months are June to September, with dry, mild weather, though fog on the coast is common in summer mornings. Winter is wet and gray, and the west coast road can be slick with rain and fallen needles. Watch for deer, which are bold and plentiful here, and for cyclists on the narrow shoulders.
t.buxton@53.3,-1.9:
Buxton is England's highest market town, give or take a rival's claim, perched at about three hundred meters in the hills of the Peak District, and it has the cool, brisk air to prove it. The Romans knew the place for its warm spring, which rises from deep in the limestone at a constant temperature of about twenty-eight degrees, and named it Aquae Arnemetiae. In the eighteenth century the Duke of Devonshire turned it into a fashionable spa, building the great Crescent in the 1780s, a curved Georgian terrace modeled on Bath.

The town is full of well-kept Georgian and Victorian architecture. The Opera House, a gilded theater from 1903 by Frank Matcham, hosts an annual festival, and the Pavilion Gardens, with their glass pavilion, make a pleasant park. St Ann's Well, a public fountain outside the Crescent, lets you fill a bottle with the warm, soft spring water, and Buxton Water is bottled and sold across the country.

For motorcyclists, Buxton has a mixed reputation, because it is the gateway to some famous, and notorious, roads. The A537 over the Cat and Fiddle, a high moorland road toward Macclesfield, is a fast and exciting run with sweeping bends and big views, but it has a long history of accidents and is heavily policed, with reduced limits and cameras. The A515 and A53 lead through limestone dales and over open moor, with stone walls, sheep and sudden views, and the White Peak lanes are narrower and quieter. The weather is the issue: Buxton is damp, misty and cold even in summer, and the moors are exposed.

Buxton has fuel, supermarkets, pubs and cafes, and it is a convenient stop. Chapel-en-le-Frith, nearby, has more. The best months are May to September, though morning fog and sudden rain are common, and winter ice on the moor roads can be dangerous. Weekends are busy with bikers, cyclists and walkers, so weekdays are quieter.
t.pickering@54.3,-0.8:
Pickering lies at the southern edge of the North York Moors, and it is the town where the moor begins. A castle of Norman origin stands on a mound above the market place, with a ruined keep and walls that once held kings, and in the parish church, medieval wall paintings of saints and scenes from the Bible, found again under whitewash in the nineteenth century, cover the nave. The streets are lined with warm honey-colored stone, and the market, held weekly, has been going for centuries.

The North Yorkshire Moors Railway, a heritage steam line, runs from Pickering through the moor to Whitby, via Goathland, and the station, with its old signs and gas lamps, is a favorite for photographers. The line was built by George Stephenson in the 1830s, and on summer days the whistles of steam locomotives echo along the valley. Thornton Dale, a village a few miles east, is often called the prettiest in Yorkshire, with a stream running through, thatched cottages and flower beds.

The A169 north from Pickering is the classic road onto the moors, and a good ride. It climbs steeply out of the town, past the great hollow of the Hole of Horcum, a huge natural amphitheater said in legend to have been scooped out by the giant Wade, then runs across high, open moorland with heather, sheep and views toward the golf-ball domes of Fylingdales radar station, before dropping to Whitby on the coast. Bends are open and moderate, and the surface is generally good, but the moor is exposed, with strong winds and sudden fog. In August the heather blooms purple.

Pickering has fuel, supermarkets, pubs, cafes and hotels, and it is the best base for the southern moors. Kirkbymoorside, to the west, has a market too. The best months are May to September, with August for heather, though the moor weather can turn cold and wet at any time. Winter snow can close the high road. Sheep wander across the road, so keep your speed in check, and give walkers and cyclists room on the lanes.
t.cheltenham@51.9,-2.1:
Cheltenham is a spa town of the Regency age, all pale stucco, iron balconies and tree-lined avenues, and it wears its elegance lightly. A mineral spring was found here in the early eighteenth century, and when King George III visited in 1788 the town became fashionable overnight, with grand terraces and a promenade lined with trees built to match. The Pittville Pump Room, a Greek-style building of 1830, still offers a glass of the water for the brave.

The town's best-known event is the Cheltenham Festival, four days of horse racing in March at Prestbury Park, with the Gold Cup the highlight, drawing crowds from across the country and, especially, Ireland. The composer Gustav Holst, who wrote The Planets, was born here in 1874, and his birthplace is a small museum. Edward Wilson, who died with Captain Scott on the return from the South Pole, also came from Cheltenham. The government's communications headquarters, GCHQ, sits in a ring-shaped building on the edge of town, a secretive presence.

For riders, Cheltenham is the western gateway to the Cotswolds, the limestone hills that rise abruptly to the east in an escarpment. The roads climb from the town to Cleeve Hill, the highest point of the Cotswolds at about 330 meters, with views across the Severn Vale toward Wales. Beyond, narrow lanes wander through honey-colored villages such as Winchcombe, Stanway and Broadway, past stone walls, sheep pastures and manor houses. The surface is generally good, but the lanes are narrow and busy with tourists, cyclists and tractors, so patience is essential, and summer weekends are slow.

Cheltenham has every service, with fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, though town traffic can be heavy at rush hour. Charlton Kings and Shurdington, nearby, are smaller. The best months are May and September, with warm days and fewer crowds, and October brings golden foliage on the beech woods. Winter is damp and cold, with the odd frost on the hill roads. Watch for horse boxes and farm vehicles in the lanes.
t.caernarfon@53.1,-4.3:
The first thing you see in Caernarfon is the castle, and it is meant to be. Edward I began building it in 1283 after conquering the Welsh princes, and he designed it to impress as well as to defend, with polygonal towers and bands of different coloured stone in imitation of the walls of Constantinople. It was the seat of English power in north Wales, and in 1284 Edward's son, later Edward II, was born here and became the first English Prince of Wales, a title since given to the heir to the throne. The castle, along with Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the sheer scale of it, rising above the Menai Strait, is staggering.

But Caernarfon is not simply a museum. It is a living Welsh town of nearly ten thousand people, where Welsh is spoken in the shops and cafés as the first language, and the atmosphere is friendly and unpretentious. The old town inside the walls has narrow lanes, pubs and small shops, and the quay on the Seiont is a pleasant place to sit. Fuel, supermarkets and anything else you need are easy to find, and the town makes a good base for exploring Snowdonia. A narrow-gauge railway, the Welsh Highland, runs from here to Porthmadog through the mountains.

The ride from Caernarfon through the Llanberis Pass is among the best in Wales. The road runs southeast along the shore of Llyn Padarn, past the old slate quarries at Llanberis, whose huge terraced steps mark the mountain across the lake, and then climbs into the pass itself, a steep-sided glacial valley with a river and walls of boulders. Snowdon, at 1,085 metres the highest peak in Wales, rises to one side. The road narrows as it climbs to Pen-y-Pass, with tight bends and rock on both sides, and it is spectacular, but it can be crowded with walkers, cyclists and cars in summer.

The weather in Snowdonia is changeable and often wet, with low cloud and sudden showers even in July, so wet-weather gear is essential. The surface can be greasy, and sheep wander across the road without warning. Early morning is the best time, when the light is clear and the traffic is thin. Have a good breakfast before you leave, and keep an eye on the clouds.
t.llanberis@53.1,-4.1:
Llanberis is the town at the foot of Snowdon, and it carries slate in its bones. Behind it, the huge terraced scar of the Dinorwic quarry climbs the mountainside in steps, a reminder that for most of the nineteenth century this was an industrial valley, with thousands of quarrymen blasting and splitting rock that roofed half of Britain. The quarry closed in 1969, and the old workshops beside Llyn Padarn are now the National Slate Museum, with working water wheels and a foundry. Inside the mountain across the lake, a vast hidden power station, Dinorwig, known as the Electric Mountain, can supply Britain's grid at short notice.

The town itself is a long, straggling street of grey stone, with outdoor shops, cafés and chip shops catering to walkers, climbers and families heading for the summit. The Snowdon Mountain Railway, a rack-and-pinion line opened in 1896, climbs from here to just below the top of Wales's highest mountain, at 1,085 metres, and in summer its little steam and diesel trains chuff past the end of the high street. On a quiet morning the lake, with the ruined tower of Dolbadarn Castle, built by Welsh princes in the thirteenth century, makes a fine photograph.

For riders, Llanberis is the starting point for the Llanberis Pass, one of the best mountain roads in Wales. The A4086 climbs east out of the town, following a glacial valley between the Glyderau and Snowdon, with rock walls rising on either side and boulders scattered across the valley floor. The road is narrow and winding, with tight corners and sheer drops in places, and the surface is generally good, but the weather is the key. Rain is common, cloud sits on the tops, and the wind can be strong. On a clear day, the views are magnificent, but even in summer, bring waterproofs. Weekends and bank holidays are very busy, with walkers' cars parked along the verges.

Nature here is Welsh mountain nature: sheep on the road, red kites in the sky, ravens on the cliffs, and a smell of wet slate and bracken. The Snowdon lily, a rare arctic-alpine plant, grows on a few high rocks. Welsh is widely spoken in the town, and you will hear it in shops and cafés.

Llanberis has what a rider needs. There are cafés, pubs and shops, and a fuel station in the valley is possible, but it is safer to fill up in Caernarfon, about ten kilometres to the west, or Bangor. Parking is available by the lake. A bacon sandwich and strong tea in a walkers' café is the right way to start the day.
t.pen y pass@53.1,-4.0:
At 359 metres, Pen-y-Pass is not high by any alpine standard, but it is the highest point on the A4086, and it feels like the doorway to something big. The road tops out here between the shoulders of Snowdon and the Glyderau, with the cliffs of Crib Goch and Lliwedd on one side and the long glacial trough of the Llanberis Pass falling away on the other. Mist often fills the gap, and on a day of low cloud it can feel like the top of the world. When the sun comes out, the contrast is astonishing, with the green valley stretching down to the lakes.

It is also the starting point for the best-known paths up Snowdon. The Pyg Track and the Miners' Track both begin here, and on a summer morning the car park, one of the most expensive and crowded in Wales, fills before eight. The old Gorphwysfa Hotel, now a youth hostel, was where early climbers gathered at the end of the nineteenth century, and nearby, the Pen-y-Gwryd Hotel was where the 1953 Everest expedition team trained before their successful ascent. Their signatures are still on the ceiling of the bar.

The ride up from Llanberis is a sequence of tight bends and sheer rock, with the road narrowing in places to barely two cars wide. The surface is good, but there are cattle grids, sheep, cyclists and walkers' cars stopping suddenly, so it is no place for speed. On the east side, the road drops toward Capel Curig past the Pen-y-Gwryd hotel, and from here you can continue along the A5 or turn south through Beddgelert. Weather is important. Cloud can fall quickly, and winter ice is a real risk, so check conditions before you set out.

The mountains above hold plenty of natural interest. Cwm Glas, a hanging valley, has some of the best examples of glacial features in Britain, and the rocks are rich in fossils. Alpine plants cling to the high crags, and choughs, the red-legged crows, nest on the cliffs.

Parking at the pass is limited, and a park-and-ride bus runs from Nant Peris in summer to relieve the crowding, so a bike makes things easier. Fuel is not available here. Llanberis, about six kilometres down the hill, has services of a sort, and Bangor, a bigger town, is further away, so keep an eye on the tank. The café at the pass is handy for tea and a bacon roll in season.
t.beddgelert@53.0,-4.1:
Beddgelert is a village of grey stone cottages at the meeting of two rivers, the Glaslyn and the Colwyn, surrounded by steep green mountains, and it is famous for a dog. The legend says that Llywelyn the Great, a thirteenth-century Welsh prince, left his baby son in the care of his hound Gelert, and returned to find the cradle overturned, the dog covered in blood and the child nowhere to be seen. Believing the dog had killed him, he drew his sword, and only after the dog was dead did he hear the baby crying and find a dead wolf nearby. He is said to have buried Gelert with great sorrow, and the village's name means Gelert's grave.

The story is almost certainly a later invention, probably popularised in the eighteenth century by a local innkeeper who wanted to attract visitors, which, if true, is a good piece of marketing. Still, a stone marks the supposed grave, in a meadow beside the river, and it is a pleasant ten-minute walk. The village itself has a tidy stone bridge, tea rooms, outdoor shops and pubs, and it fills with hikers on summer weekends. Walks start from the village up Snowdon and into the Aberglaslyn Pass, a rocky gorge just south of the village where the river tumbles over boulders.

The ride that ends here, from Llanberis over Pen-y-Pass, follows the A498 down through the Nantgwynant valley, past the lakes of Llyn Gwynant and Llyn Dinas, with Snowdon's flanks above you. The road is good, with gentle bends and wonderful views, and it descends gradually into the village. The Welsh Highland Railway also runs to Beddgelert, and a steam train puffing through the valley is a fine sight. The Sygun Copper Mine, a Victorian copper mine now open to visitors, lies a short distance away.

Parking in the village is limited and fills quickly in summer, so arrive early. Rain is frequent, and the damp air smells of bracken and wet slate. After a long ride, a pot of tea and a slice of bara brith, Welsh fruit bread, by the river is a pleasure.
t.tintagel@50.7,-4.7:
Tintagel has been selling King Arthur for a long time. The twelfth-century writer Geoffrey of Monmouth first placed Arthur's conception here, in his History of the Kings of Britain, and the legend grew from there, helped by a Victorian love of chivalry and a ruined castle on a dramatic headland. Archaeologists have since found that the site was an important trading post in the fifth and sixth centuries, when imported Mediterranean pottery and glass came in by sea, so something notable did happen here, but whether it involved a king named Arthur is another matter. Cornwall, characteristically, has chosen to believe.

The castle ruins, run by English Heritage, stand on a rocky island joined to the mainland by a narrow neck, and in 2019 a new footbridge, with a gap in the middle that gives the impression of a narrow slot between two cliffs, replaced the old stone steps. The site is dramatic: stone walls clinging to the edge of a cliff, a sea cave below known as Merlin's Cave, and the Atlantic crashing in. Up in the village, the Old Post Office, a fourteenth-century manor house with a slate roof that sags with age, is cared for by the National Trust, and the street is lined with shops selling swords, crystals and mead, in a cheerfully kitsch way.

Riding here means the A39, known as the Atlantic Highway, which runs along the north Cornish coast. It is more of a cruise than a thrill. The road is generally good, with long straights and gentle bends over open moorland, but it can be slow, with caravans, tractors and holiday traffic in summer. The better sport is on the lanes, which are narrow, hedged and winding, with blind corners and a good deal of mud and gravel, so approach with caution. The weather here is Atlantic: wind, mist and sudden rain can arrive at any time of year, but a clear evening on the cliffs is one of the glories of Cornwall.

Nearby, the slate quarry at Delabole has been worked for six hundred years and is among the largest in England, and next to it stands one of Britain's first onshore wind farms, from 1991. The coast is a protected landscape, with sea cliffs, wild flowers and seabirds such as fulmars, kittiwakes and choughs, which are Cornwall's emblem.

Tintagel village has pubs, tearooms and pasty shops, a few small hotels, and a car park near the castle. For fuel, Wadebridge, about seventeen kilometres to the south, is the best option, though there is a small garage at Camelford, near the main road, so plan your fill-up. A hot pasty eaten on the cliffs, preferably out of the wind, is the traditional pleasure.
t.padstow@50.5,-4.9:
Padstow has two reputations, and they get along rather well: it is an old working fishing port on the Camel estuary, and it is the town that Rick Stein turned into a food destination. His seafood restaurant opened in the 1970s and drew so many diners that the place became known to locals, half in jest, as Padstein. Today the harbour is packed with restaurants, delis, bakeries and pasty shops, and on a summer day the quay is a crowd of holidaymakers eating crab sandwiches and ice cream in the sun, while the gulls plot the theft of their chips.

Beneath the polish, the town has a deeper tradition. On May Day, Padstow hosts the 'Obby 'Oss festival, an ancient ritual in which two dancers in black or red costumes and huge hooped masks whirl through the streets accompanied by drums, accordions and singing. It is one of the oldest surviving folk customs in Britain, and its origin is lost in time. The town fills with people, and the streets hum with music from dawn until dusk.

The Camel Trail, an old railway line converted into a path for walkers and cyclists, runs from here upriver to Wadebridge and beyond, past mudflats, salt marsh and woods. Across the estuary, the village of Rock is linked by a small passenger ferry, and the sand dunes and the deceptive Doom Bar sandbank at the river mouth, named after the many ships it has wrecked, have given the name to a famous local beer.

For riders, the approach is along the A389 from Wadebridge or from the A39 on the coast, and the road is not particularly demanding, though in summer it is slow with holiday traffic. The streets of Padstow itself are narrow and crowded, with parking difficult, so the best option is to leave the bike in the large car park at the edge of town and walk. Spring and autumn are the best times, with fewer people and good light, though wind and rain are possible at any time. In winter the town is quiet, and some restaurants close.

The coast beyond is a delight, with sandy beaches, such as Harlyn Bay and Trevone, and cliff paths where thrift and sea campion bloom in spring. Fuel is not sold in the middle of town, so Wadebridge, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest big settlement, with stations and supermarkets. A proper Cornish pasty, with beef, potato, swede and onion, crimped at the side, is the lunch to look for, though fish and chips on the quay is hard to resist.
t.eskdale@54.4,-3.3:
Eskdale is the quiet, long valley on the western edge of the Lake District, running from the high fells down to the Irish Sea, and it is the sort of place where the road narrows, the sheep multiply and the mountains seem to lean in. At the top end stand the peaks of the Scafell range, including Scafell Pike at 978 metres, the highest in England, and below them the green valley floor is dotted with stone farms, drystone walls and small woods. The hamlet of Boot has a pub, a watermill and a station, and the setting is extraordinarily pretty.

The station belongs to the Ravenglass and Eskdale Railway, a fifteen-inch gauge steam line known affectionately as La'al Ratty, which runs for about eleven kilometres from the coast at Ravenglass up the valley to Dalegarth. It was built in the 1870s to carry iron ore and later converted to carry passengers, and today the little locomotives pull open carriages through woods and fields. Riding beside the track with a train chuffing alongside is a nice experience. Ravenglass has a Roman bath house and Muncaster Castle, with its owl centre and gardens, near the coast.

The real draw for motorcyclists is what lies to the east. The road climbs out of Eskdale over the Hardknott Pass, one of the steepest roads in England, with a gradient signed at one in three on its tightest hairpins. The road is narrow, single-track in places, with passing bays, and it requires a steady hand and a clear head. At the top, at about 390 metres, the remains of a Roman fort, Mediobogdum, stand on a ledge with a view across the valley, built in the second century to guard the route to the coast. Beyond, the road continues over the Wrynose Pass to Little Langdale.

Fuel is not available in Eskdale, and the nearest options are Egremont, seventeen kilometres away, and Seascale, so arrive with a full tank. The passes can be dangerous in ice, snow or heavy rain, and they are frequently closed in winter. Come in late spring or early autumn, early in the day, to avoid the crowds. Wear a layer even in summer, because the weather here changes fast and cloud can drop onto the road. The silence at the top, with only wind and sheep, is something to remember.
t.hardknott pass@54.4,-3.2:
Hardknott Pass has a reputation among British riders that is partly earned and partly exaggerated, but the earned part is considerable. The road climbs from the Eskdale side in a series of short, sharp hairpins with gradients of up to one in three, among the steepest on any public road in England, and the surface is narrow, rough and often slick, with no barriers on the outside of the bends. At the summit, 393 metres above sea level, the road crosses a high saddle between the valleys of the Esk and the Duddon, and then drops again, nearly as steeply, to Cockley Beck. Take it slowly, in first gear, with both hands on the bars and a good look ahead.

Beyond the challenge, the pass has a fascinating history. Just below the summit on the Eskdale side stand the remains of Hardknott Roman Fort, called Mediobogdum by the Romans, built in the second century to guard the road from Ravenglass on the coast to Ambleside. The fort commanded one of the loneliest postings in the empire, and on a clear day you can walk around the foundations of the granary, the commander's house and the bath house, with a spectacular view to the Scafell range. It is easy to imagine a legionary from the Mediterranean, standing here in the rain, wondering what he had done wrong.

The Lake District here is at its roughest and most remote. Bare crags, bracken and heather cover the slopes, and the lakes are far below, out of sight. Herdwick sheep, the tough, grey-faced breed of the Lakes, graze the hillsides and wander across the road without concern. The weather matters: low cloud and mist can reduce visibility to a few metres, rain makes the surface treacherous, and in winter, ice and snow close the road. It is best done in dry, clear conditions, in spring or early autumn, and many riders prefer to approach from the west, climbing the steeper hairpins rather than descending them, though opinions vary.

There are no facilities on the pass. Fuel is available in Ambleside, about twenty kilometres to the east, and at villages on the coast such as Seascale, and the Woolpack Inn at Eskdale and the café at Boot may serve food, though opening hours vary. Carry a warm layer and a drink, and make sure your clutch and brakes are in good order before you go. The pass is not for large vehicles or caravans, and drivers who ignore the warnings often cause long delays, so be prepared to wait.
t.wrynose pass@54.4,-3.1:
If Hardknott is the show-off, Wrynose is its older, grumpier sibling. The two passes are usually ridden together, linking Ambleside and Langdale in the east with Eskdale and the Cumbrian coast in the west, but Wrynose comes first for those heading from the east, and it sets the tone. The road is single-track for much of its length, narrow, with passing places, rough edges and a gradient of one in four on some of the hairpins. At the top, at about 393 metres, there is a bare saddle of grass and boulders, and a modest stone marker in the road called the Three Shire Stone.

The stone stands where three old counties met, Cumberland, Westmorland and Lancashire, and it has stood here since 1816. Today all three lie inside the modern county of Cumbria, but the stone remains, and children like to stand with one foot in each former county. The high ground around is known as Wrynose Bottom, and there is a ford where the River Duddon rises, a short walk away. Fell ponies and sheep graze freely, and they pay little attention to bikes.

The ride from Little Langdale is a fine one, climbing through stone-walled fields, past slate quarries and then onto open fell. The road is narrow and the surface variable, with loose gravel at the sides and potholes after winter, and visibility around the bends is poor, so ride within your limits and be ready to stop. Cars and walkers come in the other direction, and in summer, the pass can be busy with coaches and cyclists, though the road is not suitable for large vehicles. Cloud is common, and rain makes the rock slippery. The best times are a dry spring day or an autumn morning, when the bracken is bronze and the air is clear.

Wrynose Pass is beautiful in an austere way, and it gives access to some of the great walks of the Lake District, including the climb of Pike of Blisco. In the valleys, you pass dry-stone walls, small farms and old slate workings, a reminder that this was industrial country as well as pastoral. The Duddon Valley, which Wordsworth wrote sonnets about, runs from the foot of the pass.

Windermere, about fourteen kilometres away, and Ambleside, a little nearer, have fuel stations and cafés. Check your fuel and carry water. If you plan to ride both Wrynose and Hardknott in one go, allow plenty of time and expect delays.
t.little langdale@54.4,-3.0:
Little Langdale is a small, secretive valley in the central Lake District, with a hamlet of slate-roofed farms, a tarn and a stream, and it feels as if the rest of the world had been forgotten. The valley lies at the foot of the Wrynose Pass, and the road you ride in on climbs from the head of the valley to the pass, past a stone known as the Three Shires Stone, where the old counties of Cumberland, Westmorland and Lancashire once met. The stone is a simple marker, but standing at a point where three historic counties joined is a pleasing small thrill.

The Wrynose Pass is narrower than Hardknott, with steep gradients and tight, blind bends, and the Little Langdale side drops at around one in four. The road runs in a single track for much of its length, with passing places, and meeting a car head-on at a bend is a daily event, so use patience and good manners. The surface is generally good but can be wet and gritty, and it is not a road to rush. In winter, ice and snow can make it dangerous, and the pass is sometimes closed.

The landscape is classic Lakeland, with grey-green fells, drystone walls and Herdwick sheep, the hardy local breed with grey wool and white faces, which Beatrix Potter, a farmer as well as an author, helped to preserve. The slate that roofs the houses was quarried in the hills, and old quarries and tunnels honeycomb the area, with the remains of a few workings visible near the road. A packhorse bridge, Slater Bridge, crosses the river Brathay on a path, a graceful old structure of slabs, and it is a gentle walk from the hamlet. The Langdale Pikes rise above to the north.

A pub in the hamlet serves food and local beer, popular with walkers and riders, and the garden looks over the fells. Weather can change in minutes, so carry waterproofs, and note that the roads can be slow in summer with walkers and cyclists. When you finish, the soft light on the tarn in the evening makes it hard to leave.
t.mount rainier sunrise junction@46.9,-121:
This is the place where Highway 410 and the road to Sunrise part company, and it is worth knowing about because the turning leads to the highest point you can reach by road on Mount Rainier. The junction lies near the White River entrance on the park's north-east side, in a valley of old-growth fir and cedar, with the White River running cold and milky beside the road, and the mountain hidden behind the ridges until you climb out of the trees.

The Sunrise road is a spectacular, tidy piece of mountain engineering. It climbs about fifteen miles in a series of switchbacks and gentle bends to a height of around 6,400 feet, where Rainier stands directly in front of you, 4,392 metres of ice and rock. The Emmons Glacier, the largest in the lower forty-eight by area, is spread across the mountain's north-east face. The road is generally open only from early July until September or October, and snow can fall at any time at the top. Wildflower season in late July and August brings meadows full of lupin and paintbrush, and marmots whistle from the rocks.

Highway 410 itself, the Chinook Pass Scenic Byway, is a joy. It leads south-east from Enumclaw along the Greenwater and White rivers, climbing toward Chinook Pass at 5,430 feet, with a sequence of flowing bends under big timber. The road is closed in winter, normally from about November until late May, and the pass often sees cloud and drizzle even in July. There are few places to stop or turn, so be wary of traffic behind you, and be aware of the cold wetness of the forest roads, where moss and shade keep the surface damp.

There is a park entry fee payable at the White River entrance, and a limited timed-entry system has sometimes been in place for Sunrise in recent summers, so check ahead. Enumclaw, to the west, is the last big town with petrol, and the small communities on Highway 410 have limited and sometimes seasonal supplies, so fill up before you leave. Bring warm clothing even in August, because Sunrise can feel like early spring.
t.naches@46.7,-120.7:
Naches is a very small orchard town in the Yakima valley, at the place where the Naches River comes down out of the Cascades, and it is the dry-side end of the Chinook Pass road. The change from west to east is dramatic. On the Seattle side the slopes are wrapped in dripping fir and cedar, and over the crest the forest thins into ponderosa pine and then sagebrush, with sun, orchards and irrigated fields. Naches is where the green gives way to gold.

The valley produces much of America's apple crop, and also pears, cherries, hops and wine grapes, thanks to water from the mountains and a dry, sunny climate. Fruit stands appear along the road in late summer, selling peaches, apricots and cider, and in autumn the air smells of apples and wood smoke. The cascades act as a barrier to rain, so the east side gets only a fraction of the precipitation that falls on the west. The change in climate is something you can feel in a single afternoon.

Chinook Pass Scenic Byway, State Route 410, climbs along the river and crosses the Cascade crest at about fifty-four hundred feet, running along the edge of Mount Rainier National Park. Rainier itself, at over fourteen thousand feet, dominates the western horizon, a huge, glacier-covered volcano. The road is good, with smooth bends, forest and big views, and the descent east follows the river past cliffs of basalt. The pass is closed in winter, usually from November to late May, because of heavy snow, so check conditions.

You can find basic services in Naches, though the larger town of Selah, about fifteen kilometres away, or Yakima, offers more fuel and food. Fill the tank before the climb, since stations are scarce on the pass. A roadside fruit stand is a great reward after a day's ride. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, with cold rain or even snow in summer, so bring a waterproof. In September and October, golden larch and red vine maple add colour to the slopes, and the light is warm.
t.sedro woolley@48.5,-122.2:
Sedro-Woolley is two towns that stuck together. Sedro and Woolley were separate rivals on the Skagit River until they merged in 1898, and the double-barrelled name, with its hyphen, has stayed ever since. It is a working town of about eleven thousand people on the flat, green floodplain of the Skagit valley, in north-western Washington, with farms, sawmills, a timber heritage and a loggers' festival in July. For riders it is the start of the North Cascades Highway, and the last easy place to buy supplies.
