Be gentle with the throttle through the farm country, as tractors and horses use the same roads.
t.crown point@45.5,-122.2:
Crown Point is a rock buttress rising about two hundred metres above the Columbia River, and the view from the top is among the great viewpoints of the Pacific Northwest. On the summit stands the Vista House, an octagonal stone building completed in 1918, built as a memorial to the pioneers who came west along the Oregon Trail and to serve as a rest stop for motorists. Its walls are carved stone, its dome is topped with copper, and inside there are marble floors, small exhibits and a modest cafe. From the terrace you look east along the river gorge, with the cliffs falling away on both sides and the Columbia curving into the distance.

The road that brings you here is a landmark in its own right. The Historic Columbia River Highway, built between 1913 and 1922 under the engineer Samuel Lancaster, was one of the first paved scenic roads in America and was designed to show off the gorge rather than simply cross it. Lancaster had been inspired by the mountain roads of Europe, and he built it with graceful stone bridges, masonry walls, tight bends and tunnels, taking care that the road would fit into the landscape. Parts of it were abandoned when the interstate was built along the river, and in recent decades sections have been restored, so the old road can be ridden again.

Riding it is slow and delightful. The curves are tight and well graded, the surface is generally good, and the forest closes in on either side, ferns and moss everywhere. It is a road to take at a gentle pace, with cyclists, tourists and the occasional sports car for company. In wet weather, which is common, the stone bridges and painted lines can be slippery, so ease through them. In winter ice can close the road at short notice. The famous waterfalls, Latourell, Bridal Veil and the great Multnomah Falls, are stops along the way, and the crowds at the last one can be thick on summer weekends.

Wind at Crown Point is a real force, funnelled by the gorge, and the temperature at the top is often a handful of degrees cooler than at the river. Come early or late for the best light and the fewest people. Dress for weather, and bring a lens that can capture a very wide view.
t.ruby beach@47.7,-124.4:
Ruby Beach is where the Olympic Peninsula puts its raw side on show. A short, steep trail leads down from the highway through spruce and fern to a wide shore of dark pebbles, strewn with enormous bleached driftwood logs, with tall sea stacks standing offshore and a creek spilling out across the stones. The name comes from the pinkish tint in the sand, said to be caused by tiny garnet crystals, and when the sun hits wet pebbles the colour is genuinely warm. In the distance, Destruction Island and its old lighthouse, built in the 1890s, sit on the horizon like a model.

The beach belongs to Olympic National Park, which here protects a long strip of the Pacific coast, and it is wild in the proper sense. The surf is cold and strong, the logs are heavy enough to crush a person if a wave moves them, and the tide changes fast, so you do not want to wander far along the rocks without checking the tables. Tide pools among the stacks hold starfish, anemones and crabs, and you may see bald eagles overhead and seals offshore. The smell is of salt, kelp and wet spruce.

Riding in is part of the experience. US 101 follows the coast from Forks southward, through temperate rainforest of huge moss-covered trees, and the road is well surfaced, curving gently with the land and breaking out occasionally to views of the ocean. It is among the wettest places in the continental United States, so be ready for rain at any time of year and for fog that can fall quickly. Summer is the driest and busiest season, but even then mornings can be cold and grey. Logging trucks use the road, so give them room, and watch for elk crossing in the early morning.

Forks, about twenty-seven kilometres north, is the nearest town of any size, a logging community of less than four thousand people that found new fame as the setting for a series of vampire novels. It has fuel, cafes, and motels, and you should fill up there or to the south before you come, because services along this stretch of coast are few. The Hoh Rain Forest, a short way inland, is worth the detour if you want to see ferns and moss in unlikely quantities. Bring a warm layer even in August, and boots for the stony trail.
t.horseshoe bay@49.4,-123.3:
Horseshoe Bay is the place where Vancouver stops being a city and becomes a coast. It lies at the north-west end of West Vancouver, a small harbour with a ferry terminal, a marina and a strip of seafront cafes, and the mountains of Howe Sound rise out of the water behind it. The ferries run from here to Nanaimo on Vancouver Island, to Bowen Island and to the Sunshine Coast, so the harbour has a constant rhythm of arrivals, departures, and cars lining up for the next sailing.

The Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 99, starts at Horseshoe Bay and runs north along the east shore of Howe Sound toward Squamish, Whistler and Pemberton. It was upgraded in the years before the 2010 Winter Olympics, with passing lanes, wider shoulders and safer corners, and it remains one of the finest scenic roads in Canada. From the bay, it climbs above the water in long, graceful bends, with views of the fjord, its islands and the high peaks beyond. It is easy to ride, but it demands attention, because traffic is dense, particularly on summer weekends.

Howe Sound is a fjord, a drowned glacial valley, and its steep sides drop straight into water that is very deep. The sound was badly polluted by a copper mine and a pulp mill in the twentieth century, and fish and marine life have returned in recent decades, with herring, salmon, orcas and even humpback whales being seen again. Whytecliff Park, a short ride away, is a well-known diving spot, with seals and sea stars visible in the clear water.

The village has a pleasant character, with fish and chips from the harbour stalls, coffee, bakeries and a small beach. In summer it is crowded, and the car parks fill with people waiting for ferries, so take care when manoeuvring a bike around queues of cars. Parking for motorcycles is usually easier than for cars, but be wary of loose gravel and spilt oil near the terminal. Wind can come off the water and the weather turns rainy from late autumn to early spring, so a waterproof layer is a good idea.

Fuel is plentiful, with several stations in West Vancouver, and it is wise to top up here before heading north, since the stations along the highway are fewer. The best time to ride is early on a weekday morning, before the commuter and ferry traffic builds, or in the shoulder seasons of May and September, when the air is clear and the mountains are sharp.
t.porteau cove@49.6,-123.2:
Porteau Cove is a small provincial park on the edge of Howe Sound, where the railway and the highway squeeze together along the shore and the fjord stretches out toward the mountains. A pier extends into the water, a beach of pebbles and driftwood curves around the cove, and across the sound the peaks rise steeply, with cloud lying in the valleys. It is one of the best places on the highway to stop, and the pull-out is quick and easy.

The park is well known to scuba divers, because several old vessels were sunk here deliberately to create artificial reefs, and they have become homes for anemones, rockfish, crabs and the occasional giant Pacific octopus. The cold, clear water gives good visibility in winter, and on a calm day you may see divers in drysuits preparing to descend. For non-divers, the pier is a good place to watch the activity, and a short walk along the beach gives a view of the railway, where freight trains run along the shore and tourist trains pass in summer.

The railway is part of the story. It was built in the early twentieth century to link Vancouver to the interior, and its route along the shore of the sound, under cliffs and across bridges, was an engineering challenge. Along the road, the Britannia Mine Museum at Britannia Beach, a former copper mine, tells the story of the industry that dominated this stretch of coast, and Shannon Falls near Squamish drops over a high cliff beside the road. A great granite dome, the Stawamus Chief, towers above Squamish, and rock climbers can be seen on its face.

The riding on this stretch of the Sea-to-Sky is a delight, with wide, sweeping bends, the sound glinting below and the mountains close. The surface is excellent and the road has several passing lanes, though it can be congested on summer weekends, and police enforce the speed limits. Fog and low cloud can drift down and reduce visibility, and in winter the road is wet or icy in places. Aim for morning, when the light is soft and the traffic light, and watch for pedestrians crossing at the cove.

The park has a campground, and day use is charged in the busy season. Lions Bay, a small village about twelve kilometres south, has limited services, and Squamish, seventeen kilometres to the north, has stations, restaurants and supermarkets. Pack a thermos or buy a coffee on the way, and take a few minutes at the end of the pier to watch the water.
t.multnomah falls@45.6,-122.1:
You hear Multnomah Falls before the trees give it up, and then it is simply there: a thin white thread dropping 620 feet in two tiers off a basalt wall, with a little stone footbridge hung across the gap between them. It is the tallest waterfall in Oregon, and the car park behind it is built to match. This is not a place you have to yourself. Come on a weekday morning, outside high summer, and it feels almost private; arrive on a sunny Saturday and you will be circling for a space beside half of Portland. The stone lodge at the foot, built in the 1920s, serves meals and is a decent spot to warm up on a wet day.

The Historic Columbia River Highway is the reason a motorcyclist is here at all. Samuel Lancaster laid it out in the 1910s as a deliberate work of art, with masonry viaducts, tunnels, curved guard walls and bridges in the Roman style, because he wanted a road that belonged in the gorge instead of scarring it. Much of it was later bypassed by the interstate, which is a gift: the old alignment is slow, curling, and lined with moss-draped maple and Douglas fir, and the bits that survive are a pleasure on two wheels. Go gently on the old surfaces, which can be damp, leaf-slicked and patched, and watch for cyclists and walkers. Vista House on Crown Point, a few miles west, is worth a stop for the view up the gorge.

The falls themselves are fed by springs and snowmelt from the slopes of Larch Mountain, and the spray keeps everything around the base unreasonably green. A paved trail zigzags up to the bridge, steep enough to make you aware of motorcycle boots but short. The gorge is also famous for wind, funnelling between the Cascades, so a calm morning at the bottom does not guarantee a calm ride along the cliff-edge sections.

The falls sit right beside Interstate 84, which is how most people actually reach them, and in recent summers there has sometimes been a timed-entry system for the access road, so check before you commit. For fuel, Troutdale to the west and Cascade Locks to the east are the closest towns that sell it. Hood River, further east, is the one for a proper lunch and a brewery.
t.glacier washington@48.9,-121.9:
Glacier, Washington, is more a crossroads than a town: a handful of buildings, a general store, a ranger station and a bridge, in a damp green valley where the pavement turns decisively toward the mountains. It is the last place of any kind on the Mount Baker Highway, which is why riders pause here. After this the road climbs for about twenty kilometres through old forest to the foot of a volcano, and nothing along the way is going to sell you a sandwich.

The highway follows the North Fork of the Nooksack River, which is a milky, glacier-fed colour for much of the year, and the first miles are a gentle ride through second-growth forest with the river in view. Nooksack Falls, a short way east, drops into a gorge beside the road, and you can look down from a fenced viewpoint. Beyond that the forest gets bigger, the moss gets thicker and the road starts to climb with a sequence of rolling bends that suit a relaxed pace. This is some of the wettest country in the lower forty-eight, so rain gear is not optional, and mist and cloud can erase the volcano completely.

The name belongs to the mountain's ice. Glacier is the old gateway to Mount Baker and Mount Shuksan, and the hamlet grew up to serve miners and loggers before it served hikers and skiers. The Mount Baker ski area up the road holds the world record for snowfall in a single season, 1,140 inches in 1998 and 1999, which is a fact that comes up quickly when you ask the locals about winter. In practice the upper part of the road is closed with snow for many months, and the final stretch to Artist Point usually opens only in July.

For practicalities, Glacier has a small shop, and I would not assume it has fuel at every hour. Plan to fill the tank at Bellingham or at the small towns of the Nooksack valley before you start east. The ride back down is easy enough for a tired rider, and the evening light along the river is excellent, with mist rising off the trees and the smell of wet cedar everywhere.
t.heather meadows@48.9,-121.7:
The Mount Baker Highway ends in a small paradise of lakes, ridges and tilted meadows, and Heather Meadows is the part where the road gives up and the walking begins. You are at about 1,300 metres, which does not sound high until you realise how much of the scene is made of snow: Mount Shuksan is a great jagged pyramid straight ahead, Mount Baker is a white whale to the side, and pocket lakes flash in the hollows between. Picture Lake, with Shuksan reflected in it on a still morning, is one of the most photographed views in the state.

The road up from Glacier is a lovely climb, especially in the last ten kilometres, where the trees give way to subalpine fir, the bends tighten, and the walls on the uphill side get taller. Expect cool, damp air and frequent changes of weather. The road is kept open for the ski area in winter, though ice and storms can shut it, and the final stretch to Artist Point only opens when the snow clears, usually in July. In August the meadows are full of heather and lupin and the berries ripen, and in autumn the huckleberries and blueberries redden the slopes.

The ski area here is where the 1998-99 snowfall record, 1,140 inches, was recorded, which tells you everything about the climate. The wet Pacific air hits the volcano and dumps in vast amounts of snow, so even in early summer you may find walls of old drift beside the road. Ancient volcanic and glacial activity shaped everything in sight, and Baker itself is an active volcano, though quiet for now. Marmots whistle among the rocks, and black bears feed on berries in late summer, so keep food secure and give them space.

Glacier is about 25 kilometres back and has little; Bellingham is the sensible refuelling stop, and Chilliwack in Canada is the other nearest sizeable town. The parking area has toilets and trailheads, a short easy walk gets you to viewpoints, and a Northwest Forest Pass may be needed for parking. Bring a warm layer even in August.
t.hood river food@45.7,-121.5:
Hood River is where the Columbia Gorge turns into a playground. The town sits on the Oregon bank of the Columbia River, about ninety kilometres east of Portland, at the point where the river squeezes between high basalt walls and the wind funnels through with almost reliable force. That wind made Hood River one of the windsurfing and kiteboarding capitals of the world, and from summer afternoons through early autumn the water is dotted with colourful sails. Across the river, the Washington side climbs into green hills, and on a clear day the white cone of Mount Hood rises to the south over the orchards.

The valley behind the town is also fruit country. Pears, apples and cherries grow in the volcanic soil, and in spring the blossom is a sight, while roadside stands in late summer sell fruit, cider and jam. A loop of farm roads known locally as the Fruit Loop links orchards, tasting rooms and a lavender farm, and it is a pleasant ride for a relaxed afternoon. The surfaces are good, the bends gentle, and the traffic light outside the weekend.

Downtown, the streets slope toward the river, with a mix of old brick buildings and more recent cafés, shops and breweries. It has a young, outdoorsy feel, with cyclists and kiteboarders in the cafés and a good selection of food. Fresh salmon, local cheese and fruit pies are easy to find, and the breweries, many of which have outdoor tables, serve a variety of beers with burgers and pizza. If you are riding, one pint is about the limit, and a coffee afterwards is wiser.

The Historic Columbia River Highway, an early scenic road built in the 1910s with stone bridges and viaducts, passes close by, and parts of it are open to traffic, offering a slower and prettier alternative to the interstate. Waterfalls, including the famous Multnomah Falls, lie to the west along it.

Fuel is easy, with stations along the main road, and the town has about seven and a half thousand people. Parking for motorcycles is available near the waterfront, but weekends and summer are busy. Across the bridge to White Salmon, a small toll applies, so keep some change handy.

Expect wind. A gust off the river can push a bike sideways on the bridge or on exposed stretches of the interstate, so grip the bars and lean into it. The best time is early morning or evening, when the wind drops and the light is gentle on the cliffs.
t.mount hood timberline@45.3,-121.7:
Mount Hood is Oregon's highest peak at 3,426 metres, a glaciated volcano that can be seen from Portland on a clear day, and the road to Timberline Lodge takes you right up onto its flank. The lodge sits at about 1,800 metres, above the treeline, where the forest gives way to open slopes of ash and snow, and it is a remarkable building. It was constructed in the 1930s as a Works Progress Administration project during the Depression, with local craftsmen carving the timbers, forging the ironwork and weaving the rugs, and President Franklin Roosevelt dedicated it in 1937. Its exterior was later used in the film The Shining, which is why you will see visitors taking photographs of the front door with slightly worried expressions.

The ride up starts at Government Camp, a small ski village on US 26, and follows a spur road of several kilometres that climbs through noble fir and mountain hemlock. The road is paved and well maintained, with moderate bends and good views opening as the trees thin. Snow can fall early and linger late, so the road may be closed or require chains in winter, and even in summer fog can fill the upper slopes. Expect temperatures far cooler than in the valley, and wind that cuts straight through a mesh jacket.

Skiing continues at Timberline long after most resorts have closed, thanks to the Palmer snowfield, and you may see skiers carrying their gear across snow in July. The mountain's glaciers are shrinking, but the upper slopes are still white, and the contrast with the green forest below is striking. In summer, wildflowers bloom in the meadows, and hikers follow the Timberline Trail around the mountain. The old Barlow Road, the last stage of the Oregon Trail, passed nearby, and pioneers hauled their wagons over these slopes in the 1840s.

Mount Hood Village, about twenty kilometres away, and Sandy lower down are the places to fill up, and Government Camp has limited services. The lodge has restaurants and a café where you can warm up with a hot drink, though it can be crowded in peak season. Bring layers, gloves and a rain shell, even on a bright day.

The view from the terrace, with the cone of the mountain above and the forested ridges falling away below, is worth the ride. Late afternoon light is lovely, and the air is thin and clean.
t.sandy@45.4,-122.3:
Sandy is a small city on the road between Portland and Mount Hood, and it does the job of a gateway very well. It sits at the point where US 26 leaves the suburbs and heads into forest, with the Sandy River running nearby, and for a rider coming down off the mountain it is the first place where fuel, food and flat ground come together. It has about ten thousand people, and the main street, with its murals, shops and bakeries, has the air of a town that knows most of its visitors are passing through and has decided to be friendly about it.

History runs through here in a quiet way. The Barlow Road, which opened in 1846, was the final overland route of the Oregon Trail, built by Sam Barlow to let pioneers avoid the dangerous rafting of the Columbia River. It crossed the shoulder of Mount Hood and came down to the valley near here, and the settlers who made it often arrived exhausted, with a few belongings and a lot of nerve. A toll was charged, and the road made its builder some money. Markers and museums in the area tell the story, and the old route still exists in places as trails and back roads.

On a ride, Sandy marks the return from the mountain. The road from Government Camp descends in long, gentle curves through forest, with the traffic building as you approach the city. The run down is relaxed after the climb, with good surface and clear lines, but it can be busy on Sunday evenings when skiers and hikers head home. Deer and elk occasionally cross at dusk, so keep your eyes open.

Fuel is plentiful, with several stations along the highway, and there are fast food outlets, cafés and a few local restaurants for a proper meal. Parking is easy, and the town has a grocery store if you need supplies. Bakeries are a good choice for a pastry and a coffee. Estacada and Damascus are close alternatives if Sandy is crowded.

Check your gear before you continue. The temperature in Sandy can be ten degrees warmer than at Timberline, and it is worth taking off a layer. The ride on toward Portland is straightforward, but the traffic grows heavier, so settle in, and keep the mountain in your mirror as long as you can.
t.cardiff@51.5,-3.2:
Cardiff Castle tells you a lot about the city in one place. There is a Roman fort wall, a Norman keep on a mound, and, behind it, a fantastical Victorian palace designed by William Burges for the third Marquess of Bute, one of the richest men in Britain, whose money came from the coal that was shipped through the docks. In the nineteenth century, Cardiff was the world's biggest coal-exporting port, and it grew from a small town into a capital in a few decades. Wales formally recognised it as capital in 1955.

The city is compact and friendly. The Principality Stadium, the home of Welsh rugby, stands in the middle, and on match days the whole centre is a river of red shirts and singing. The old docks, once known as Tiger Bay, are now the Bay, with the Senedd, the Welsh parliament, and the Millennium Centre with its bronze roof, inscribed with lines of verse in Welsh and English. Llandaff, where Roald Dahl was born, has a quiet cathedral and a village green.

For riders, the day ahead is a long haul east, across the Severn estuary into England, then south-west through Somerset to the Dorset and East Devon coast, the so-called Jurassic Coast, where the cliffs reveal 185 million years of geology. The motorway is the quick way, but it is worth leaving it when you can. The Welsh valleys north of the city, with their steep terraced streets and the brooding hills above, are another day's ride, and the Brecon Beacons are an hour away.

Fuel is easy in the city and along the motorway. Welsh cakes, cooked on a griddle, and a bowl of cawl, a lamb and leek broth, are the local comforts. The weather is, as in most of Wales, changeable, so a waterproof layer is sensible even in summer. Leave before the commuter rush, since the M4 around Cardiff and the Severn crossing can be slow, and be ready for a long day in the saddle.
t.liverpool@53.4,-3.0:
Liverpool owes its looks to the sea. The three great buildings on the waterfront, the Royal Liver Building with its two bronze Liver birds, the Cunard Building and the Port of Liverpool Building, are known as the Three Graces, and they were built in the early twentieth century when the city was one of the richest ports in the world. The Albert Dock, with its brick warehouses, is now a place to eat and visit museums, but it also tells the story of the trade that made Liverpool, including the dark chapter of its role in the slave trade, which the International Slavery Museum examines frankly. The city lost its UNESCO listing in 2021, after arguments over new development along the waterfront.

Music is the other pillar. The Beatles came from here, and the Cavern Club in Mathew Street, rebuilt on the original site, is still a pilgrimage. The city has two cathedrals, the Anglican one, the largest in Britain, built of red sandstone through most of the twentieth century, and the modern Catholic one, a round tent-like building from the 1960s, at opposite ends of Hope Street.

The ride that starts here crosses the Mersey through the Queensway Tunnel to Wirral, then heads west along the North Wales coast and into Snowdonia, to Blaenau Ffestiniog, where slate was quarried on a vast scale. The mountains of Wales rise ahead, and the weather changes quickly: sun on the coast, rain in the hills. The A470 over the Crimea Pass is a fine road, climbing through bleak moorland with views of slate tips, and it can be misty and wet even in summer.

Liverpool has fuel in abundance, and the city is famous for scouse, a stew of lamb or beef and potatoes, which is a hearty meal after a cold ride. Parking a bike near the docks is easy, though you should always use a good lock. Be careful on the wet setts around the old warehouses, which are slippery, and leave early so that the Welsh hills fill the afternoon.
t.leeds@53.8,-1.5:
Leeds made its fortune from wool and cloth, then from engineering and trade, and the evidence is in the arcades. The Victoria Quarter, with its glass roof and stained-glass windows, the Corn Exchange, an oval hall of iron and stone, and Kirkgate Market, where Marks & Spencer began as a penny bazaar, all reflect the confidence of the Victorian city. Today it is the biggest legal and financial centre outside London, and a university city with a young crowd, which gives the evenings plenty of life.

The canal and river, the Aire, run through the city, and the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, which links the Pennines, starts here. A short way out, the old mills along the river are being turned into flats, galleries and cafes, and the Royal Armouries Museum on the waterfront holds one of the great national collections of arms and armour.

For riders, Leeds sits conveniently between the Yorkshire Dales to the north and the Peak District to the south. The ride from here heads across the Pennines toward Cheshire, to Jodrell Bank, where the Lovell Telescope, a steel dish seventy-six metres across, has been listening to the sky since 1957. The roads across the hills, such as the A62 over Standedge or the Snake Pass, are among the best in the north of England, with open moorland, long views and plenty of bends, though the weather up there can be fierce, with rain, wind and low cloud in any season, so dress for it.

Fuel is easy in Leeds and in the towns of the Pennine foothills, but the high moors have few stations, so fill the tank before you climb. Locals will recommend a Yorkshire pudding with gravy, a pork pie or fish and chips, and a pint of the local bitter. Leave before the morning rush, which backs up on the Aire valley roads, and keep a close eye on the surface after rain, when the hills run with water.
t.fes@34.0,-5.0:
Fes holds the largest car-free urban area in the world, or so it is often said, and walking through it for an hour makes the claim credible. The old medina, Fes el-Bali, is a maze of nine thousand alleys, according to the usual count, wedged into a valley and descending in terraces toward a stream. It was founded in the late eighth century and grew into one of the great intellectual centres of the Islamic world. The Al-Qarawiyyin, established in 859 by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri, is often described as the oldest continuously operating university in the world, and its library and mosque remain at the heart of the old city. The medina is on the UNESCO list.

Arriving by motorbike, you leave the machine outside the walls. Bab Boujloud, the blue-tiled gate, is the usual entry. Inside, goods are carried by donkey and handcart, and the smells shift from leather to mint to woodsmoke every few steps. The tanneries at Chouara are the famous sight: round stone vats of dye, laid out like a palette, where workers tread hides in the liquid. The best view is from a terrace above, and you will be handed a sprig of mint to hold under your nose. The smell is strong. Do not take it personally.

The riding around Fes is the draw for motorcyclists. To the south, the road climbs into the Middle Atlas toward Ifrane, a town of alpine-style roofs and cedar forests that looks transplanted from Switzerland, and then on to Azrou, where Barbary macaques hang about the cedars. Roads there are smooth and wind through rolling hills, with fresh air and views. In the other direction, the motorway runs west to Meknes, about sixty kilometres away, and on to Rabat.

Fes is a big city with fuel everywhere and cheap, excellent food. Pastilla, a sweet and savoury pigeon or chicken pie dusted with sugar, is a local classic, and mint tea comes with everything. Spring is the best season, with green hills and mild air. Summer is very hot, and in winter the nights are cold. Roads can be icy in the Middle Atlas from December to February.
t.olympia@47.0,-122.9:
Washington's capital is a small, rather relaxed city at the very southern tip of Puget Sound, and it is where Highway 101 makes its last stand. The road, which begins its long loop of the Olympic Peninsula here, runs up the coast of the continent from California, and anyone arriving from Newport in Oregon will have been riding beside the Pacific for much of the way. Olympia itself sits on the shore of Budd Inlet, with the white Capitol dome on the hill above and the ferry-scarred waters of the sound just below.

The approach from the south passes through damp forests of Douglas fir, western red cedar and hemlock, the sort of green that looks almost black under a grey sky. That grey sky is part of the deal. Rain is frequent from autumn to spring, and the coast road can be slick with moss and fallen needles, so a good rain suit is more useful than a clever playlist. Summer, from July to September, is the proper season, with long light evenings, warm days and clear views of the Olympic and Cascade peaks. Traffic around Olympia, Lacey and Tumwater can be heavy on weekday afternoons because of the I-5 corridor.

The city has a lively streak. It has a waterfront farmers market, a number of independent bookshops and music venues, and it was the home of a well-known independent music scene in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The state Capitol campus is pleasant to walk through, with the Legislative Building a fine example of domed American classical architecture. Oysters are the local food, especially from the small bays around Totten and Eld Inlets, and many places serve them fresh, alongside craft beer from the region's many small breweries.

In terms of practicalities, there is no worry about fuel here. Olympia and its neighbours Tumwater and Lacey together form a sizeable urban area with petrol stations, motorcycle shops, supermarkets and plenty of places to sleep. It is also a sensible place to buy supplies before the thinly populated western reaches of the peninsula, where services get farther apart. Walk the harbour at dusk, and the lights, ferries and gulls make a fitting end to a long road.
t.village de songo@14.4,-3.7:
Songo stands on the edge of the Bandiagara escarpment in central Mali, the long sandstone cliff that is the heartland of the Dogon people. From the top, the land drops several hundred metres to a sandy plain, and houses of mud and stone cling to the rock face, stacked like swallows' nests, with granaries topped by pointed thatched roofs. The area is a World Heritage site, valued for both its landscape and its living culture.

Songo is best known for its caves, decorated with red, white and black paintings of circles, animals and masked figures that relate to the Dogon circumcision rites. The paintings are made with natural pigments and have a flat, graphic power. Dogon traditions are rich and deep, from the elaborate masks of the Dama funeral ceremonies to a cosmology that attracted anthropologists such as Marcel Griaule in the twentieth century. The Dogon moved to the cliffs long ago, displacing or absorbing an earlier people, the Tellem, whose small cliffside granaries and burial caves still dot the rock higher up.

I have to add a serious note. For some years, parts of central Mali, including Dogon country, have been affected by armed conflict and insecurity, and many governments advise against travel here. Anyone considering a visit must check the latest official advice and local conditions carefully, and should not go on the strength of an old guidebook. The road to the area, from Bandiagara, which is about eleven kilometres away, is usually a mix of tarmac and rough track, dusty in the dry season, and the climate is hot, with a rainy season from June to September when tracks turn to mud.

Bandiagara has about seven thousand inhabitants and is the place for fuel, food and basic supplies, since Songo itself is small. Carry water and cash in West African francs, and hire a local guide, who also helps to explain customs and sensitive places. Respect is crucial: ask before photographing people, never touch sacred objects, and follow your guide's advice on where to walk. The silence in the evening, with the cliff turning red and children calling across the plain, is hard to forget.
t.fes el bali@34.1,-5.0:
Fès El Bali is the old walled city of Fez, founded at the end of the eighth century by Idris I and made a capital by his son Idris II, and it is often described as the largest car-free urban area in the world. Nine thousand lanes is the figure people quote for its maze, and anyone who has lost an hour there believes it. The medina fills a bowl in the hills, with roofs stepping down toward the Fez river, and from the heights above it the whole place looks like a pile of sand-coloured dice.

The Qarawiyyin, a mosque and teaching institution founded in 859 by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri, is claimed as one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world, and it anchors the city's reputation as a centre of learning. Around it grew the madrasas, such as the Bou Inania with its carved cedar and zellij tilework, and the funduqs, the old merchants' inns with wooden galleries around a courtyard. Fez was the intellectual and religious heart of Morocco for centuries, and its pride shows in its craftsmanship and cooking.

A motorcycle cannot go inside, and shouldn't. Donkeys and handcarts carry the loads, and you walk. Park the bike at a guarded lot near Bab Boujloud, the blue gate, or outside the walls, and agree a fee with the attendant. Official guides are worth hiring for a first visit, since signage is scarce and the lanes confuse everyone. Stay out of the way of the loaded mules, who do not stop, and keep a hand over your pockets in the busiest streets.

Summers are very hot, so mornings and evenings are best, and winter can be cool and wet. From the city, the roads lead south into the Middle Atlas cedar forests toward Ifrane, and west toward Meknes and the Roman ruins of Volubilis. Fuel is readily available around the new town. Eat bastilla, the sweet-savoury pigeon pie, or a lamb tagine with prunes, and drink mint tea in a rooftop cafe as the call to prayer drifts over the roofs.
t.fes jedid@34.1,-5.0:
Fès Jedid, the New Fez, is a funny name for a district that is over seven hundred years old. The Marinid dynasty founded it in 1276 as a royal city beside the older medina, with its own walls, palace and mosque, and put the government and army there, leaving the old town to scholars and merchants. It remains a quieter quarter, where wide streets and gardens give relief from the crush of Fès El Bali.

The Royal Palace, Dar al-Makhzen, still serves the king and is closed to visitors, but its monumental gate is worth a visit all the same. Seven great brass doors, with enormous knockers, stand in a line before a patterned wall of green and blue tile. They are best photographed in early morning light, when the metal glows and the street is still empty. Behind them are gardens, courtyards and a palace used for official ceremonies.

The Mellah, the old Jewish quarter, lies within Fès Jedid, and it was created in the fifteenth century as a protected area for the community, close to the palace. Its houses have wooden balconies facing the street, unlike the inward-looking houses of the Muslim quarters, and there is a Jewish cemetery with whitewashed tombs and a restored synagogue, the Ibn Danan, now a museum. Many families left in the twentieth century, but the memory is kept alive.

The road system around Fès Jedid is a knot of one-way streets and roundabouts, so ride slowly and park carefully; a guarded lot is best. From here the road runs southwest to Meknes, another imperial city with huge gates and stables built by Sultan Moulay Ismail, and the countryside between is rolling olive groves and wheat. Fuel is in the new town, Ville Nouvelle, a few kilometres away. Spring is best, with green fields and mild air, and August is brutally hot, so go early and rest in the afternoon.
t.medina of fez@34.1,-5.0:
The tanneries are what everyone remembers. In the Medina of Fez, at the Chouara quarter, round stone vats stand in rows like a giant palette, filled with white lime, red, yellow and brown dyes, and men stand knee-deep in them soaking hides of goat, sheep and cow as their ancestors have done for centuries. The smell is strong, and visitors are handed sprigs of mint to hold under their noses from the leather shops above, where you watch from a terrace.

Fez is more than leather. Coppersmiths hammer large pots in Place Seffarine, weavers work at looms, and carpenters carve cedar in tiny workshops, with guilds that go back to the Middle Ages. Sweet makers sell almond pastries, and bakers carry trays of bread to the communal ovens. The Fassi kitchen is regarded as the most refined in Morocco, with dishes such as pastilla, a pie of pigeon wrapped in paper-thin pastry and dusted with sugar and cinnamon, and tagines with quince or prunes.

Finding your way is part of the experience. The medina has no real map in the mind, and the best advice is to choose a landmark, such as the Bab Boujloud gate or the Qarawiyyin mosque, and to accept that you will be lost. Someone will always point the way, sometimes for a tip. Shops close on Fridays at midday for prayer, and the streets quieten at dusk. Shop prices are negotiable, and a calm sense of humour helps.

Ride in from the new town and leave the bike at a guarded lot, since the lanes cannot take a motorcycle. Traffic around the old city gates is thick, with petit taxis and carts. Roads leave toward the Middle Atlas, where cedar forests shelter Barbary macaques near Azrou, and toward Meknes. Fuel is easy in the new town. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with summer heat strong and winter nights cold.
t.duffy lake road@49.4,-122.9:
Anmore is a small village in the forested hills above Burrard Inlet, a short ride from Port Moody and the eastern edge of Vancouver's urban area, and the dot sits here because the Duffy Lake Road loop ends back in this part of the Lower Mainland. The land is dense with hemlock and cedar, the air is damp and cool, and the roads wind between lakes and ridges with a sense of being close to wilderness while only a few kilometres from the shops.

Nearby, Buntzen Lake and Sasamat Lake offer swimming and paddling in water that is warm enough for a dip by midsummer, and Indian Arm, a long fjord that cuts north into the mountains, can be seen from several viewpoints. Port Moody, at the head of the inlet, was once the western terminus of the Canadian Pacific Railway before the line was extended to Vancouver, and it has a pleasant waterfront and a number of craft breweries.

The Duffy Lake Road, which gives the ride its name, is one of British Columbia's finest mountain roads. It links Lillooet, in the dry interior, with Pemberton in the coastal rainforest, over Cayoosh Pass at about 1,250 metres, and in the course of fifty-odd kilometres, the landscape changes from desert hills to glaciers and wet forest. Steep gradients, tight bends and a few narrow sections require focus. Joffre Lakes, a trio of glacier-fed turquoise lakes, lie beside the road and can be reached by a steep trail. In winter, snow and ice can make the pass difficult, and snow tyres are required for cars.

The return to the coast follows the Sea to Sky highway past Squamish and through the fjord country of Howe Sound, one of the best roads in the province, though busy in summer. Speed cameras and police patrols are common, so keep to the limits.

Fuel and food are easy in Port Moody and Coquitlam, with large stations, supermarkets and cafes. The restaurants of Port Moody's Shoreline Trail serve good seafood, and a short walk by the inlet is a calm way to end the day. Rain is common in the Lower Mainland, even in summer, so carry waterproofs. The best months for riding are July to September.
t.olympic peninsula@47.7,-121.9:
The Snoqualmie Valley, where Carnation sits, is a quiet pocket of dairy farms and berry fields in the western foothills of the Cascades, a short way east of Seattle's suburbs. It is a place where cows graze in sight of snow-capped peaks, with the Tolt and Snoqualmie rivers winding through the flats and the dark ridge of the mountains behind. The village of Carnation takes its name from the Carnation Milk company, which once ran a famous model dairy farm here. Lake Marcel-Stillwater, nearby, is a scattering of houses on the forested slope.

To the south, Snoqualmie Falls drops about 82 metres over a lip of rock into a misty pool, and has been a sacred place for the Snoqualmie people for countless generations. The town of Snoqualmie nearby is better known to some as the setting for the television series Twin Peaks, and diner fans will find the cafe made famous in the show. The valley's light, in early morning mist, is particularly beautiful.

The Olympic Peninsula and Hood Canal, the first part of the ride, lie across Puget Sound to the west, and they are some of the greatest riding in the Pacific Northwest. Hood Canal is not a canal at all but a natural fjord, a long, narrow arm of the sound with steep forested shores and oysters in the shallows, and the highway along it passes through small towns with names like Brinnon and Quilcene. Further inland, the Olympic mountains rise to glaciated peaks, with the road to Hurricane Ridge climbing about 1,600 metres to wide meadows and views that sweep across the range.

By contrast, the Snoqualmie Valley is for gentle winding and quiet. Roads are narrow, lined with fir and maple, and the surface is generally good. Rain is common from autumn to spring, and fog fills the river bottoms in the morning. Farm stands sell fruit and vegetables in summer, and there are good stops for coffee in Duvall and Fall City.

Fuel in Carnation itself is limited, so use the larger stations in Duvall, Fall City or Redmond. Weekend traffic can be busy near the falls, and elk, which have become common in the valley, sometimes wander onto the road, so be careful at dawn and dusk.
t.beijing@39.9,116.4:
Beijing has been a capital, on and off, for most of the last eight hundred years, and the centre of the city still carries the weight of that. At its heart sits the Forbidden City, the vast palace complex from which Ming and Qing emperors ruled, with its red walls, yellow-tiled roofs and nine hundred or so buildings, and just south of it lies Tiananmen Square, one of the largest public squares in the world. The city's grid of boulevards and ring roads is laid out around this axis, and anyone who has looked at a map will see the logic.

The afternoon trip described here goes north-west to the Ming Tombs, the burial ground of thirteen of the sixteen Ming emperors, set in a broad valley ringed by mountains about fifty kilometres from the city. The site was chosen according to feng shui principles, with hills to the north and a stream to the south, and it is reached by the Sacred Way, a long avenue lined with pairs of stone animals and officials, including lions, camels, elephants and horses, which seem to stand guard over the valley. The tomb of the Wanli emperor, Dingling, has been excavated, and visitors can descend into a vast underground palace. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Riding in Beijing needs a clear head about the rules. Motorcycles face strict controls in the city centre, with registration and licensing rules that make it nearly impossible for visitors to ride their own bike. Traffic is heavy, the ring roads can be jammed at any hour, and signage is mostly in Chinese. If you travel here, the metro is cheap, clean and efficient, and taxis and ride-hailing apps are plentiful. The air can be hazy, particularly in winter, and the best weather is in spring and autumn.

Fuel and food are no issue in a city of this size. The hutongs, the old alleys around the Drum Tower and Houhai lake, are full of small restaurants, and Peking duck is of course the dish to try, carved at your table with crisp skin, pancakes and sweet bean sauce.

If you can, walk the lanes of the old city at dusk, when the lanterns come on and the cooking smells drift out of doorways.
t.old course of yellow river estuary@38.1,:
The Yellow River is the most restless big river on earth, and this is one of the places it used to leave the land. Over the centuries it has carried so much silt out of the loess plateau that it keeps building its own floor, rising above the plain, bursting its banks and changing course. In 1855 it broke out in Henan, gave up its long southern route to the Yellow Sea and swung north to the Bohai Gulf instead. The channel that ended here, on the low coast of Shandong, is one of the old mouths of that restless history, and the land around it is still being made by mud.

Do not expect mountains or corners. This is delta country: dead-flat, wide-skied, with raised embankments, drainage channels, reed beds, tamarisk scrub and salt-crusted flats that shimmer in the afternoon. The roads are straight and long, often with trucks serving the oil wells and chemical plants of the Dongying area, and the riding is about distance and light rather than technique. Early morning and the hour before sunset are the times to be here, when the reeds turn copper and the haze flattens out. Wind off the sea can be steady and tiring, and in summer the heat sits on the tarmac.

What makes the place worth the detour is the birdlife. The delta wetlands are a major stopover on the East Asian flyway, and the protected reserve here and at the present river mouth holds huge numbers of migrating and wintering waterbirds. Spring and autumn are the seasons to come, and on a good day the sky over the reed beds is busy with geese, cranes, gulls and waders. Cranes and storks are among the species the reserve is known for, though you will want binoculars and patience, not a motorbike engine, to see them.

The data for this point gives no named town nearby, which tells you how empty it feels, so plan fuel and water before you arrive. Fill up in a city on the way, and carry a little extra if you can, because filling stations thin out on the delta roads. Gates and access rules around protected land can change, and some tracks near the mouth are closed to vehicles, so treat the final approach as something to check locally. Come to look at a coastline that is still arriving, grain by grain, from the other side of a continent.
t.bellingham@48.8,-122.5:
Bellingham is the last substantial city before the Canadian border, a place of eighty-five thousand people on a sheltered bay in the north-west corner of Washington state. It is a university town, with a lively cafe and brewing scene, a revived waterfront, and the kind of outdoorsy, independent character you find in many Pacific Northwest cities. The old Fairhaven district, a Victorian district with brick buildings and bookshops, is a nice place to wander, and the ferry terminal for Alaska sits at its edge.

The mountain looms over everything. Mount Baker, a glacier-covered volcano of over ten thousand feet, stands to the east, and on clear days the white cone fills the horizon. It is one of the snowiest places on Earth, and in the winter of 1998 to 1999 the ski area on its flank set a world record for snowfall in a single season, with over a thousand inches. The Nooksack River runs down from its glaciers, and the valley below is full of dairy farms, berry fields and small towns.

The Mount Baker Highway begins here and runs about fifty-seven miles east, first across the flat farmland of the Nooksack valley and then, beyond the village of Glacier, climbing into deep forest of cedar, hemlock and Douglas fir. The road is well paved, with easy bends and a few tighter sections, and it follows the river through a gorge before ascending toward Heather Meadows. The final section is closed in winter, usually reopening in summer after the snow clears, so check conditions. Rain is frequent, even in summer, and cloud often covers the upper mountain, so be ready for wet roads.

Fuel and food are easy in Bellingham, and it is wise to fill up, because the services on the highway are limited to the villages of Deming, Maple Falls and Glacier. The Pacific Northwest is famous for coffee, and the city has many independent roasters, so a good cup is never far away. Spring and early summer bring waterfalls, and September and early October are often the best time, with stable weather and fewer visitors. Take a warm layer for the top, where the air is cool even in August.
t.artist point@48.8,-121.7:
The pavement ends at a car park on a ridge, and a short paved path leads to the best view in the North Cascades. Artist Point stands at around fifty-one hundred feet at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, and from the edge you look straight across a valley to Mount Shuksan, a jagged pyramid of dark rock and white ice, while the rounded, glaciated cone of Mount Baker sits close at hand to the west. Painters and photographers have been coming for a century, hence the name.

The road up is only open for part of the year. Heavy winter snow buries it, often deeply, and the last stretch is cleared in early summer, sometimes not until July, and shut again with the first big storm of autumn. Even in midsummer, snow patches survive beside the car park, and wildflowers bloom in a rush as soon as the ground thaws, with lupines, paintbrush and avalanche lilies making the meadows look painted. If you ride up in August or September you will probably have the best chance of clear weather.

The final miles climb through Heather Meadows, a high basin of subalpine meadow and small tarns, passing Picture Lake, where the mountain reflects in still water on a calm morning. The road is narrow, with steep drop-offs in places, sharp turns and a patchy surface after winter, so ride carefully, especially if mist or cloud rolls in. Temperatures can be twenty degrees lower than in the lowlands, and the wind can be sharp. Marmots whistle among the rocks, and mountain goats sometimes cross the high slopes.

A recreation pass is normally required for parking at trailheads and lots in the national forest, so check before you go. Short trails lead from the car park, including a gentle loop around the lookout and routes toward Table Mountain, but the weather is changeable and you should wear proper footwear. Fog can close in within minutes, so if the view is hidden, wait a while, because it often clears.
t.midelt@32.7,-4.7:
Midelt is a market town on a high, windy plain between two mountain ranges, at about 1,500 metres, and it feels like a place that exists in order to be passed through. The Middle Atlas lies to the north and the High Atlas to the south, with the great bulk of Jbel Ayachi, close to 3,750 metres, rising to the south-west, often snow-capped into spring. The town has about forty-five thousand people, a long main street of shops, cafés and mechanics, and a surrounding landscape of orchards, mines and open steppe.

It lies on the main road from Fez and the cedar forests of the north toward the Sahara, so many riders arrive here after crossing the Middle Atlas via Azrou and Ifrane, over a pass where in winter the snow can be deep. South of the town the road drops through the Ziz gorges toward Er-Rachidia and the desert oases. Between towns, the road is long and open, with wide views and sometimes strong wind, and the temperature swing between day and night is large, so pack layers.

Midelt is known for its apples, grown in the surrounding valleys, and for minerals: stalls along the road sell fossils, crystals and rocks from the mountains, some real and some carved to order, so look carefully before buying. The mines nearby have produced lead and other minerals for decades, and the area has a long history of Berber settlement. The town is also the starting point for the road east and then south into the high country toward Imilchil, for those who prefer something less travelled.

With a population this size, fuel, repairs and food are easy, and the town is the best place to stock up before the remote roads. Cafés on the main street serve tagines, grilled meat and mint tea, and hotels range from simple to comfortable. Winters are cold, with frost and snow common between November and March, so check conditions before setting out, and in summer the sun on the plateau is fierce. Starting early gives you the best light and the calmest air.
t.fez@34.0,-5.0:
Fez is the oldest of Morocco's imperial cities and it has been busy for well over a thousand years. The medina, Fès el-Bali, founded in the late eighth and early ninth centuries and listed by UNESCO, is a maze of thousands of alleys, many too narrow for anything but a donkey, and it is often described as the largest car-free urban area in the world. Inside are workshops, mosques, madrasas, fountains and markets, all packed so tightly that the sky is often a thin strip above your head.

At the centre sits the University of al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri, and regarded as one of the oldest continuously operating educational institutions in the world. The tanneries, where leather is still dyed in stone vats of red, yellow and white, are the sight everyone wants, and you can watch from a terrace above, with a sprig of mint under your nose against the smell. Metalworkers, weavers and ceramicists work in their own quarters, and the food is excellent: pastilla, a pigeon or chicken pie dusted with sugar and cinnamon, is the classic.

For the rider, Fez is both a place to leave the bike and a starting point. The medina is impossible on two wheels, so park securely in the newer city, and explore on foot with a guide if you want to avoid getting lost. From Fez, the road north to Chefchaouen climbs through the hills of the Rif foothills, with olive groves, villages and long views, and it is a ride of changing scenery, with tidy tarmac in some places and potholes in others. Traffic around the city is heavy, so leave early.

Fès has a population close to a million, so fuel, workshops, parts and every kind of food and lodging are easy to find, and the old town of Fès al Bali alone holds well over a hundred thousand people. Summers are hot and winters are cool and damp, so spring and autumn are best. Be polite but firm with unofficial guides, agree prices in advance, and keep valuables out of sight in the medina.
t.merzouga@31.1,-4.0:
The tarmac stops being the main attraction at Merzouga, because here the Sahara starts for real. Erg Chebbi, a wall of orange dunes more than a hundred metres high, rises out of the stony plain in the far south-east of Morocco, a short distance from the Algerian frontier, and the village sits right at its foot with a scatter of guesthouses, cafés and camel stables. In the early morning the sand has the colour of burnt sugar, and at sunset it turns the red of a hot stove.

The riding to get here is long, flat and hot, on the road through Erfoud and past the oasis town of Rissani, once the capital of the Tafilalet region and the cradle of the dynasty that still rules Morocco. Reçani, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town and the place where you should be thinking about your fuel gauge. Beyond it there is a surfaced road and a number of tracks into the dunes, and the tracks are where the problems begin: soft sand grabs a loaded motorbike without mercy, so be honest about your skills, ride with a partner, and do not wander off alone in the heat.

Wind is the main enemy. In spring a hot dry gust carrying fine sand can make visibility poor and fill your visor, and in midsummer the temperature is brutal, so the sensible months are autumn and spring, with the early morning the best hours. Nights in the desert can turn surprisingly cold. A few kilometres south lies the village of Khamlia, where the community of descendants of sub-Saharan musicians plays Gnawa rhythms with iron castanets and drums, and it is a rewarding evening if you can arrange it. Out on the flats, Dayet Srji, a lake that fills after rare rains, can draw flamingos.

Nearly everything here is arranged around visitors. You can take a sunrise camel trek, sleep in a tented camp, and eat bread baked in the sand, a kind of Berber pizza called madfouna stuffed with meat and onion. Fill the tank in Rissani or Erfoud before arriving, carry more water than seems sensible, and keep your phone charged. The ride on to the Todra Gorge to the north-west is a good way to leave, and it feels like the first sip of cool water.
t.historic columbia river highway point 3@:
Multnomah Falls drops about two hundred metres in two main tiers, and it is the most visited natural site in Oregon, which tells you what to expect from the car park. The classic stone lodge stands at the bottom, the arched footbridge spans the lower pool, and a path zigzags up to a viewing point above it. From a motorcycle seat you cannot see the whole thing at once, so the usual routine is to park, take off your jacket and walk the few minutes to the base.

Getting here is half the point. The old highway meanders past Latourell and Bridal Veil, each with its own waterfall, before reaching this one, and the road is at its most enjoyable on those stretches: tight, tree-lined, fenced by mossy stone walls and mostly shaded. Heavy rains can send rocks or branches onto the pavement, so keep an eye on the surface. The modern interstate runs just below, and motorcycles can drop onto it if time is short, but the old road is plainly the better ride.

The falls are fed by springs and snowmelt from Larch Mountain above, and the flow is strongest in winter and spring and weakest in late summer. Local legend, as told for generations, ties the falls to a Native American maiden who sacrificed herself for her people; whatever its origin, it is part of the place. The lodge and visitor services are right by the car park, with food and restrooms, though it gets busy at midday and long queues on summer weekends are normal.

Troutdale to the west and the gorge towns to the east are the reliable places to refill. Plan the day around the crowds if you can: arriving before nine or after late afternoon gives you the falls with room to breathe, and the cooler evening air in the gorge, with the mist rising off the lower tier, is the nicest time to be on foot here.
t.olympic peninsula loop point 3@48.0,-123:
West of Port Angeles the highway climbs into forest and the character of the ride changes. This stretch hugs the northern edge of the Olympic Mountains, and the road alternates between tall evergreens, small creek crossings and sudden glimpses of Lake Crescent, a deep and strikingly clear glacial lake whose water is a cold blue-green. The lake is only a short distance on, and it is among the best parts of the whole loop.

The riding here is a real pleasure. The road is two-lane, mostly well surfaced, and it follows the contours of the hills with long, rolling bends and a few tighter ones that need attention. Trees close over the road in places, and in the morning the light filters through the branches in a way that makes the tarmac patchy with shadow, which can hide a damp spot or a bit of loose gravel.

The Olympic Peninsula holds one of the largest remaining areas of temperate rainforest in the Northern Hemisphere on its western slopes, and the park contains glaciers, wild beaches and herds of Roosevelt elk. Here on the north side the forest is drier than the famous Hoh, but the scale of the trees is still impressive: old Douglas firs and western hemlocks thick enough that two people could not link arms around them.

Nature sets the schedule. The weather can change in minutes, and a morning of sunshine can become an afternoon of drizzle, so waterproofs belong in the pannier. Summer and early autumn are the best seasons, and the lake is calm at dawn. Pull over only at the signed turnouts, since the road has little shoulder and blind bends, and be respectful of the cyclists and campers who share it. If you need a break, the lake lodge area has seasonal services, though I would not rely on their hours.
t.olympic peninsula loop point 4@48.1,-123:
Past Lake Crescent the road turns west and wanders on through country that feels properly remote. This section runs through the valley of the Sol Duc and the Soleduck River area, with thick forest, ferns, moss on the trunks and the occasional logged hillside showing where timber has been cut.

The road is where the pleasure lies. Highway 101 here is a classic two-lane mountain-edge highway with long straights broken by flowing curves and a few tighter turns where it follows a creek. Traffic thins out the further west you go, and on a weekday morning you can have sections almost to yourself. The surface is good for the most part, though the logging trucks wear grooves in places, and the shade means damp patches can hang around well into the day.

The Olympic Peninsula has a long Native American history, and the Quileute, Makah, Hoh and Klallam peoples have lived on this coast for thousands of years. Logging and fishing shaped the later settlement, and the timber industry still shapes the economy: small mills, log trucks and clear-cuts in various stages of regrowth mark the landscape. The tension between old-growth protection and logging was the defining political fight of the Pacific Northwest in the 1980s and 1990s, and you can read it in the scenery here, with protected forest on one side of a ridge and working timberland on the other.

Wildlife is the extra. Black-tailed deer step out at dawn and dusk, elk occasionally appear in meadows, and bald eagles hunt over the rivers. Slow down at those times of day, and watch the verge. The climate is mild but wet; even in summer a cold front can roll in from the Pacific, and temperatures drop quickly. A packable layer, a visor that shields rain, and a bit of patience for slow vehicles all make the ride better.
t.olympic peninsula loop point 6@47.7,-124:
South of Forks the highway bends away from the coast and runs on through rolling forest, passing the mouth of the Hoh and tracing the shore of the Pacific for stretches, with grey-green sea beyond the trees. This is remote country, and the nearest town is Forks, about twenty-seven kilometres back.

Riding here is calm and gently rhythmic. The road rolls through logged and regrowing forest, over small rivers, past occasional turnouts with views of the Pacific. The curves are mostly moderate and there is little traffic apart from logging trucks and the occasional camper van. It is a good place to settle into a steady pace and enjoy the landscape without stress, and on a dry day it is some of the easiest and most pleasant riding on the whole loop.

The coast here belongs in part to the Quinault and Quileute, and to the national park, whose Pacific strip runs for roughly seventy miles and is one of the wildest coastlines in the lower forty-eight. Beaches are strewn with driftwood the size of tree trunks, and tide pools shelter starfish and anemones. If you stop at a beach, check tide tables, because in places the tide can cut off headlands. The smell of salt, kelp and rain-soaked spruce is distinctive and gets into your gear.

Weather is the variable. Summer fog can drift in from the sea and cover the road for hours, while winter storms bring wind and heavy rain, and trees occasionally come down. Between June and September the odds are best, and the mornings can be foggy, clearing by noon. Bring a spare visor or an anti-fog insert. Further south the road leads to Lake Quinault and the Grays Harbor towns, where fuel is plentiful again, and Aberdeen, about an hour on, is the next substantial place for a proper meal and a bed.
Hardknott Pass tops out at about 393 metres, and the Romans got here first. Just below the summit on the Eskdale side stand the ruins of Mediobogdum, a fort built in the second century to guard the road from Ravenglass to Ambleside, and its stone walls, gateways and parade ground are laid out on a shelf with a view down the valley to the sea. Soldiers were posted here from as far away as Dalmatia, which makes the place feel even more remote. It is free to visit, and the walk from the road is short.

The road is the other attraction, and it asks for respect. Coming up from Eskdale the gradient reaches one in three on the hairpins, the surface is narrow and sometimes rough, and there are no barriers at the worst drops. The hairpins are tight enough that a loaded bike needs a firm hand, a low gear and a steady clutch, and stopping on the steepest part for a photograph is a bad idea. Wet leaves, gravel and sheep add to the challenge. In ice or snow, the pass is simply impassable, and signs warn drivers to turn back.

Come with a full tank and pack a flask. Mobile signal comes and goes. Brakes get a workout on the descent, and engine braking in first gear is better than riding the lever. If you meet a car on a narrow stretch, the usual courtesy applies: the vehicle going uphill generally has priority, as it is harder to restart.

The scenery is hard to beat. The pass runs over the shoulder of the high fells, with the great mass of Scafell and the crags of the Scafell range to the north, and on a clear day the Irish Sea shines in the west and the Isle of Man shows on the horizon. Herdwick sheep, hardy and grey, graze the verges. The wind blows constantly, and cloud can drop in minutes. A calm, clear morning in late spring or autumn is the best time to try it.

t.vancouver@49.2,-123.1:
Vancouver is a city that sits between mountains and sea, so closely that you can ski in the morning and sail in the afternoon, as the local line goes. Glass towers crowd a peninsula with the North Shore peaks rising directly behind, and Stanley Park, a huge, forested park on the tip of the peninsula, wraps around the downtown with a seawall path and old-growth cedar. Gastown, the historic quarter, takes its name from a talkative saloon keeper, Gassy Jack Deighton, whose statue stands in the square.

The Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 99, leaves from the Lions Gate Bridge, a graceful suspension span opened in 1938, and rises along the edge of Howe Sound, a deep fjord with mountains tumbling straight into the water. The road is one of the best in Canada, with smooth tarmac, curves that follow the cliff edge and views across to the islands. It was widened and improved for the 2010 Winter Olympics, and it is now safer, though traffic is heavy on summer weekends. Squamish, about an hour north, lies at the foot of the Stawamus Chief, a huge granite dome beloved by rock climbers, and nearby Shannon Falls drops more than three hundred metres. Further on is Whistler, the ski resort, and Pemberton beyond.

The road continues beyond Pemberton as the Duffey Lake Road, which crosses the Coast Mountains in a wilder fashion, with tight bends, steep grades and a great view of glaciers and turquoise lakes. It is less forgiving than the first part, and the surface can be damp and patchy, so ride carefully. Rain is the great theme of Vancouver's weather, particularly from October to March, when grey skies can persist for weeks, but in summer the days are long, dry and warm. In late spring and early autumn, the mountains offer clear air and fewer visitors. Snow can linger on the high passes until early summer.

In the city itself, practicalities are no problem, with fuel stations, motorcycle dealers and repair shops. Eat well before leaving: Vancouver has superb sushi, dim sum and fresh salmon, and its coffee culture is serious. Parking downtown is expensive, so find a secure lot in advance. Bring waterproofs, whatever the forecast, because weather on the coast can turn within an hour, and wildlife, including bears, appears on some of the northern sections.

t.tintagel@50.7,-4.8:
Tintagel has been selling King Arthur for a long time. The twelfth-century writer Geoffrey of Monmouth first placed Arthur's conception here, in his History of the Kings of Britain, and the legend grew from there, helped by a Victorian love of chivalry and a ruined castle on a dramatic headland. Archaeologists have since found that the site was an important trading post in the fifth and sixth centuries, when imported Mediterranean pottery and glass came in by sea, so something notable did happen here, but whether it involved a king named Arthur is another matter. Cornwall, characteristically, has chosen to believe.

The castle ruins, run by English Heritage, stand on a rocky island joined to the mainland by a narrow neck, and in 2019 a new footbridge, with a gap in the middle that gives the impression of a narrow slot between two cliffs, replaced the old stone steps. The site is dramatic: stone walls clinging to the edge of a cliff, a sea cave below known as Merlin's Cave, and the Atlantic crashing in. Up in the village, the Old Post Office, a fourteenth-century manor house with a slate roof that sags with age, is cared for by the National Trust, and the street is lined with shops selling swords, crystals and mead, in a cheerfully kitsch way.

Riding here means the A39, known as the Atlantic Highway, which runs along the north Cornish coast. It is more of a cruise than a thrill. The road is generally good, with long straights and gentle bends over open moorland, but it can be slow, with caravans, tractors and holiday traffic in summer. The better sport is on the lanes, which are narrow, hedged and winding, with blind corners and a good deal of mud and gravel, so approach with caution. The weather here is Atlantic: wind, mist and sudden rain can arrive at any time of year, but a clear evening on the cliffs is one of the glories of Cornwall.

Nearby, the slate quarry at Delabole has been worked for six hundred years and is among the largest in England, and next to it stands one of Britain's first onshore wind farms, from 1991. The coast is a protected landscape, with sea cliffs, wild flowers and seabirds such as fulmars, kittiwakes and choughs, which are Cornwall's emblem.

Tintagel village has pubs, tearooms and pasty shops, a few small hotels, and a car park near the castle. For fuel, Wadebridge, about seventeen kilometres to the south, is the best option, though there is a small garage at Camelford, near the main road, so plan your fill-up. A hot pasty eaten on the cliffs, preferably out of the wind, is the traditional pleasure.
Stanwood and the northern end of Camano Island lie at the edge of the Skagit Delta, where the Stillaguamish River spreads into a flat, fertile plain and meets the waters of Port Susan. The land is as flat as a table, and the horizon is filled by the Cascades to the east and the Olympics to the west. This is a landscape of dairy farms, fields of peas and potatoes, and drainage ditches, with huge skies and a strong smell of earth and sea.

In winter the delta becomes one of the great bird-watching sites of the Pacific coast. Tens of thousands of snow geese arrive from Siberia, along with trumpeter swans and swarms of raptors, including bald eagles, peregrine falcons and snowy owls in some years. The fields turn white with geese, and the air fills with their noise. In April, the nearby Skagit Valley comes alive with tulip fields in yellow, red and pink, and the whole area is thick with visitors.

The label mentions the Olympic Peninsula, which lies across the water, and a ferry from nearby Whidbey Island will take you there. But this corner has its own pleasures. Stanwood was settled by Scandinavian farmers in the late nineteenth century, and its old buildings and cemeteries reflect that heritage. Camano Island State Park offers beaches, forest paths and views over the sound, and the water is cold but clear.

Stanwood has about seven thousand people, with a fuel station, supermarket and some cafes, while Camano, a larger area, has a few shops and a small marina. The roads are flat and straight, with fields on either side, and a strong crosswind is common, so keep a firm hold of the handlebars. In misty weather, the fields look like a painting, with soft light and dim shapes. For a quiet day beside the water, with plenty of birds and few people, it is hard to beat.
t.goring on the way back@51.5,-1.1:
Where the Thames squeezes between the Chiltern Hills and the Berkshire Downs, the river has had to cut a passage through a chalk ridge, and the result is the Goring Gap. The pin sits on the Oxfordshire bank just upstream, a few kilometres from Goring, with Wallingford to the north and Pangbourne across the water. It is the sort of place that looks very English from a distance and even better up close: willows, pastures, narrow locks and a weir, with the brick railway bridge at Moulsford that Brunel built crossing the water.

The river is the reason this stop is marked for a swim. On a warm day the banks upstream of the locks fill up with picnic blankets, paddleboards and children in the water, and the Thames here is clean enough that the small swimming spots by the meadows are well used. Take care near weirs, where the current is stronger than it looks, and remember the river is also a busy navigation channel.

There is a good deal of quiet history in the neighbourhood. The Ridgeway, said to be Britain's oldest road, crosses the river here between Goring and Streatley, and walkers have been using it for thousands of years. Pangbourne is where Kenneth Grahame, the author of The Wind in the Willows, lived in his later years, and the riverside scenery has more than a little of the book about it. Nearby Cholsey is where Agatha Christie is buried. At Whitchurch-on-Thames, a small toll bridge still takes your coins to cross the river, which is a fine thing to do on two wheels.

The roads here run along both sides of the valley, with a mix of fast A roads and winding lanes. Climb out of the river onto the Downs and the lanes become narrower, with wide views over the Vale of the White Horse and old beechwoods, and traffic drops away. Weekends in summer are crowded near the river, so go early or late.

For practical matters, Wallingford, with ten thousand people, has fuel, a market square and plenty of cafés, and Goring has a couple of good pubs and a railway station. The way home to London is either the quiet road along the Thames or a faster run on the M4, depending on how much daylight you have left.
t.sutton on the way back@52.1,-0.2:
The Greensand Ridge runs across Bedfordshire like a low spine, and Potton and Gamlingay lie on its eastern edge, a pair of small towns of brick and clay tile that once made their living from the soil. Potton, with nearly five thousand people, was famous for its market gardens, and Gamlingay, with about thirty-two hundred, has an old heath and woodland, the Gamlingay Wood, which has been managed for nearly a thousand years and is one of the oldest in the county. Everton, a tiny village nearby, sits on the ridge with views over the Ivel valley.

Biggleswade, six kilometres away with over sixteen thousand people, is the nearest large place, and it has fuel, shops and cafés on the River Ivel. Not far off, Old Warden is home to the Shuttleworth Collection, a remarkable museum of historic aircraft and vehicles, many of them still flown on summer weekends, and the sight of a biplane over the fields is one of the pleasures of the district. The RSPB reserve at The Lodge, near Sandy, has heathland, woodland and birds.

The label calls this a swim stop, but the local waters are small and mostly private, so treat it as a rest. The riding is gentle, with lanes among arable fields and hedgerows, and the Greensand Ridge gives enough relief for bends and short climbs. The soil is sandy, and the roads can be gritty on corners, particularly after dry weather. Traffic is light apart from the A1 and the A603, and the cyclists are many.

As the start of a ride toward the Chilterns and the Thames, this is an easy place to begin. Fill the tank in Biggleswade, buy a coffee at a bakery, and set off along the ridge while the dew is still on the grass. In spring the woods are bright with bluebells, and in autumn the hedges are rich with berries. It is a quiet country of unhurried pleasures.

Darrington is a logging town in the north Cascades foothills, about ten kilometres from this stop, and it sits at the confluence of the Sauk and Suiattle rivers, in a valley overshadowed by the cone of Whitehorse Mountain. To the east, the snowy volcano Glacier Peak rises to 3,213 metres, the most remote of the five Washington volcanoes, and on a clear day it can be seen from the roads around town. The country is wild, wet and steep, covered in dense forest, and the rivers run milky green with glacial silt.

The town has a quiet, independent character, shaped by timber, bluegrass music and a history of Southern settlers who came to work the woods. Every July it hosts a bluegrass festival that has run for decades, drawing musicians and fans from across the country, and the sound of banjos and fiddles drifts across the valley. Darrington is small, with a fuel station, a store and a few cafes, but it welcomes visitors.

The Mountain Loop Highway runs through the area, connecting Darrington to Granite Falls and the Cascade foothills, and it is one of the great rides in the state, with rivers, old-growth trees and views of the peaks. Parts of the road are unpaved or rough, and some sections close in winter due to snow or washouts, so check conditions before you go. The ghost town of Monte Cristo, a former gold and silver mining camp, lies at the end of a rough track, and its story of boom and bust is evocative.

For swimming, the rivers are cold and fast, and deep pools are best approached with care, but on a hot day a dip can be refreshing. Rain is common, and mist hangs in the trees, giving the landscape a mysterious look. Wildlife includes elk, black bears and eagles, and in autumn salmon run in the river. Fill the tank in Arlington before heading up the valley, and carry spare layers.
